div.p: TO-DAY AND TO-MORROW. Don't tell me of to-morrow; Give me the boy who'll say When a good deed's to be done, ".Let's do the deed to-day." We may all command the present, If we act and never wait; But repentance is the phantom Of a past that comes too late. Don't tell me of to-morrow; There is much to do to-day That can never be accomplished If we throw the hours away. Every mongnt has its duty; Who the future can foretell? Then why put off till to-morrow What to-day can do as well? Don't tell me of to-morrow; If we look upon the past, How much we have left to do, We cannot do at last. To-day! it is the only time For all on this frail earth ; It takes an age to form a life, A moment gives it birth.
THE, DEPARTURE OF WINTER. From the hills of the East, from the home of the Sun, Whence each morning in splendour his journey's
begun, In his chariot of gold, drawn by dragon-files twain, Hailed with gladness by all, cometh young Spring again; And adoi,vn Time's worn path, where, ',with lingering

tread, Went the year 'B5 to the Land of the Dead, Compelled yet unwilling, and hastened yet slow, Loth, loth to depart, see old Winter now go. Stalwart youths ever ready for anything new, And maidens whose cheeks vie with roses in hue, Hail with joyful delight as he comes from afar The Boy-King who rides in the glittering car; And with equal delight they bid Winter "Farewell," Though the joys that he brought them were loved for a spell; "Base ingratitude," murmurs he. Nay, nay, old King, Mortals want constant changes, they'll tire yet of

Spring. • Cheer up, Spring. Monarch, a time there will be When the beautiful Spring shall depart even as thee; When Summer, though lovely, shall too pass away, And when Autumn, the golden, no longer must stay. Then, then, noble King, shall be thy turn again, Then shalt thou once more o'er the ceded Earth reign, Once more shalt thou sit on the year's yielded throne, And the sceptre of power shall be thine, thine alone. Oh ! 'tis pleasant to ramble along through the vale, O'er the heath-covered hill and the flower-pied dale, To list to the wild bee, who merrily hums, His welcome to Spring as o'er meadows he comes, To watch the bright butterfly play round the flowers, To hear the birds sing in the Eden-like bowers; While far, far above, in the clear azure sky, The lark pours its welcoming song from on high. Old Winter the flowers in a deep sleep had- cast, But the Spring has appeared, and their sleeping is past, For, cheered by the rays of the bright shining Sun, Each flower wakes again, glad that Winter is done. The primrose, the daisy—so modest, yet fair,— The violet, the snowdrop, the lily are there, Each clad in its beauty, each fair to the eye, Not the glory of Solomon these could outvie. As we wander through valleys -where Spring casts around His beauties, his treasures, above, on the ground; As we pass over hills decked in'verdant attire, And watch the lark circling still higher and higher, May our thoughts be led onward and upward through Time, From the beauty of Earth to Heaven's beauty sublime, Till we soar far above where the joyful birds sing, To the land of eternal Spring, beautiful Spring. March, 1886. EXCELSIOR.

div.head: Varittirs.
div.p: Varittirs.

—Genius makes its observations in shorthand; talent writes them out at length. We are always using the word "sympathy ;" but do -we know what it means ? It means "suffering with"— nothing less. The avaricious man is like the barren, sandy ground of the desert, which sucks in all the rains and dews with greediness, but yields no fruitful herbs or plants for the benefit of others. _ _

There must be an intrinsic likeness between that which we seek and the way in which we seek it, or we shall never find it. We may catch at its shadow, but the reality will elude us. He who is truly, deeply ho:iest, loves honesty so much better than any possible reward that he chooses it every time, apart from any consideration of its results, and neither hope nor7ear, neither bribe nor threat, could tempt him away from his loyal allegiance. To-morrow may never come to us; we do not live in to-morrow—we cannot find it in any of our title-deeds. The man who owns whole squares of real estate and great ships on the sea, does not own a single thinute of to-morrow. To-morrow! It is a mysterious possibility not yet born; it lies under the seal of midnight, behind the veil of glittering constellations. It is not calumny or treachery that does the most harm in the world—they are continually crushed, and are felt only in being conquered—but it is the glistening and softly-spoken lie, ,the amiable fallacy, the patriotic lie of the historian, the provident lie of the politician, the jealous lie of the partisan, the merciful lie of the friend, -and the careless lie of each man to himself which darken and degrade our life. Books are teachers whose influence is peculiar to them- selves. They !speak not to you unless you: speak to them. You must go to them, or they will not come to .you. They teach when 'other teachers sleep, or travel, cr die. In the silencp of the midnight hour, or in the seclusion of a mountain or forest retreat, with none but yoU and your book, there you and it, in stillness and fZlitude like death, may converse together. Not a sound shall pass from either to the!other, yet you and it shall talk as though you had a veritable living person by your side. In the indelible form of printed words passing as rapidly as the weaver's shuttle before your eyes, it holds .converse with you in the secret chamber of your mind. Enfolded in those magic syllables and sentences is a voice which none can hear but the invisible ear of your own soul.

ANECDOTES or Josn BILLINGS. Before leaving New York the writer called on Josh Billings with an album and modestly solicited his autograph. He took it on his ,knees, gave his mouth a comical twist, and wrote:— Thrice is he armed who hath his quarrel just. —The Bard of Avon. Ancijour tirfig be who gets his blow in fust. —J. Billings.

uJosli /as extremely fond of animals, and had a cat in his at Albany which he gravely addressed as " I suggested that that was a dignified name for 'puss, as eats were usually called " Toni," or "Tip," or a quick short cognomen. "But that's a special, swell, blue-blooded specimen of the feline race, I wish you to know," rejoined the humourist. " Recently, poor fel- low, he has had fits, and since then I call him ' Fitz- William.' " When Rubinstein was over here he was pre- sented to Josh, and the pianist was careful to impress .the American with accounts of the nobility of his ances- tors. "My family," said he, loftily, " goes:back to the time of the Crusaders. My researches in :this direction enabled me to discover that one of my ancestors accom- panied the Emperor Barbarossa.." Josh smiled, and, affecting to be immensely impressed, immediately re- marked, "On the piano, of course." IA story is told of the humorist being thrown on one occasion amongst a batch of students in a country town near New Haven. He was tramping along with a rusty yellow dog, and entered the bar-room of an hotel for some refreshments. A group of the Yale lads chanced to be there on a frolic, and immediately interviewed Billings, whom they evi- dently mistook for a farmer. They inquired with affected interest after the health of his wife and children, and Josh, with counterfeited simplicity, gave them a graphic account of his family and farm. "Of course you belong to the Church?" asked one of the boys. "Yes, the Lord be praised, and my father and grandfather before me." "Now, I suppose you would not tell'a lie?" said one of the students. "Not for the world." "What will you take for that dog?" pointing to Josh's cur, which was crouching beneath his chair. "I won't talieo dols. for that dog." "Twenty dols.! Why, he's not worth 20 cents." "I assure you I would not take 20 dols. for him." " Comeimy friend," said the student, who, with his companions, was bent on having some fun with the old man, "now, you say you won't tell a lie for the world. Let me see if you will not do it for 20 dols. I'll give you 20 dols. for your dog." "I'll not take it." "You will not ! There! Let mei see if this will not tempt you to lie," added the student, producing a small bag of half dols., which he built up in small piles on the table. Josh was sitting by the table with his hat in his hand, apparently unconcerned. "There," added the student; "there are 20 'dols., all in silver; I will give you that for the animal." Josh quietly raised his hat to the edge of the table, and, as quick as thought, scraped all the money into it except one half dol., and then ex- claimed, "I won't take your 20 dols. Nineteen and a half is as much as that dog is worth; he is your pro- perty IA tremendous shout from his fellow-students clearly showed the would-be wag that he was completely qsouladr,taenr, o h and he need not look for sympathy from that good-humouredly acknowledged himself beaten.

Snatches of suitable weather have allowed some pro- gressto be made in the vegetable garden, and potato planting and seed sowing have been performed in most gardens. Last week we incidentally mentioned the Car- rot amongst other seeds that might be sown, and it was our intention to give instructions how to secure some good roots where the natural soil will not grow them, but space did not permit As more Carrots are sown in April than in March, our remarks are still timely. If we look round the vegetable tables at our late summer or autumn shows, we find many of the collections minus this vegetable, or those staged showing traces of canker, which considerably detract from the merit of the collec- tion, and obviously accounts for a more common but well-grown vegetable being substituted for it. If the following plan is adopted Carrots fit for exhibition may be grown in any garden, and a square yard of ground will produce several dishes' But ‘thatever space may be decided upon, throw out all the soil to the depth of 15in., which. will be the depth of the spade, and shovel- lings, then loosen the bottom, and fill the hole with de- cayed manure or a mixture of this and half-decayed leaves. Over this place :six inches of the soil thrown, and the remainder can be regulated round the sides, as they will be considerably higher than the normal level of the soil. The surface of the bed may have a gentle beating with the back of the spade, and afterwards break the surface with the rake, if the seeds are to be sown broadcast; but if in drills this will not be neces- sary. In either case the seed should be covered over with half an inch of the finest soil, and to measure this kwe would sift it through a half-inch riddle. if we only sowed one sort we would select James' Intermediate, as it is larger than Early Horn or Early Nantes, but these come in earlier, and it answers well to sow them in drills alternately with the Intermediate, inasmuch as their earliness admits of them being drawn for use, which allows more space for the others to develope.. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The grassplot this time of the year invariably has a very soily appearance. Continually walking over it, drip from overhanging trees, and poverty of soil are some of the causes that produce this result. The best renovator, as far as we have experienced, is to mix fresh horse droppings and soil in equal portions, and pass these through a half inch sieve over the plot, walking backwards as the work proceeds. In a few days this may be rolled or beaten with the spade. Soot, either alone or in conjunction with soil, will improve the ap- pearance of the grass at anytime. Any mixture contain- ing soil is best applied at this time of the year, as it al- lows time for it to settle well down before the grass requires cutting, and the roots of the grass will rise and take possession of it. Should the grass in two or three. weeks appear weakly in places, a handful of grass seeds thrown over them will work wonders. Bulbous plants, such as Snowdrops and Crocuses, should, as they go out of flower, have some mark put to them to indicate their position, and in case of the latter, the colours should be marked if it is intended to move them or make any alteration in the arrangement another year. THE WlNDOW.—Tuberose Begonias: For two seasons past we have watched one of these growing in a cottage window, which is conclusive proof that they are suitable for the purpose; indeed, most of the hardier kinds are so. Even those grown in our stoves for the sake of the foliage have been frequently well grown in a window by painstaking cultivators. We have also observed two or three of the tuberous class flowering freely in the front garden, where they had been planted in May or June, and taken up in autumn and potted and covered with ashes for the winter. They naturally begin to make their growth now, and those intended for pot culture should be turned out of the pots they are now in and the old soil shaken away, when they may be placed in pots an inch larger and good soil of a sandy nature placed round them. SMALL ALLOTMENTS.—The Earl of Pembroke has ar- ranged with the tenant of a bolding near Salisbury for 20 acres to be given up for the purpose of allotments. The ground has been marked out in about a hundred plots ranging from 20 perches to half an acre, and about 80 lots have already been taken. The rent per perch. The Earl will pay all rates, taxes, and tithes. A gentleman from Salisbury intends offering prizes for the best cultivated plots, and also purposes placing seats In the field. These garden allotments are much needed in the vicinity of many towns- and villages, as they afford a healthy and remunerative occupation to our opera- tives who are confined during the day an the stuffy atmosphere of the mill.

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE FRENCH BREEDS Or POULTRY. —From the remarks which we have made lately regard- ing the show of poultry held at the Palais de l'lndustrie, Paris, it will have been gathered that the french breeds are bred for their economic rather than their fancy merit's. We do' not say that by this the purity of race is disregarded, for that this is not sods abundantly proved by the number of high-class varieties which are to be found in France. But the utilitarian element is much more kept in view than is the case in British shows. Another instance of the continued study of this aspect in poultry keeping is shown by the cards exhibited on the pens of M. Lemoine at the Paris shcicr. Thesecontained, in addit*Pn to a specimen of the eggs laid by each, the qualitievand characteristics of each breed, as learnt by M. Lemonine in his experiments in. his poultry estab- lishment a Crosne. These tables: have been translated, and were given in a recent number of the Lire Stock Journal. They are so valuable that we take the oppor- tunity of giving a few particulars with respect to the French breads, specially for the advantage of those who have not read the articles thereon whiclthave, fmm time to time, been published in these columns. The tables are well worth careful preservation, and, must have en- tailed a vast amount of careful stud Y- and trouble on M. Lemoine. CravEcalum—This is one of the most* valuable of the French breedfor table• purposes: It owes its origin to Normandy, and undoubtedly is indebted' for its delicate flesh to the rich pastures of that country. It is en- tirely black in the plumage, has adarge crest and beard, with a horned comb. It has hitherto been, found rather delicate in tills country, though there are those who have had little or no trouble with, it even on the most unfavourable land.' JOHN RYLAND& OF MANCHESTER = MILLIONAIRE AND HOW HE BECAME SO, We take the following interceding sketch from "The North Eastern Weekly Gazette The father of the Manchester millionaire was originally a hand-loom weaver at Parr, • near St. Helens. He rose to be manager and partner of a small factory, and eventually opened a draper's shop in St. Helens, where the bulk of the goods produced at the little factory was sold. The plan of being both manufacturer and retailer soon told its tale in his banking account. He gradually rose to be known as a substantial business man. His three sons were taught to fight their own way in the world and expect no help frora their father. John was the youngest, and the best scholar of the three. He seems to have been a money-maker even when a boy. When about fourteen be spent his pocket-money in buying a lot of trinkets, put up at an auction sale. Having sold these at a good profit he found himself with an unusually large sum of money in his pocket. He told his good luck to an old woman who had nursed him in infancy. She and her husband had been hand-loom weavers. "Why don't you buy a little warp and weft with the money you've got, and let us weave. them ?" she said. John took quite a fancy to the suggestion,. bought some material for the old dame to work up, and the investment proving profitable continued to employ her. He thus became both a manufacturer and mer- chant in a small way, though still a schoolboy.. After school hours he acted as assistant in his father's shops and earned quite a good wage for a boy. By the time his schooling was over he was pro- moted to be regular assistant at a large salary for those times. His earnings and his holidays he spent in weevily.... All his savings were put into warp and weft, and before he was seventeen he had several families employed working up his material. There was no romance in such a beginning as this, but there was promise of a great success so far as -ea- cumulation of wealth goes. His eldest brother, Joseph: started a mill in Wigan, and did wonderfully well. In i•B2-1 he had succeeded so-far as to ask Johns then only eighteen, to join him as partner and act ate commercial traveller for the firm. He entered into the arrangement, and started out on horseback with' his samples fastened on to the scale. His journeys were mostly to the towns in Lancashire, Yorkshire Cheshireeand North Wales. His patterns were prin • cipally ginghams, calicoes, and other cotton goods. He proved himself a successful traveller, and used to make it his boast that he never tried to sell to a man without succeeding sooner or later. The two brothers soon built up &larger trade than they had capital for,- and their father offered to be- come a third partnerrand find more-capital. The re- sult was the establishment of thenow famous firm of Rylands and Suns. At this time they had weaving mills at Wigan and St. Helens, and a large draper's shop in St. Helens-, • Chester was then a larger place. than Manchester, so far as trading went. The Rylande used to send all their goods by carte to Chester. In 1822 John saidto hie brother " Instead of send- ing goods to Chester-fair, let us send' them to Man- chester fair, and open up a warehouse in that town." The suggestion was a good one, and soon carried out. In a few weeks a, house in High-street was rented ancl- filled with cotton goods. ;Tohn removed there and lived on tire premises, and made this the centre of the business operations. Hie first house in the metropolis of Cottendom•was not so, grand as his present one. At this date all calicoes were woven, with a linen warp. The Rylands soon began to bay their linen direct from the fix-growers and spinners in the North of Ireland, thus saving any intermediary profits. As their capital increased they added other-' branches to their businen, such as-dyeing and printing. In 1824 they found t would be necessary to enlarge their works. With this view they bought two large estates near Wigan—one containing dyeing and bleach- ing works; on the Other they built a spinning mill for producing both cotton and linen yarn— This was reckoned a tremendous establishment when it was opened, but in comparison with their present factories is small. The purchase of these estates was the gigantic, stride that lended John 11#/ands among_the million- aires of the world. As -it happened, there-was a rich vein of coal underlying part of the land that was use- ful for both domestic and manufacturing purposes. A colliery was soon, sunk, and the house coal was sold, while the coarser kinds they cox:seamed in their works. In this way all the coal dealers' and colliery proprietors' profits- were saved, and the firm was able to devote more capital to their already enormous trade. Joseph Rylands eatired from the firm, in 1840, and went into business in Hull. Soon after-31am and his father bought a large cotton mill ab Ainsworth, where they now spin about twenty ton.s of cotton a-week, and weave 30,0G0 lbs. of calico. Nearly i,OOO operatives are employed in this one mill alone. In 1847 the old man dietA leaving. Min as the sole representative of Rylands and Sons. Unhampered now by any partners, and having plenty of capital and almost unlimited credit, he launAed out larger than ever. The warehouse in High-street was en- larged, and other branches of mercantile business were added, until 'a deeper-could furnisle himself com- pletelyout of Rylands's stock. He was thus the pro- ducer of nearly all that he sold, right prom the coal mine, the flax field, the spinning mill, the weaving shed, the bleach works, the dye worbet. the printing works, up to the dealer's-warehouse. He saved eight or nine profits, and paid, nothing for distributing his goods.

- By 1864 his profits luta so increased in his ham. that he was able to buy- some large cotton mills at Gorton, which he enlarged and made into one of the largest factories. in Bug land. They cover 16, square yards, and emplby 1,600 hands. In 1865 he built a larger facto 7 near Wigan, known as the Ciid- low Works. This magnificent mill is,fireproof. The top room is for receiving cotton, brought from the railway oven, a viaduct 300 feet /tag. The second floor contains the machinery for cleaning, opening, and making ready for the cardroom. The bottom Door is for boilers and engines. It contains 6c-noo spindles, and produces. 75.000 lbe. of yarn weekly. Rylands's three mills. at Gidlow, Gorton, and Ains- worth give employment to 5,000 people.

FATS OE A COMMERCIAL TRAVELLER.—Abont eleven o'clock on Monday night the body of a man was founcl in a railway tunnel near Ratherley, Cheltenham. The head had been cut off at the nook, and it lay some distance away. The body was removed to the railway station, and papers found in the clothing showed that he was a com- mercial traveller named George Riley, in the employ of Messrs. Chadwick and Taylor, paper manufacturers, Man- chester. It is supposed he was killed by the nine o'clock train.

A young lady being asked if there were many beauti- ful women in the place, innocently replied, "Oh, no, there are only six of us at present." "A genuine patriot," said an election orator recently, "must at all times be ready to die for his country, even though it should cost him his life." (Thundering ap-

plause.) "What amused me most at the opera," said an Arab chief who had been taken to hear "Faust," "was a musician in the orchestra, seated a little higher than the I rest, who performed on an invisible instrument with a

stick." A gentleman mentioned to Archbishop Whateley that he had been night in the rain and was wet through. "Are you really wet through 9" said the archbishop, "I was never wet through in my life—never further than

my skin." "Don't talk to me about beginning at the bottom the ladder," observed a "crushed" actress to a friend. "I began there ten years ago, and lam there still. If it was to do over again, I'd begin at the top. It's much easier to fall down than to climb up." Patrick was a true son of Erin, always happy and , always ready for a joke. One day a farmer, in passing him, shouted good-humouredly—" Bad luck to you, Patrick !" "Good luck to you, sir !" was the immediate Iresponse; "and may nayther of us be roight !" Housemaid: "It does my heart good to see you and the baby together; it's a pretty picture. Sure and he's the image of you." Fond mother: "But they all say that he looks like his father, Mary." for that:" FRENCH AS SHE IS SPOKEN.—The Browns spend their New Year's Day at "dear Parry."—Brown pere : Gar- song, bring us some lunch.—Garcon Oui, m'sieu—pour quatre ?—Brown: Cat ! No, hang it all. Cat "Will you please give me some dinner, ma'am ?" begged a tramp. "I guess, so," was the reply. "Will you have a plate of soup ?" "I'm not particular," said the tramp. There was a time," he went on mourn- fully, "when I wouldn't think of sitting down to dinner without soup; but things is different now. You kin start me on roast beef, or pie, or even an ontry, for all I care." A lady said the other day at a friend's dinner table— at which she found several strangers seated—in response to a remark made about a certain lady of uncertain age, "Why, good gracious! she is as old as the hills !" and could not imagine in the least what had caused the general consternation. She did a little later, however, when it was explained to her that two maiden sisters at the table, whose names she did not catch in the intro- duction, were called Hill, and were extremely sensitive on the subject of age. GREAT CnnacttEs.—The following is the comparative capacity of the most celebrated churches in Europe : St. Peter's, Rome, will hold 54,000 persons; Milan Cathedral, 37,000; St. Paul's, Rome, 32,0001 St. Paul's, London, 25,000; St. Petronia, Bologna, 24,000; St. Sophia, Constantinople, 23,000; Florence Cathedral, 24,300; Antwerp Cathedral, 24,000; St. John Lateran, 22,900; Notre Dame, Paris, 21,000; Pisa Cathedral, 13,000; St. Stephen's, Vienna, 12,000; Cathedral of Vienna, 11,000: St. Peter's, Bologna, 11,400: St. Dominic's, Bologna, 11,000; and St. Mark's, Venice, 7,000. A SEASHELL WITH EIGHT THOUSAND Eras.—The Coat- of-Mail shellfish has its eyes not on its body, where we should naturally look for them, but on its shell. The surface of the shell is, in fact, full of eyes. They glisten at us like crystals, as we view them in their calcareous setting. One might as soon expect to see eyes em- bedded in the back of the tortoise or turtle, or on the surface of one's finger-nail. The sight is so strange, and the discovery so new to science, as to lead us to a closer inspection. These eyes of the Coat-of-Mail shell- fish are minute, highly-refracting rounded bodies, for the most part arranged in rows. In one case there are 24 of such rows, with an average of 15 eyes in each, so that there are in all 360 eyes. In another shell, of which the eyes are very small, the almost incredible number of 8,500 eyes can be counted. We are not wrong, therefore, in speaking of the "myriad-eyed" Coat-of-Mail shell. A PRESCRIPTION IN DISGUISE.—GeneraI D— was more distinguished for gallantry in the field than for the care he lavished upon his person. Complaining, on a certain occosion, to Chief Justice Bush% of Ireland, of the sufferings he had endured from rheumatism, that learned and humorous judge undertook to prescribe a remedy. "You must desire your servant," he said ,to the general, to place every morning by your bedside a tub three-parts filled with warm water. You will then get into the tub, and having previously provided yodr- self with a pound of yellow soap, youl must rub your whole body with it, immersing yourself occasionally in the water, and at the end of a quarter of on hour the pro- cess concludes by wiping yourself dry with towels, and scrubbing your person with a flesh brush." "Why," saidl the General, after reflecting for a minute or two, "this , seems to be neither more nor less than washing one's self." "Well, I must confess," rejoined the judge, "it is open to that objection." THE STORY or POPE JOAN.—TO many persons the story of "Pope Joan" (Redway, London) is just as worthy, or unworthy perhaps we might say, of credence as any other legend of the Dark Ages, a period prolific of doubtful miracles and legends. Historical research, however, puts a very different complexion upon the matter. It is surprising to find what a hest of authori- ties there is in support of this astounding incident. Many of these are quoted in the little volume now before us. The title of Pope Joan is said to have been Johnl VIII. She was born at Mayence, of English parentage; I is described as beautiful, talented, and learned, but by no means chaste. In connection with her amours she assumed male garb, and subsequently retained it when Ale devoted herself to study. She gained distinction in Rome by her secular and theological lectures, and her popularity became so great that on the death of Leo IV. she was elected Pope. The date of her accassion to the tiara is stated to be A.D. 855, and that she reigned two years, five months, and four days. While taking part in a procession a most scandalous event put an end at once to her Pontificate and her life. One can hardly realise contemporary feeling on the matter. There is no. evidence that any one was shocked by the occurrence; it was a period, indeed, when immorality was rampant in high places, when public opinion had no weight, and the superstitious and ignorant populace was described as "no better than a herd of animals." In commamora- tion of the singular death of Pope Joan a statue was erected at the spot. There it remained until 1585, when Pope Sixtus V. cast it into the Tiber. It is also assnted as a fact beyond denial drat the bust of Pope Jorxi re- mained for upwards of two centuries between those of Leo W. and Benedict 111. in the Cathedral of Sienna,and' that then it was removed and a bust bearing the name of Zacharias put in its plate. The ridicule and scorn. cast upon the pretensions and vices of the Papacy Ur the Reformers seem' to have first given rise to the desire to remove all traces of Joan in the Ronran hierarchy. It is sought finally to clinch the whole story-as truthful lir' citing from the official minutes the uneontradicted ferences of John Huss- to Pope Joan when before the Council of Constance, which, in violation of his saffy conduct, consigned him to the frames. " NETER MIND."—Tn 1862 litince Bfamarck, than Ambassador of Prussia at the Cburt of St. Petersburg,. was invited to the imperial hunt.. Being awenthusiastic hunter, he went to the designated' place on the evening'i before the appointed day in order-to have a' little spout by himself. Game was abundant,. and Bismarck had a* god time, but somehow he lost his way-.. When the. time for the imperial hunt approached' Bismarck fowl& himself fourteen miles-away from the place:. A offered his services to take Bismarck to the sight place. He appeared with a team of ponies-and a:village sleigh.. Bismarck doubted that the Russkurdrivereould get him' there in time to engage in the hunt. "Itrelreu sure you. can get me there in time?" asked-Bisniarek: *-Nitchego answered the mouja quietly. ("-Nitehego" is th Russian for "Never mind." or " All right.") "These are- rather rats than horses,' remarked' Bismarck, taking his, seat in the sleigh. "Nitchego !". was- the answer. Th peasant whipped up his horses, and they went as swiftly as a pair of falcons. Bismarck could. hardly keep his. seat. "You do not spare your horses- at all,r'remarked} the famous passenger, gasping for breath. "-Nitchego !" said the driver. "You say ‘Nitchego,' but they ma fall dead on the way!"' " Nitchege, The road w hardly distinguishable through the Ibrest, but the peasant continued Sus mad run. brushed against the big trees and went on and on. "You will' break my neck finally exclaimed Bismarck, scared in good earnest- " Nitchego!" answered the Russian, with a bit of a smil on his face. Presently there was a smash.. Bismarchi flew against a tree and bruised his face. He jumped tip, very angry, snatched an iron rod from the sleigh, and rushed at the peasant, swearing vengeance. The driven coolly picked up a handful of snow, with which he goo& naturedly wiped the blood-stains from Bismarck's face: "Nitchego !" he:muttered as he finished the operation: 'That invariable Russian Nitchego' disarmed me," said' Bismarck, telling the story to a Russian diplomatist. "I gave myself up to the will of my driver, sa,t quietly in the sleigh, and made no more remarks. My driver brought me to the place in time; I paid him welt, thanked him warmly, and preserved that him rod. When I returned to St. Petersburg I ordered a jewelter to malt% me a ring from that rod, with the inscription in Russian* Nitchego.' " The Russian " Nitchego" became the watchword of Bismarck's policy. "Whenever," said he, "I meet troubles and dangers, I say in Russian Nitchego then I push ahead."—St. Petersburg T'ecinnosti.

MILK AS A STIMULANT.—The greater my experience becomes, writes Dr. Clauston in the annual report of the Royal Edinburgh Asylum for Insane, I tend more to substitute milk for stimulants. In very acute cases, both of depression and maniacal exultation, where the disordered working of the brain tends rapidly to reduce the strength, I rely more on milk and eggs made into liquid custards.

Mr. W. SATTERTHWAITE, of Colthouse, Hawkshead, has sold (per Mr. R. W. Ashburner) to Mr. J. P. Brockbank a very grand bull calf of the famous Bright Eyes branch of the Wild Eyes tribe, by Baron Newfield Winsome, from Estliwaite Wild Eyes, a half-sister to Conishead Wild Eyes, bought by Sir H. Allsopp, Bart.. for 610 gs, when not five months old. The youngster, a September calf, is very promising, and, being a heifer's first calf, is of good size, with grand head, neck, back, and quarters. AGE OF HORSES.—A discussion on the subject of the age of horses has been going on in the columns of a sporting paper, and some very aged animals have been brought to light. The horse comes to maturity very early, and in many cases retains his good qualities for a surprising length of time. The doings of thoroughbreds at two years old are frequently astonishing, and in many cases a racehorse is never better—that is to say, never performs greater feats—than during the autumn of his three-year-old career. A horse on the turf is called aged when he is over six, and the number of such horses in training as flat-racers is comparatively very small, though often steeple-chasers last longer, and on the flat there are some exceptional animals, such as Herald, who won three races last year, and is still in training at the age of fourteen. Horses that pursue less exciting careers last much longer. Animals well over thirty do not seem to be rare; there are authentic instances of ponies over forty, and accounts appear to be forthcoming of horses "said to be" over sixty, but one would like to have something very definite in the way of proof. CALF REARING.—Mr. Primrose McConnell writes "Calf rearing is almost a business in itself, and there is not space to say more than a few words about it. When newly born, the young animal should get its own mother's milk, as this colostrum' has a beneficial purga- tive tendency. Afterwards from two to four quarts daily of new milk, according to breed and age, increas- ing as the animal is able to take it. Never give cold, but always a little warmed. At a fortnight, a little porridge composed of linseed-cake meal and barley meal mixed may be added to the milk, and the latter may be reduced gradually by adding skim-milk, butter-milk, or whey. Hay or grass should be within the reach of the youngsters until they go out to the fields, when they may be gradually weaned off pail-feed. It will scarcely pay to rear calves if sd. or 6d. per gallon can be got for the milk, but by proper management several "crops" of calves may succeed one another on the produce of the same cows. The most of us are still sceptical as to the great merits of milk substitutes." CROPS AND SYSTEMS.—I am glad to see you are direct- ing public attention to a more rational rotation on strong land. In these times the growth of roots on strong lands is a grave mistake. During an unfavourable autumn the soil is parched, and injured by the horses and vehicles used in their removal, whilst no ordinary cultivation and manuring will keep land in condition where the root crops are all drawn off. Even the ' strongest clays, if -well drained and judiciously cropped, will grow a certain amount of food for the nation, find employment for the labourer, and still leave a remnant for rent. I have had considerable experience in the growth and ploughing-in of green crops on strong lands, and maintain that there is no better or cheaper method of increasing the fertility of such lands. Dwarf rape, tares and mustard are the best crops for the purpose. The fend soon sickens of broad clover, and to plough in a good crop must be considered a wasteful practice. Clover should be folded off with sheep, which should have, say, one pint of oats, barley, or peas per day. I still maintain that at present prices wheat meal is not only the cheapest but the best artificial food, either for dairy cows or young store stock. In this way our clay lands can be cultivated and improved in manurial con- dition on the self-supporting system, and with benefit to the country.—Gilbert Murray,-Elvasion. Mn. JAMES HOWARD ON HAYMAKING.—A few days ago Mr. James Howard, the eminent agricultural authority, read a paper before the Farmers' Club, London, on "Haymaking." Mr. Howard's paper dealt with the sub- ject under three heads, the time for cutting, treatment in the field, and carrying and stacking_ Of these none is more important than the best time for cutting grass for hay. Practical experience shows that over-ripe grass makes hard and woody hay. As the grass becomes ripe the sugar and other ooluble nutritious matters in the stems and blades become more or less converted into cellOose or fibre, while the' cellulose that eiready exists in the younger grass, and is' by no means wholly indiges- tible, becomes gradually less, tender and more indurated as the plant matures, and censequently less digestible. The maximum proportion of really nutiitive matter occurs in, most grasses at flowering time. and Mr. Howard's experience is in accord with that of others when he recommends this as the proper time at which, weather permitting, to cut the- grass. Too early a cut- ting, on the-other hand, he regards as wastefAeseeing that while the plant is actively 'Stiking up carbonaceous matter from tlie air and daily forming fresh substance, as it does right up to flowering,, we more than ibse ri substance what we might perhaps gain in digestibility. Mr. Howard's practical rule, dedheed from his own ex- perience, is to take the sorrel plant as his guielbeand "when the sumer begins to ripen "'to mow his meadows. He estimates that the annual money-saving in the-king- dom due to mechani•aal aids in the -harvesting of the-hay . crop can hardly fall short of two millions sterling on a crop of seven million, acres. Mr. Thaward was last year struck while travelling in Baya,ria-with the plan there adopted of making hay-cocks, or rather substitutes- for what we in England know as hay-cocks. The plan alluded to consists in piling the grass round a species-of tripod made of three hop-poles, furnished with pegs mm the shape of ceress-pieees, about twanty tripods being. used per acre. Although the grass is piled green, thee space in the centre of the tripod give& sufficient yen/elle- time to prevent undere heating, evaporation readily goes. on, and excellent, hay is made. SUICIDE oF A FARISIBIL—Mr. John Mannings, a well- known Cheshire farmer, residing near Crewe, committed suicide on Monday evening. He had been to Sandbach with his horse and trap, and returned to his farm in the afternoon. Later on he was found in an outhouse dead, a bottle containing poison on a bench near leading to the be- lief that he had committed suicide. It is said the poison was carbolic acid, and that the quantity he took would have poisoned 30 people. Deceased was a quiet man, but is said to have been drinking lately. feared the bill would lead to civil war. The Oppogition ad- hered to the declaration they placed in the Queen's Speech, and they would not at any- time or for any reason in- terfere with the legislative union between England and Ireland. Mr. GLADSTONE, who was received with loud cheers, rose at twelve o'clock to reply on behalf of the Government. He denied that the safeguards provided in the bill were dictated by distrust of the Irish people. OK the contrary, they were inserted in consequence of the mistrust, no doubt honestly, felt by others. It was said that there had been no formu- lated demand from Ireland, bat the Government recognised the wisdom of yielding to reason what it would be far better not to have to yield to necessity. The right hen. gentleman recapitulated the conditions he had in his opening speech laid down as the guidiog principles of the proposed legisla- tion, adding that he had had no intention to put the control of the Customs and Excise and the absence of the Irish members from the House as vital principles of the bill. Since then it had been suggested that Irish members might come with limited powers. or with diminished number, and he (Mr. Gladstone) did not think it would be right for the Government to take upon themselves at this stage ef the bill to close the door on the consideration of those matters. Having defended and justified his previous references to the analogies for what he proposed in the cises of Sweden and Norway and Austria-Hungary, Mr. Gladstone pro- ceeded to argue that the fundamental fear of those who had. attacked the measure was that the Irish people would neces- sarily do wrong—that the administration of the country would necessarily be changed. (Cheers.) In regard to the question of the veto proposed by the bill, the right honourable gentleman stated that there was no limitation to that proposition; and in reference to the income-tax that would necessarily be as separate in Ireland as it would be in England. Of the bill generally, he said it proposed to give to the Irish people a reasonable satisfaction of their demands, without imitating the example i set by a former Government in the case of America. The wants of Ireland were to be considered in relation to the fact whether it would be harmful to others that they should be granted. He ridiculed the fear that had been expressed as to further demands on the part of the Irish members if this bill were passed, and as to the question of tneir having been no mandate for this measure he contended that, inasmuch as there had been no mandate for coercion, or for maintain- ing the law, so no mandate was necessary for a proposal to attengthen the means of maintaining the law. He com- pared the criticisms on the bill, and pointed out that no one speech agreed with another; and speaking of the measure as a plan, he remarked that it migla be improved, but at any rate it held the field, as did also the subject. (Cheers.) It was for Parliament to say whether It would make a bold I attempt to establish a system of Irish laws, under an Irish I Parliament, or whether they should struggle on as before, I leaving England and Scotland to a famine of needful legisla- tion, and Ireland to a continuance of social disease and in- ternal discord. (Loud and prolonged cheers.) The motion that leave be given was then, at five minutes bast one, put by the Speaker, and agreed to amid protracted and enthusiastic cheering. Mr. GrArteroNE stated that the second reading would be fixed for the 6th May. The Municipal Franchise (Ireland) Bill was withdrawn, and order for the second reading discharged. The House adjourned at 20 minutes to three o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDaY. The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve o'clock. THE ROME RULE BILL.—Mr. ARNOLD MORLEY, on be- half of the Prime Minister, announced that the second read- ing of the Government of Ireland Bill had been postponed from the 6th to the 10th of May.—Mr. J. O'CONNOR an- nounced the postponement of the second reading of the County Government (Ireland) Bill from that day to the 26th May. POLICE PENSIONS BILL.—Sir H. SELWIN-IBBETSON, in moving the second reading of the Police Constable Pension Bill, stated that its object was to provide fixed pensions to the police after 25 years' service, in lieu of the present sys- tem, under which the provision made by the superannua- tion fund, to which the men were compelled to contribute, was uncertain and precarious.—Mr. CHILDERS stated that he was prepared on behalf of the Government to bring in a bill soon after Easter, and he therefore hoped the motion for the second reading would be withdrawn until the House had had the opportunity of discussing the Government measnre.—Sir H. SELWYN-IBBETSON expressed his williog- nese to accept the suggestion of the Home Secretary, and moved the adjournment of the debate to the 24th May.— The motion was agreed to. LAND CULTIVATION BILL.—Mr. BRADLIXON, in Moving the second reading of the Land Cultivation Bill, admitted that he was not satisfied with it, because it did not go far enough. There were hundreds of thousands of acres of land now uncultivated in the United Kingdom which could be cultivated at a profit which the bill would not reach, and if the bill were read a second time it would undoubtedly re- quire large amendment in Committee. There were four pro- positions which he desired to lay down. The first was that there was a large quantity of land in an uncultivated state, and which ought to be forced into cultivation; secondly, that there was a very considerable proportion of this land which might be cultivated with profit; thirdly, that the ownership of cultivable land ought to carry with it the duty of cultivation; and fourthly, that the cultivation of the now uncultivated land would provide remunerative employ- ment for the whole of the unemployed portion of the pop- ulation throughout the kingdom. The total area of the United Kingdom was, he stated. 77,606,146 acres, the cul- tivated area being 47,708,095, and the extent of land un- cultivated or unaccounted for was 29,847,488 acres. The bill proposed to empower the local authorities to take on payment of compensation to the owner land beyond 100 acres that was kept waste, and to let it for cultivation.— Mr. W. LLOYD opposed the bill, and complained that no es- timate had been given of the value of the land it was pro- posed to bring into cu)tivation.—Mr. Tyssen-Anaherst and Mr. Jacks opposed the bill.—Mr. BROADHURST speaking on behalf of the Government, said the honourable gentle- man (Mr. Bradlaugh) had done good service by showing that land at present uncultivated could be broueht into pro- fitable cultivation, and, baying succeeded in raising an in- teresting and useful debate, he hoped the honourable mem- ber would be willing to withdraw a bill the incompleteness of which he had himself admitted.. Sir WALTER BATATTILOT moved that the bill be read a second time that day six months. Mr. LABOUCHERE ad- vised that the measure when brought forward should as- sume the more drastic form, and should include urban as well as agricultural land.—Mr. JOSEPH Ariel{ regretted that his friend Mr. Bradlaugh did not intend to press the bill. If the bill was withdrawn, he should do his best to buoy the agrioaltural labourers up with the hope that their rights were on the eve of being recognised, aud he trusted, please God, of being conceded,—a tter further debate, Mr. Brad- laugh offered to withdraw the bill, and the bill was by leave withdrawn. 'NET; Brus.—Leave was given to bring in the following bills:--Mr. Morgan Howard—Bill to amend the Medical Act, 1858.--Mr. Howard Spenseley—Bill for the better preven- tion of fires within the metropolis.--Mr. Thomas Blake— Bill to provide for the fencing of quarries. The House adjourned at a few minutes before six o'clock.

population out of the account it was supplying an alcoholic revenue less than in 1875-6 by £4,379,000. Roughly speaking, it might be said that the dimi- nution in revenue from alcoholic sources was about £41.500,000 in the last eleven years, and the fall last yes,- -£1,179,000—was the largest. While there had been this great diminution in the consumptic n of alcohol there had been an enormous increase in the consumption of the other comforts of life. The income tax, he hoped, might long be the Chancellor of the Exchequer's sheet anchor ; he did not mean that he wished it to remain at its present rate, but, but that it still might be found a staunch and solid resource. The fact that the tax in spite of the depression of trade yielded £50,000 per penny more than in 1882 could net be considered unsatisfactory. It was also SA tisf actor!' to find that the people had been saving more, for whereas in 18V5—the high tide prosperity—the savings banks showed savings of £2 Is 3d per head, in 1885, after years of depres- sion, there was a saving per head of £2 133 6d. As to the growth of expenditure, the great increase in eleven years had been upon the army and navy, and 6d out of 8d of the income tax was the result of that growth of expenditure. Upon the interesting question of the estimated expenditure for the coming year, he- said, if they balanced the income against the expenditure there would be a deficit of £543,599; and the question was how the deficit was to be met. He knew of no class or trade in the country at present in a condition to bear additional taxa- tion; the deficit mast therefore be met by some reduction in the fund now appropriated to the reduction of the National Debt. They ought not to have a surplus of less than ,£250.000; he proposed, therefore, to take from the Sinking Fund £BOO,OOO, which would convert a deficit of £544,000 into a surplus of £274,000 and prevent the necessity of borrowing. With such a surplus it was clear he could not undertake any serious operation for the remission of taxes. He should, however, relieve the cottage brewers inhabiting houses under £8 valuation of their 4s license—the license reduced last year from OS tO 4s. This would cause a loss to the revenue of £16,000, and the final 6alance would leave a surplus of £258,721. It they wanted a reduction of taxa- tion they must go back to economy. In his opinion we were living too fast. and the fact was that habitual spend- thrifts were very like habitual drunkards—they had no reserve to fall back upon. It would be well for them to note what were the causes of the gigantic debt and increased expenditure of the French Budget. They were extensions of dominion, foreign expeditions, great public works under- taken to give general employment to the people. He men- tioned these things not to disparage the energies or discour- age the exertions of the people of this country, but in order to entreat the House to resist the perpetual demands which came from all quarters for fresh expenditure. Sir M. firms-Beans regretted that in a normal Budget they should be asked to retain the income tax at 8,1 in the pound, and contended that the Budget was a remarkable justification of the amendment he carried last year.—The debate was continued by Mr. Childers, Dr. Cameron. Mr. W. H. Smith, Mr. Hubbard. Mr. Baden-Powell, Sir G. Camp- bell, Mr. Ainsley, Mr. J. More, Mr. S. Hill, Mr. S. Mason, Mr. M. Stewart, Mr. L. L. Cohen, Colonel Blundell, Mr. Illingworth, Sir J. Gorst, and Sir R. Fowler.—The Budget resolutions were agreed to, and were ordered to be reported to the House. CROFTERS' (SCOTLAND) BILL.—The Committee on this bill was resumed. On an amendment by Mr. A. J. Bar, FOUR, further amended by Mr. Catalcs, providing that the Land Commissioners may take into consideration whether the granting of the application of the crofters for part of a deer forest would injuriously affect the district. the Com- mittee divided—For the amendment, 165 ; against, 102- 63. Clause 13, which was the only clause dealt with, was passed by 120 to 89, and, progress having been reported, the House resumed. The Metropolitan Police Stations Bill was read a second time; and the Companies Acts Amendment Bill passed through Committee. On the motion of Mr. Childers, the Select Committee on he Rent Charge (Extraordinary) Bill was nominated. • The House adjourned at a quarter to two o'clock.
AMONG THE CONSONANTS-

BY JOHN PEERS. ; Intelligent reader I Doubtless thou bast seen, in wild and windy weather, geese on a common, or ducks in a pond, flapping impotent wings and mak- ing as though they would mount upon the air and ride on the wings of the wind. With them, indeed, the spirit is willing but the flesh is too abundant. Adiposity forbids what old instincts impel. Well, I confess to a similar feeling in simi- lar weather. Let the reader explain it as he likes ' best. With or without the help of the doctrine of transmigration of souls, I care not, if with Pytha- goras they saddle me with a goose as a remote ancestor. Be this as it may, the fact remains, and in the wild weather we experienced last September I gave way to the temptation, took train to Liver- pool, and found myself, a little before eleven o'clock,' on board the Bonnie Princess. A strong breeze from the S.W. made things rather lively. The spray which occasionally broke over the bow caused much amusement, to some of the passengers by wetting the others. The weather was very fine, clear, and warm until the Ormshead was missed, when the wind strengthened and the sky darkened threateningly. At Bangor it began to rain and continued to do so most of the night. Landing at islenai Bridge, I hastened to where shelter and a good tea awaited me. After which, to while away the time, I strolled on to the bridge in a meditative mood, induced, perhaps, by the dripping weather, and poked, pored, and pon- dered till the darkness and the gusty rain compelled a retreat. The next morning presented a complete contrast to the dank experiences of the previous evening, being fine and fresh. My route this morning was from Menai Bridge to Gaerwen by road, and thence to Holyhead by train. The road to the Anglesea column affords beautiful glimpses of Strait scenery, backed by the Snowdonians with the Llanberis Pass and the peak of Snowdon. Both bridges were in full view, and backed by the mountain range brought into prominent con- trast the works of man and the works of nature. A walk across the noble suspension bridge, com- paring even its smaller details with its compara- tively puny constructor is calculated to make a man proud of the fact of being one; proud of his race and proud of the nation to which he belongs. Here, standing upon this beautiful but stupendous structure, conceived, designed, and executed by his compeers, he feels himself tndeed the lord of the universe. I say; standing upon the .work of his hands wrapt in the contemplation of them, he feels an exultant pride in the thought that he was akin to the men who wrought these mighty works. But if pride be a sin its corrective in this case is not far to seek. The bane and the antidote are here to- gether. At the back of the dreqmer, towering above his head, are the eternal hills, whose smallest peak dwarfs his mightiest efforts, and reduces this self- styled lord of the universe to the comparative insig- nificance of a fly on the ceiling. And if his pride need further abasement, let him ascend the summit of Snowdon and try to find a trace of his handi- work in the valleys beneath him. In the Magnitude of his natural surroundings his own little efforts are lost or dwarfed into utter insignificance. And Snowdon is but as a molehill compared to the Him- alayas, which are themselves but as wrinkles on the skin of the earth, itself one of the smallest members of the solar system, whose inconceivable millions of miles of width is but as a point among the count- less number of its companions in the universe. Surely the immensity of nature must crowd out and crush the pride and self-conceit of the man who thus contrasts his own littleness with the incon- ceivable immensity of his surroundings. . And yet some of these little folk submit to be styled "majes- tic "—and this with a grave face, unconscious of the jest. Even in England, and the nineteeth century, we have this burlesque performance gone through, with the factitious majesty of a limited monarchy. And herein lies the difference between the majesty of the mountain and the majesty of the monarch. With the former it is intrinsic and inalienable, while the majesty of the limited monarch is of the leasehold kind, a majesty by suffrance, supported on the shoulders of the people, at the thunder of whose voices it will ultimately crumble to the ground. In the meanwhile we will onward toward. Holy- head. Through an undulating country parcelled out by stone walls into more or less stony fields wherein the scanty grafts give scanty crops, down into the richer valleys yielding a richer crop; among a primitive people dwelling in primitive houses, and speaking a primitive tongue. A land in which there is a deal of strong language used, that is, it is strong if a multiplicity of consonants can make it so, for the vowels seem as though they were there by accident, when not conspicuous by their ab- sence. In my inquiries as to the road I frequen- tly got Dim Sachenach, to which, of course, my answer might have been Dim Welsh— that is very dim indeed to the Welsh. But the invariable kind- ness I experienced in the island rendered a know- ledge of this ancient language of less importance. For if my informant's English was scanty the gaps were filled up with Welsh, and so we got along com- fortably, the will being taken for the deed. • So, in fine weather and among a kindly people, I tramped on to Gaerwen, and there took train to Holyhead. Here I hastened to the breakwater and dined frugally beneath its terminal light house, on the spot where some years before I had sailed into the harbour. The wind, although fresh, was off shore here and the sea comparatively calm. On the seaward face of the breakwater• iron steps and rails lead down to the wave-worn pebbles at its foot. A stroll upon these seldom trOdden stones brought to my mind the last time I walked along the breakwater, and the contrast then and now. Then a north-west gale was raging, driving before it a heavy sea, which thundered against the battlements, often sending tying de- tachments over the wall into the harbour, ren- dering the passage inconvenient if not positively dangerous. _You/ the sun shone, and the waters sparkled with just a pleasant ripple, and the para- pet was quite a delightful promenade.. Having often longed for a land view of South Stack, I bent my steps that way. The road leads over what, I suppose, is part of Holyhead Moun- tain. I was much amused, but at first rather startled, by an apparition which suddenly appeared from behind the old-world rocks around me. It was a weird strange looking animal, like a cross between a greyhound and an ichthyosaurus, and I veritably for the moment thought I was favoured by a visit from a pachydermatory palveotherium, so much in keeping was it with its palveolithic sur- roundings. A moment's •reflection convinced me that though a pachyderm it was only -a mortal pig, and not a spirit from the vasty deep. but an Old many farrowed sow of the bottle-nose breed, whose narrow flanks and spindle shanks, though well suited for mountain ranging, gave little promise of the well rounded hams and adipose flitches in which we rejoice at home. The rugged slopes of these hills afford a scanty, hardly won, existence to its inhabitants. They and my porcine friend are examples of the survival of the fittest, for they live whcke others would starve. The Stack lighthouse situated on its own little island, and surrounded by its white buildings and walls formed a very pretty picture as seen from thB heights, where it first comes in view. It is indeed a bird's-eye view, the observer being far above the lantern top. A rather heavy sea was breaking on the rocks, and fringing them with surf. The sea birds hung on motionless wings, poised on the 11D- draught, which gradually and gracefully bore them aloft. A few coasting steamers, lately weather bound in Holyhead harbour, were making the best of their way to the south. now plunging their bows into the opposing seas, the propellers churning the water half in and half out, now in a sea and now in a trough, floundering like a stranded whale. I spent the evening inspecting the harbour and the splendid steamers of the London and North- Western Railway Co., by the aid of the electric light. The juxtaposition of locomotives and stea- mers gives the place a very mixed look, and gives one the feeling of amphibiousness, a terra-aquatic sen- sation, as though the sight of a mermaid would be a thing of course. The Welsh are a very pious people, and theirpiety seems to be of that diffusive kind that spreads itself over the walls of their houses in the shape of illu- minated scripture texts. I think every room in which I passed a night while in Anglesea had these mural embellishments. One in particular I noticed 1, from the suggestive association of a portrait, which, whether by accident or design I will not say, was placed between the following texts—" The Lord shall preserve me from evil" and "Rejoice in the Lord allway." The portrait was that of Lord Deiby. In thirease I acquit my Welsh hostess of any at- tempt at a joke. I believe she was incapable of it. Next morning, after post time. I sought and found a butcher's shop, and by the modest ex- penditure of threepence became the happy pos- sessor of two pork chops intended for consump- tion. "a is Bohemian," on the day's march. The blue sky, flecked by a few fleeting clouds, gave pro-

mise of a fine day. An early start for a country walk like this is like the start in life; one is replete with the abounding, if not abiding, anticipations of delights to come. A very pleasant walk of some two miles along the fine old coach road which here skirts the western side of the beautiful bay lying between Holyhead and the Skerries took me across a fine stream of water pouring through a sluice into the bay out of a pond on the opposite side of the , road. To a stranger this seems a great waste, as , in this stream alone there is power enough to light by electricity the whole of the town. But have we ' not nearer home examples of a foolish preference of expensive artificial to inexpensive natural modes of lighting? Is there no power in Howley? Is there ; no waste of water there? The further I got from Holyhead and penetrated the hill country the less use my tongue became to express my wants and wishes. Ere half the day's , tramp was done "Dim Sassenach" reigned supreme, , and lingually I was alone in the midst of a crowd. ; But the weather and the roadside blackberries were both very good, wherein a compensation for greater 1 evils than these might be found'. This is a pictures- que country. Even the roads are conscientious in this , respect, deviating as much from the straight and level as the capabilities of the ground will admit. What most strikes the lowland stranger is the ab- sence of barns, the cause being perhaps the absencs of anything to put in them. But if there are no barns he will see plenty of barn-like edifices, which upon investigation he will find to be Methodist chapels. Hefe is a primitive people speaking a primitive language, worshipping in a primitive form, in a primitive temple. And here in these inornate edi- fices these rugged children of the hill assemble to- gether to worship God and, accompanied by the wheezy strains of an asthmatic harmonium, sing to His praise and their hearts content. Not for these "the long drawn aisle and fretted vault, where the pealing anthem swells the note of praise." And if this simple worship be acceptable and effi- cacious unto salvation, and these rude edifices fit receptacles for Him who has said" For where two or three are gathered together in My name, there am lin the midst of them ;" if this indeed be so, what a condemnation of the pomps and vanities of eccle- siastic architecture and the florid ritual of the churches, which if not a substitute for the simple truth, often overlies it and hides it from view, as we often hear the crude production of the varia- tionist smothering the harmony of the true melo- dist! And where was the first and best of Christian sermons preached? Where, out in the open air, beneath the light of heaven, in a temple not built with hands. But man, being wiser than his teacher —following the barbaric precedent of the heathen— builds himself a gloomy pile of masonry wherein to worship, from the sacred interior of which the light of heaven is excluded, or only admitted after filtra- tion through bits of coloured glass in order to create the "dim religious light" in which his weak soul delights. And then the religious voluptuary goes a step farther and treats himself to what he is pleased to call" sacred" music, on the assumption that what delights the finite must be pleasing to the Infinite. If man must have pleasures, in them- selves both laudable and useful, by all means let him honestly call them by their proper name—self- indulgencies, and not use the name of religion as a cloak under which to gratify his own tastes, lest his "mind be corrupted from the Elimplicity which is in Christ." And to say these things, however good and commenaable in themselves, are aids to devotion, or in any way neces- sary for salvation, is to impugn the eternal justice of God who has placed so many , of His creatures beyond the reach of these artificial means of grace. Were this not so, the lot of these poor hill-folk would indeed be deplorable. But , justicend common-sense alike dictate that if sal- vation be necessary to man, it will be as easy of at- tainment by the scattered population of these bleak hill-sides. worshipping in the whitewashed sheds, as by the clustered inhabitants of our crowded cities, who perform their services immured in their minsters and cathedrals, Truly, if the one be justi- fied, the other is condemned.
