A RCM ARSABLE CURE OF EPILEPTIC FITS EFBECTED BY GORDO:VS EXTRACT." D. Tgamas 74. Hoxton-street. Bradford, writes July 24th, 1885.—Gentlemen,—Permit me to attest my unsolicited and ttunible testimony to the healing and curative properties of Tour EXTRACT, not only in restoring the weak and debilitated but in the curing of Epilepsy in its most aggravated form; not only do I speak from information, but personal observation In one special case—viz that of a woman subjected to the Shove disease for upwards of twelve years; nce:, so severe at 'first, but as time went on the fits became mare frequent,•until the patient was seldom a week without the recurrence, until Ale was reduced to sheer helplessness, and almost to a state (if Idiocy; for over thee years not able to do her own household lvork, and the family had tried anything and everything that doctors and patent medicines could do without effect; in fact, she ,gradually became worse, until the doctors said there was no cure, and the patient could net sur- vive long. They had tried many patent medicines. one preparation to the amount of £7. This for a time seemed tohave a little effect, and thejamily had hopes of a cure, but so soon as the system became used to the medicine, the medi- •eine became useless and all hopes again blighted. The family. in fact, became seriously inzpoverb-hed in expending money with hope of a cure, but all to no purpose; besides, the hus- band's health became enfeebled for want of rest for such a length of time that he was laid aside for long, until the family was reduced to a nitiful condition indeed. However, as.the last effort your EXTRACT was resorted to, and with surpris- ing effect sir or seven bottles regularly taken successively until the fits became lesa frequent and the health became WI- -proved, until the woman was enabled to attend her household duties; and now, though she has not used the EXTRACT for many months, she h-s not had fits for twelve months, and is now in her 'Kauai health. Any party writing me for proof, I will gladly answer and give the full name and address of suf- ferer, and at my expense; they will most gladly reply to any inquiry, but for reasons which are justifiable, they would rather not have their name come before the public. Yet you are at perfect liberty to make what Use of my statement you like, and, believe me, yours respectfully, DAVID TEOMAS, Bookseller and Stationer.

THE WELSH ELECTORS OF NEWTON DIVISION. A meeting of same importance as affecting the 300 or 400 Welsh electors resident in the Newton Division was held on Monday night, in the Welsh Congregational Chapel (kindly lent for the occasion), Houghton-street, Earlestewn. The chair was occupied by a popular Welshman, the Rev. E. Pan Jones. Ph.D., M.A., of Mostyn. The object of the meeting was to arouse in the minds and hearts of the local Welshmen an enthusiastic interest upen political questions generally, but more partichlarly the political reforms they considered necessary for the benefit of the Principality of Wales; and to consider the best means of organising themselves so that in future the Welsh vote might be more consolidated and made more effectual in bringing before candidates their require- meats and demands. It was at the same time understood as a means to this end they should put forth every etlort to support the Liberal cause. The Chairman, in the course of an instructive address in Welsh, expressed the great pleasure it afforded him to meet such a gathering of his fellow countrymen, whose aim was the political and social advancement of the Welsh nation. There was one peculiarity about the Welsh people which had placed them at a great disadvantage hitherto, namely, their proneness to look upon others as superior to them- selves, but he thought it was high time they should show a greater amount of moral independence and pay homage only to individual worth. They had too long paid an ap- parent homage to the parson and squire, but he had latterly presumed to think himself quite as good as either the squire or the parson. (Applause.) He was gratified to find the Welsh inhabitants of that neighbourhood had formed themselves into a political band to assist as far as they could their fellow-countrymen in Wales in the political struggles which the future had in store for them. For that example they were undoubtedly indebted to Irishmen, and he could only hope their success might be i found equal to that which had attended the many efforts of Irishmen in England to assist their brethren in Ireland. The people had now the power to say what measures they de- manded, and to let it be known what laws they were willing to obey. (Applause.) One grievance of Welshmen, and which they felt severely, was the establishment of an alien church in their midst, and he was glad that subject was receiving their attention in Earlestown. (Applause.) ' Mr. L. T. Foulkes then read a lengthy and carefully pre- pared paper dealing with the Established Church in Wales. He observed that every Welshman present would be sup- posed to agree that it was necessary tht church in Wales should be disestablished, that it had been such an absurdity forgo long a period that for the sake of decency alone, and in the name of religion, of which it pretended to be an in- stitution, it was high time that the church as an establishment in Wales should cease to exist. ' Dealing with the church in its religious aspect, the speaker ' considered it was unscriptural, and opposed to the prin- ciples of cbristianity. He followed with a succinct account of the ecclesiastical history of Wales from the earliest period, and observed that Wales, unlike Scotland and Ire- land, for all legal and political purposes formed an integral part of England, was governed by the same laws, and enjoyed the same rights and privi- leges. vet, notwithstanding this, it had never been Anglicanised. To this day it had all the marks of a distinct and separate nationality. He gave statistics showing the proportion of adherents of the Established Church to the adherents of the Non-conformiet Church. In Wales Non-coxformity had done the work it was the duty of the Church to do. In asking for the disestablish- anent and digendowment of that Church they merely asked for that which they felt themselves fully entitled to, seeing that the property of the Church was in every sense national property. Mr. T. 0. Roberts then moved "That this meeting con- siders it necessary that the Welsh inhabitants of this Par- liamentary Division of Newton should unite with the object of promoting such political reforms as may be considered necessary for the benefit of the Principality ef Wales."—The motion was seconded by Mr. Daniel Owen, and passed with enthusiasm.• On the motion of Mr. L. T. Foulkes, and seconded by Mr. John Williams, the following resolution was adopted:— "That this meeting of Welsh electors of the Parliamentary Division of Newton express their indignant protest against the vote given by Sir Richard Cross, the member for the Division, on the occasion of Mr. Dillwvn moving his reso- lution for the disestablishment of the Church in Wales." Mr. Richard Owen moved, and Mr. Robert 0. Roberts seconded—" That this meeting pledges itself to co-operate as far as possible with the Liberal Council, as represented by the Liberal "300 " in this Division, to secure the re- turn ef their candidate at the next election."—The motion was passed. The following vote of confidence in the Government was also passed, on the motion of Mr. Watkin, seconded by Mr. Hugh Jones—" That this meeting of Welsh electors express their confidence in the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone and his administration in their present efforts to arrive at a just and true settlement of the Irish question, and also their fervent hope that the right honourable gentleman may live to see his present efforts crowned with success." The meeting was of an enthusiastic character throughout and closed with the usual votes of thanks.

FOREIGN NEWS. - 'THE EASTERN QUESTION.—REPORTED INTRIGUE IN MACEDONIA. PRILIPPOPOLIS, SATITEDLI .—A. decree of Prince Alexan- 4er hearing to-day's date has been promulgated abolishing the state of siege which has been maintained since the outbreak of the war both in'Easiern Roumelia and Bulgaria *roper. SOFIA, SlM:AL—Prince Alexander to-day telegraphed to the Grand Vizier announcing that he would yield to the will of Europe, while maintaining certain reservations pending the meeting of the Bulgarian Assembly. ;VIENNA, SUNDAT.—There came some rather alarming news from the Greek frontier yesterday. Evoub Pasha was reported to have ordered General Sapnnzaki to evacuate a position which the latter had taken upon Mount Kutra, near Zarkos, on the neutral zone between Greek and Turkish ter- ritory. The Greek General was said to have refused, but this statement has not beemconfirmed to-day, and it is con- sidered a rather favourable•sign that the Turkish and Greek Generals should have commenced negotiations instead of at once coming to blows. ATIIENS,`SONDAY.—After a debate lasting seven days, the Chamber to-day passed a vote of confidence in the Go- -by 129 against 83 votes. There were four blank Wen. ATHENS, MONDAY.—Late last night a great popular demonstration was made before the residence of M. Delv- acnie, the Premier, with the object of expressing joy at the adoption by the Chamber of a vote of confidence in the policy of the Government. The Premier thanked the people for this manifestation of their good-will towards him, and stated that the policy adopted in• September last was not forced on the nation by the Government, but imposed on the (Government by the nation. PERSIA AND TURKEY. TABRIE, •FRIDAY.—II is reported that the Turks have oc- cupied various strategic positions between the provinces of Van and Ooramiah. Extensive preparations continue here. The district horsemen are to be prepared for active service.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MeeNnAv. The House met at a quarter-past four o'clock. MISCMLANEOUS.—In reply to Lord Harris, Lord SUDS- TRY said the Government were prepared to afford facilities for experiments in the growth and preparation of tobacco in the United Kingdom, provided the experiments were undertaken by responsible persons. No one had, however, as yet offered to try the experiments wished for, and it was quite impossible that a general licence should be granted. —The Labourers (Ireland) Acts Amendment Bill was read a second time, after a short discussion, in the course of which the Earl of Wemyss and Lord Ashbourne urged the necessity of a careful conaideration of the details of the bill in Committee. The Contagious Diseases Acts Repeal (No. 2) Bill passed through Committee.—The Prison Officers' Superannuation Bill and the Idiots' Bill were read a third time.—The Poor Relief (Ireland) Bill and Bankruptcy Office Accommodation Act (1885) Amendment Bill passed through Committee.—Earl GRANYILLE stated that it was proposed to adjourn from Friday next to the 6th May for the Easter recess% The House adjourned at 7-10. ROUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNnAr. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONso&C.—Mr. HENRY FOWLER, in answer to a question by Lord Cranborne, said there was no regulation prohibiting Post-office servants from taking part in local or municipaleelections. With regard to Parliamentary elec- tions, the regulations of the late Pcstmaster General were still in force.—Mr. lIIBBERT, in reply to Lord C. Beresford, , was understood to say that the bursting of a Nordenfeldt , gun on board her Majesty's ship Albatross was reported to be due to carelessness. THE HOME RULE DEBATE. The debate on the Home Rule Bill was opened by Lord ReeepoEree Cannel:nue who said the measure involved such complications and contradictions and absurdities that he felt certain that if it had not been introduced by the Prime Minister it would not have been for one moment seriously ' considered. As to the proposed retention of the fiscal unity 1 of the Empire it had been agreed by the Irish party to sell ' to the British' Government and the British Parliament for £1,400,000 a year the inalienable right of a free people that representation and taxation should go together. If the ar- rangement were carried out the Irish Government would have the undisputed control of more than enough money to carry on the government of Ireland without the aid of Par- liament, and it would be open to the Irish Government to dismiss the Parliament and never summon it to Dublin at all. rle held that the principle of this bill was repeal of the Union. Dealing with the restrictions to be impoeed on the Irish Parliament, he said he thought that one of the most inalienable rights of a quasi independent Parliament was the right to pro- vide for its ovem defence, and that the require- ment that the Irish Parliament should have nothing to do with the laws relating to trade and navigatlon be- trayed the most extraordinary ignorance ot Irish history; for what had been the cause of almost every dispute between English and Irish Parliaments but this very deka of the Irish Parliament to control legislation, of this character ? That the Government had been unable to come to any de- cision with regard to the inclusion of Ulster was, in his lordship's opinion, irrefutable proof of the almost insoluble character of the problem of Home Rule. He denied that it was necessary to yield to the strength ef the new Irish party, contending that this was but a temporary strength, as experience preyed that Irish parties were never long- lived.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL (Sir C. Ressell) declared that the only true remedy for the state of Ireland was to give Irishmen the rights of domestic legislation, with an Irish Government re:monsible to and representative of the Irish people. If it ceuld he shown that the inclusion of Irish members in the Imperial Parliament was consistent with the object of this scheme, he hoped, though he had no authority to say so, that Ministers would be open to consi- der that point.—Mr. BURT spoke in favour of the scheme, and advised the Premier, if his proposals were rejected, to appeal to the country.—Mr. Jennings and Mr. Bradlaugh also supported the bill; Major Saunderson, Mr. Whitbread, and Mr. Gibson also addressed the lieuse.—On the motion of Sir W. Harcourt the debate was adjourned. MISCELLANEOUS. The Highways Acts Amendment Bill was read a second time.—Mr. JOHN SMALL intro- duced a bill to amend the law relating to County Courts in Ireland. I The House adjourned at 12-45. HOUSE OF LoaDs.—TcESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. BULGARIA AND THE GREAT POWERS.--The Marquis Of SALISBURY asked for information as to negotiations between Bulgaria and the Porte on the one hand and the Great Powers on the other. and was informed by the Earl of Rosa- salty that upon the sth of April there was signed at Con- stantinople by the representatives of the Great Powers a protocol embodying what is erroneously Called the Sofia Proposal, the effect of which is that the government of Eastern Roumelia shall be confided to the Prince of Bul- garia under the terms of the Pith article of the Treaty of Berlin. Information had been received from Sofia that Prince Alexander. while still maintaining his objections to the conditions which made his appointment as Governor General of Eastern Itournelia subject to renewal at the end of five years with 'the assent of the Powers, has announced to the •Grand 'Vizier that in view of the unanimous decision of the powers he is ready to defer to the authority of the International Act signed by the representatives' and to nominate at once the Bulgarian members of the different Commissions specified in the agreement. Basle FORWABDED.—The reports of amendments to the Bergh Police and Health (Scotland) Bill, the Marriages (Hours of Solemnisation) Bill, and the Sporting Lands Bating (Scotland) Bill were received and adopted. The Contagious Diseases Acts Repeal, No. 2. Bill., and the Bank- ruptcy (Office Accommodation) Act (1885) Amendment Bill were read a third time and passed. Their Lordships adjourned at five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE TARPQRLHY BURIAL CASH—Mr. CHILDERS, in reply to a question from Mr. J. Carvell Williams as to the Tarporley burial case, admitted. that he had bees in error in retying that the Wesleyan minister had expressed his satie- faction with the arrangements at the funeral, and expressed his regret that he had misled the House on that point. div.head: HOME RULE CRISIS.
div.p: THE HOME RULE CRISIS.

! The Press Association has good reason to believe that the resignation of Lord Suffield (Master of Buckhounds) w ill be tendered immediately. The step has been delayed only in accordance with a suggestion from Downing-street. A Yeovil correspondent states that a telegram was received on Thursday night from Lord Kil- coursie, in reference to the rumour that be inter). ded to resign his oppointment as Vice-Chamberlain. His lordship stated that he "would sink or swim with Mr. Gladstone."

• The Queen has been pleased to approve of the ap- pointment of tile Earl of Elgin as First Commis- sioner of Works, in the room of the Earl of Morley, who has resigned; and of the appointment of Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttle worth as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, in the room of Mr. Heneage, who has resigned. Earl Granville, presiding on Wednesday at a house dinner at the National Liberal Club, said he had become convinced that it would be a grave error to give to Ireland any measure which was not fully acceptable, as Mr. Gladstone's scheme was, to the great majority of the Irish people. Lord R. Churchill, speaking at a banquet in his honour at the Beaconsfield Club, on Wednesday evening, expressed the opinion that the Govern- ment of Ireland Bill had pulverised the Liberal party, and alluded with satisfaction to the defec- tions which have taken place. The London correspondent of the "Dublin Ex- press" says :—lt is said that on the passing of the Repeal Bill, Mr. Gladstone will recommend her Majesty to grant an amnesty to a large number of Irish prisoners incarcerated in English and Irish prisons. "United Ireland" says the position is one of tre- mendous peril, for Whig defections will make a fearful gap in the Liberal ranks. There is every reason to anticipate that the second reading is now safe. THE HOME RULE BILL.—The Government of Ireland Bill, introduced by Mr. Gladstone last week, is published. The Bill is divided into two parts. The first consists of twenty-one clauses, of which six deal with legislative authority, two with ex- ecutive authority, three with the constitution of the legislative body, nine with finance, and one with the police. Part two consists of twenty clauses, of which one deals with the powers of Her Majesty. two with the legislative body, one with the decision of constitutional questions, one with the Lord Lieutenancy, four with judges awl civil servants, one with transitory provisions, and ten with miscellaneous provisions. THE OUTLOOK.—The fate of the Home Rule Bill is the subject of much speculation at Westminster, and the most widely divergent opinions are being disseminated from " the lobby." We are assured by one news agency that Lord Hartington is busily en- gaged in constructing an alternative scheme of Irish government which will have the support of many Liberals and all the Conservatives. There seems to be an impression that if the Premier modifies his • scheme to a material extent it will command the votes of a majority of the Liberals and thus pass the second reading. Opinions differ as to the chances of a dissolution in case the bill is rejected. in one quarter an appeal to the country is de- scribed as "certain" in that eventuality, whilst another authority states that the Coalition Government would at once be formed and business proceeded with in Parliament. Speak- ing at Ipswich, Mr. • Mundella said that Mr Gladstone's measure might not be perfect, but it was an honest attempt to settle the Irish problem, and its vital essence was that the Irish people should be free to govern themselves within their own coun- try. The Mayor of Boston, Massachusetts, has tele- graphed to Mr. Gladstone a message from a mass meeting thanking him for his just and wise Irish policy, and expressing profound admiration and respect for him. American opinion is very generally favourable. UNION IST MEETING IN LONDON. A great Unionist meeting was held in her Majesty's Theatre, London, on Wednesday night, under the presidency of Earl Cowper (a former Lord Lieutenant of Ireland), to protest against any vio- lation of the legislative union between Great Britain and Ireland. The Chairman denounced the Government proposals, and protested against the attempt to hand over the government of Ireland to the National League. Lord Hartington, who was very warmly received, moved a resolution protest- ing against the proposal submitted by Mr. Glad- stone. The noble Marquis paid a high tribute to Mr. Gladstone and admitted the sincerity and noble- ness of his purpose, but protested that the Home Rule scheme had been sprung upon the constituencies. If the bill were carried it would be because of the anti- cipations of outrage and violence which would follow its rejection. He did not believe that the bill would be a final settlement of the Irish question. It would substitute for the present Constitution a paper Con- stitution patched together from Various models which, in his judgment, had no application to the circumstances. The prerogatives of the Crown and the sovei eignty of Parliament were to be retained. That meant that we were to retain responsibility for the government of Ireland in the face of the world, whilst we were stripped of all executive and administrative power. The noble Marquis acknow- ledged that he had no cut-and-dried scheme, and that no statesman could see his way to a better and brighter future for Ireland; but that was no reasoa why they should accept blindfold a policy which they held to be no real cure for the evils of Ireland. —Mr. Rylands, M.P., seconded the resolution, and protested specially against the proposal to buy out the Irish landlords.—Lord Fife supported the resolu- tion, and it was carried with almost perfect unanimity.. Lord Salisbury, who had a most enthusiastic greet- ing, said there was no need to apologise for the cOm-- bination of men of various political creeds in defence of their endangered country. The statesman who had always hitherto maintained the integrity of the Empire had now, in obedience to some great dein-- aion or fanatical interpretation of party obligations, wheeled suddenly round. Home Rule, which a year ago was a chimera, was now a burning question. In the recent debate the securities which were sup-- posed to divide this project of Home Rule from a project of absolute separation had been dinven .to, the winds. There was no security for minorities or for the preservation of the fiscal union, and he hoped the conviction was coming home to all that there was absolutely nothing be- tween government at Westminster and inde- pendent and separate Government at Dublin. We wanted a wise, firm, continuous administration of the law, with no turning aside from the straight course of policy on which the people of England should decide. Mr. Goschen, in a short speech, denied that the magic phrase " self-government " would at once remove the manifold difficulties of Ireland. He vigorously condemned any idea of granting Home Rule because of the threats of evil consequences to this country. Mr. Plunket, M.P., Mr. Wodehouse, M.P., and other gentlemen ;also addressed the meeting.

MOONLIGHT OUTRAGE.—On Saturday morning a gang of " Moonlighters" raided upon several houses in the neigh- bourhood of Killarney, demanding money. The men were armed and carefully disguised. They exacted sums at dif- ferent places varying from 15e to £7. One man named Daly, a National School teacher, was fired at as be attempted to escape through a window. " BUBBLES."—It is stated that the last and most beautiful painting from the brush of Sir J. E. lillais. Bt., WA., known as " BAbles," representing a fair-haired child blow- ing sop bubbles from a pipe, has been purchaskd bv the proprietors of the well known Pears' soap for the sum of £2,200. 47e believe the painting is to be the subiect of a show card for Messrs. Pears' business. Too much credit cannot be elven to this enterprising house for the cultured tone they have introduced into advertising. FIRE AT THE BOARD OF TRADE OFFICES.—A fire was discovered shortly after four o'clock on Saturday morning in the room of the commercial branch of the Board of Trade Offices, White! all. The seat of the flames was the centre of the building on the first floor • and the conflagration at one time threatened to envelope the whole department. Several engines were soon on the spot, and it was an hour before it was got under, when it was found that two rooms had been almost wholly desrroyed, and a large mass of official docu- ments damaged. A SURVIVOR OF WATERLOO —The last survivor of Waterloo in Chelsea Hospital, John Mackay, who fought in the ranks of the 42nd Highlanders, enjoys excellent health, and is generally in good spirits. There is little reason to doubt that this sturdy Scot is actually 103 years old. He is a broad-shouldered, big-chested man, below middle height, and is still fairly erect. The old fellow seldom gets up now, not from debility, but because he is getting fat. He likes his pipe and his glass, and occasionally sings a little song after his fashion. His memory is rather "mixed," but otherwise he is wonderfully well. JUMPING FROM A TRAIN.—On Saturday, Daniel Hardy, Burton-on-Trent, was found in the six-foot way in Meir Tunnel, on the North Staffordshire Railway, with his head fractured, both legs broken, and otherwise maimed, having lain in that condition seven hours. When taken to the Infirmary he stated that be suffered from weak serves, and, acting upon medical advice, was going to Liverpool by ex- press for a sea trio. When the train entered the tunnel he became so terrified that he jumped out of the window of the compartment of which be was the sole occupant, and thus met with his injuries.

div.head: --THE EXAMINER.
div.p: --THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY APRIL 17, 1886

HOME Rule for Ireland—to be or not to be; that is the question; and it is a question Which is just now shaking society to its centre. The PRIME MINISTER'S scheme in- volves great constitutional changes, and the Tories are united in opposing it, as they are usually united in opposing great reforms. But the strange thing is to see leading members of the Liberal party not only refusing to fol- low Mr. GLADSTONE' but resolutely en- deavouring to block his path. That Lord RARTINGTON and Mr. GOSCHEN should hesi- tate might be taken as a matter of course; but who that remembers the biting sarcasm With which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, less than twelve months ago, referred to one as Rip VAN WINKLE, and to the other as the Skeleton of the Feast, can fail to be astonished at the sight of the apostle of Radicalism allying himself with HARTINGiON, and GOSCHEN, and CHURCHILL in the attempt to defeat the radical proposals of a Liberal PRIME MINIS- TER! We are not blaming Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN---we• simply point to the extraordinary spectacle. He has a perfect right in such a-grave crisis to exercise independence of Judgement, and equal independence of ex- pression, always assuming, as we do assume, that he is actuated by patriotic and not by Personal motives. We are willing to confess that up to the middle of last year we always looked on Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S plan of giving Ireland Home Rule by developing the prin- ciples of local self-government as-much to be Preferred, as a solution of the Irish problem, to granting a Parliament in Dublin with legislative and administrative functions. Twelve months ago, Ireland,. there is reason to believe, would have accepted such a scheme, and been content to work it for some years. But during twelve months many things have happen(' d, and amongst them a very high Tory bid for Irish votes, which has caused the Nationalists to increase their de-" raands. CHAMBERLAIN and Sir CHARLES Dium should have gone to Ireland to advocate their proposals - but the in- tended visit was suddenly and indefi- zitely postponed. And why ? Because in • the meantime Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL had taken the wind out of their sails; he had fentered into such an alliance with the Par- tellites as caused them to reject the idea of 'contenting themselves with anything less than a Home Rule Parliament. It has not to be forgotten that the Tories . when they came in office paid for Parnellite support by allow- ing the Crimes Act to lapse. They thereby 'Made it all but impossible to resort to coer- cion afterwards; but so incapable were they of governing Ireland when the opportunity 'as given them that, when they came to meet T'arliament in January of this year, the only policy which they had to suggest was the policy they had themselves discarded—the Policy of coercion. From the moment this 'Was seen, their fate was sealed, and they suffered the penalty of their double-dealing and incompetency by being ignominiously turned out of office. They had but a short innings, but they did a great deal of mischief. They made it, we repeat, all but impossible to resort again to repressive legislation, and . thus paved the way for the stupendous bill for the better government of Ireland which is now before the country. With regard to Mr. GLADSTONE?S Home Rule Scheme, we cannot but admit that we feel considerable misgiving as to the work-

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: ing of some of its provisions. Irishmen may be content for a while with directing their energies to the management of purely Irish affairs, and, if the bill pass, there will be plenty for them to do for some years ; but the time must come when they will demand a voice in Imperial affairs, and there, as it seems to us, is the rock ahead. It has been suggested, as one way out of the difficulty, that Ireland might be allowed to send repre- sentatives to Westminster in Proportion to her quota of taxation ; but, as this would give her less than 30 representatives in the Im- perial Parliament, against 90 or so to which she would be entitled on the ground of population, it cannot be said that this would be likely in the end to prove satisfactory to Ireland—to say nothing of the objection that Englishmen. Scotchmen, and Welshmen , might have to even 30 Irishmen having a pie , of their own, and their coming to England to dip into another dish. The PRIME MINISTER in expounding his scheme was understood to refer to the exclusion of Irish representatives from Westminster as a vital point; but in replying on Tuesday night on the whole de- bate he said it was a matter which the Government would regard as open to con sideration. There is reason, therefore, to hope that the measure will, in this important respect, be amended in Committee. It is a matter of suprise—of agreeable surprise, we may say—that the Irish members, do not seem to be in the slightest degree concerned as to the prospect of being relieved of attend- ance at Westminster. Their thoughts are evidently centred upon a Parliament in Dub- lin; and this is exceedingly gratifying as showing that they are earnestly and hope- fully looking forward to the opportunity of fully occupying themselves with legislation and administration in their native land. Nothing could be more emphatic than the affirmative response which the Parnellites made to the question which Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH put on Tuesday night as to whether they would be content with the bill before the House as a final settlement of the question. The cordial acceptance on the part of the people of Ireland of any measure that may be proposed must be taken as a sine qua non; and, looked at from this point of view, the PRIME MINISTER'S scheme leaves every other that has been suggested ridicu- lously in the rear. But apart from this essen- tial consideration, it remains to be said of Mr. GLADSTONE'S plan that the more it is examined the more it is seen that it has been conceived in that spirit of lofty patriotism which marks his unique career, and carried out with that marvellous regard to detail which makes him the first statesman of the age and "Britain's chief of men."

THE Warrington Football team did all that was expected of them on Saturday in beating Aspull in the final tie, and in thus becoming the first winners of the Challenge Cup of the West Lancashire and Border Towns Rugby Union. It has been noticed all through the season how the interest in football was growing in Warrington, "the gates" being larger as team after team were defeated by "WARREN'S lads." Sober- minded steady-going business men who at first hardly liked to own to them- selves that they took great interest in the game got to taking it as a matter of course that they must "see the match ; " and the contagion spread until, we do not hesitate to say, there was more rejoicing on Saturday over the winning of the cup than there was over the passing of the Ship Canal Bill. It was felt that the •real tug of war had come when Warrington and Runcorn met, and both contests between these teams showed how nearly on a level they were with each other. Runcorn having been beaten, there was a disposition amongst outsiders to regard the Aspull team as "small beer ;" but the style in which they held their ground on Saturday showed that the War- rington team, at any rate, had done wisely in not under-rating the strength of their op- ponents. Warrington won what is generally conceded to have been a well-earned victory. Mr. FRANCOMB, in receiving the cup as President of the club, appropriately remarked that the game ought to be played fairly, and with the greatest respect for opponents. This can hardly be too much insisted on, for in a game like football, where physical powers are for the most part called into requisition, there. is a tendency to hardness of feeling as well as of muscle. Saturday, as will be seen from our news columns, was a day of final ties, the most notable being the con- test for the English Cup, under the Association Rules, between Blackburn Rovers and West Bromwich Albion. After playing a drawn game on Saturday week, the two teams met again on Saturday last, and the Rovers won the national trophy for the third time in succession. This is a feat which has not been equalled except by the Wan- derers ; and, indeed, it can hardly be said that the Wanderers have equalled it, for, al- though they carried off the cup for three years in succession, there was no such struggle for it then as there is now-a-days. The Black- burn Olympic team were the first to teach the Londoners a lesson; and with the Blackburn Rovers following on for three years together the Cockneys may be said to have had some of the conceit taken out of them. The West Lancashire Union is in its infancy; but it has offered a splendid cup for competition; and we congratulate the Warrington team on the way in which they won it on Saturday last.

"TOUCH AND GO." The National Press Agency, 13, White- friars-street, London, has published (price one penny) an edition of 60,000 copies of Mr. Gladstone's great speech on introducing his Home Rule measure.

A revised and enlarged edition of the "Popular Guide to the House of Commons" has just been issued from the office of the "Pall Mall Gazette." It is a capital six- pennyworth, and should be in the hands of every politician.

The Welsh electors of the Newton Diyi- s ion are asserting themselves. They wish it to be understood that the Irish are not alone in having grievances to remedy. There is an Established Church in Wales which is about as great an anomoly as the English Church was in Ireland.

"Fair play is a jewel," but the watch is badly jewelled which is presented to the public as one of English make when the case only is English. -Prescot watchmakers are just now suffering from the prevalence of frauds of this kind; and they are making a move with a view to putting an end to these malpractices. They ask to be protected— not from free competition, but from unfair traders.
A contemporary tells us of the wonderful things Protection is doing in the United

Think of that, you horny-handed toilers, who are working 5+ hours and are suffering from Free Trade—think "how delightful it would be" if the Fair Traders could step in and "REDUCE the hours of labour to sixty per week!

• A good son is an angel on earth. PAT- RICK MADDEN Ins a son whom he brought before the St. Helens magistrates, on Wed- nesday, fo r striking him and threatening to knock out his brains. The mother stood UD for her broth of a boy. She said he was "only in drink," and was "as good a son as was ever reared." Fancy half a dozen of such sons—what a heavenly time the family would have of it!

Some of the Burn-ley Liberals are highly indignant at the course their representative, Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., has taken in join- ing the opponents of Mr. Gladstone's bill. It is but just to Mr. Rylands to say that dur- ing the campaign of the General Election he was emphatic in declaring that he was op- posed to a separate Parliament for Ireland. He may have taken up a wrong position, and we think he has, but he is at least sticking' to his gun.

Professor Huxley, talking not practical but unpractical politics, ploughs his way like an engine off the track. "Government by aver- age opinion," he says, "is merely a circui- tous method of going to the devil." But what is government without average opinion? Is it a direct method of going the wrong way? Professor Huxley should not have put on the prophet's mantle in order to shriek like Carlyle at his worst. He looks much better in his plain coat, making plain the mysteries of ,science in his own quiet way.

The defeat of Mr. Darbyshire in the Guar- dians ejection is reacting on the Conserva- tive .party—it is so scandalous in many of its features. There is at least one Conserva- tive who is ashamed of what has been done, and he makes the suggestion "that steps be taken with the object of Mr. Darby- shire's appointment as a county magis- trate, in which position he would be a most useful public man, and also an ex-officio Guardian." This is an excellent idea; it would be a fitting acknowledgment of fifteen years' faithful service; and a compliment to the tenant farming class of which Mr. Darby- shire is a typical representative.

The agriculturalists of Germany are "pro- tected," but Protection has not proved to be their salvation. In reply to a demand for further prohibitive duties, tbe Minister of Agriculture was constrained to admit, on Monday, that "the introduction of a duty on wool, although it. might be beneficial to agriculture, would be a severe blow to the woollen trade." Really now, how can this be? The Fair Traders must explain. If a duty is put upon everything, everybody will be protected and prosperous. That is the Fair Trade doctrine—is it not? Or is it the agriculturalist alone—thc; happy farmer—who is to be neglected while everybody else is " protected."
POORS RATE FOR atvrorr.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magistrates siened a new poors rate of 9d in the £ to realise £155 9s 10i for the township of Clif- ton.

RE•OPENING OF Sr. PAUL'S CIP,PEL, RUNCJRN.—The services in connection with the reopening of St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel were continued on Sunday, when there crowded oongrega- ions. NELSON STREET BADTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES--Tin Rev. R. Yeatman, on Sunday, preached twe specirl sermons under the titles 'Witnesses for good " and "The rich fool." The interest in these discourses still continues. Tug WIDNES VOLUNTEERS.—The 21st Lancashire Rifle Yolunteers will this year go into camp at Southport for ex- ercise and instruction, from June 11th to June 184 h. The Government allowance to the corps on this account is £237 He COURT MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN.—Livermore's Court Minstrels, on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, •performed in Runcorn Public Hall to moderately good audiences, who were not slow to show their appreciation of the capital en- tertainment arranged for their delectation. FOOTBALL AT RUNCORN.—A match between the second teams of the Runcorn and Widnes Clubs took place on the Runcorn ground' on Thursday in the presence of a large assembly of spectators, who cheered with an impartiality that was commendable. A very even game resulted in a victory for Runcorn by one goal and two minors to one minor. The goal which was obtained from a try was a very " fluky " one. Riley for Runcorn and Stirrup for Widnes were the shining lights amongst the backs. WIDNES SCHOOL SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to Widnes School Board on Wednesday at Widnes Petty Sessions prosecuted the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school e-Eliaa- beth Sparkes, Thomas Rowles, George Whitley, Elias Roberts, Thomas Burke, Wm. Fallon. Philip Riley. John Smith, Anthony Armstrong, Peter Ford, Jno. .Mularkey. and Peter McLoughlin. The usual penalty of 5s was im- posed in each case. • PRESENTATION AT. THE MERSEY MISSIONS, RUNCORN.—A social tea party was held at the Mersey Mission Room, on Wednesday evening, those present being workers and Sun- day school teachers. During the evening Mrs. Hodson, a Sunday school teacher was presented with a beautifully bcinnd volume of "Pilgrim's Progress" on behalf of her fellow teachers, as a mark of their respect on her leaving Runcorn. Mr. W. Shaw occupied the chair, and the presen- tation was made by Mr. Allen. Mrs. Littler responded on behalf of the recipient. MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF A SEAMAN AT RUNCORN. —On the afternoon of Saturday, 3rd inst., a seaman named John Coram, of Teignmouth, about 25 years of age, unmar- ried, then serving on board the schooner " Rare Plant," of Padstow, left his vessel at Weston Point Docks for the pur- pose of transacting some businees in Runcorn, and as he has not since turned up at his vessel it is conjectured he has been drowned somewhere on the route between Runcorn and Weston Point, as the canal between these two places is insufficiently lighted. He was last seen leaving Runcorn about 11 p.m. the same evening. His clothing, wages, &c., have been handed over to the Customs Authorities till claimed by his 'nearest relatives. SACRED CONCERT AT DZINCORN.—The Runcorn Parish Church Glee Class brought a successful season to a close on Thursday night, when they gave a sacred concert in the National Schools, to a numerous audience. The first part of the excellent programme consisted of Dr. Stainer's can- tata, "The Daughter of Jairup," and we have nothing,but praise for the chorus. Precision, expression, and harmony prevailed throughout its performance, and Mr. Warhato, the conductor, is to be congratulated upon the succ•-ss of his efforts. The recitatives were taken by Miss Hampson and Miss Howard. and these ladies acquitted themselves with an ability that elicited marks of cordial appreciation from the audience. The bass solos were rendered with care and appreciation by Mr. Gates, and Mr. James Littler sang '' 'My hope is in the everlasting" with much feeling and ex- pression. A pretty piece of vocalisation was the duet, "Love Divine," by Miss Howard and Mr. Littler, and the enthusiastic encore accorded the vocalists was well deserved. The second part of the concert consisted of miscellaneous items. Mr. Warham sang the air, "Come up hither ; " Miss Hampson, "Behold, I stand at the door;' Mr. W. Pownall, Our Blest Redeemer;" Miss Howard, "Angels ever bright and fair;" Mr. Joule, "Nazneth ;" Miss Good- well, " He wipes the tears from every eye;" the glee class, Lead kindly light." Miss Hampson and Miss Goodwell were honoured with recalls. Mr. Joule sang with power and feeling. Mr. S. Wadsworth was an efficient accom- panist. MARRIED INFELICITY AT WlDNES.—Margarat Harrison summoned her husband, Joseph Hanson, to Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday on a charge of using threatening language. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the complainant and said the parties had been marriei 12 years, and they had been blest or cursed with five children, all of whom were quite young. During all that period they had net lived happily together, and on two or three occasions the defendant had sold the furniture and gone away from his wife. On one occasion he was away for nine months. For five years when together they had lived with the com- plainant's mother. Ten weeks ago the defendant without any great provocation thrashed his wife and left her, and she went to the Workhouse. She, however, left that insti- tution and again went to live with her mother. The defen- dant promised the relieving officer to pay lOs per week to- wards the maintenance of his children, but all he had paid during their separation was 15s. Last Saturday he made an appointment to meet his wife near the Central Hotel. He was, however, drunk, and she had to take refuge in a shop from his violence. He subsequently followed her home and threatened he would have her life.—The complainant swore that she was afraid of her life.—The defendant said his wife would not live with him so long as her mother lived. He was willing to keep his wife but not all her family, he hadn't married eleven of them—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for two months, himself in £lO and two sureties of a each. FELONIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, James Rourke and Frank Grayson, each aged 11 years, were charged with stealing a loaf, value 9d, the pro- perty of Mr. Richard Webster, provision dealer, Widnes- road. The loaf was on the top of a boiler were the bake- house on Tuesday night at eight o'clock, and was after- wards missed. At half-past two o'clock next morning P.C. 201 found the prisoners in a covered cart which was stand- ing in Back Salisbury-street. They had the loaf with them, and a cheque which had been also missed. Each prisoner was sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod. Margaret Hynan, an elderty woman, Mary. Ann Hynao, a young woman, mother and daughter, and Peter Keenaghan, a young man' were each charged with stealing or receiving shawls worth 3s 6d, the property of Mr. Richard Tebbutt, draper, Victoria-road. The shawls were taken from the door Of the shop, on Saturday night, the 10th inst., and subsequently Keenaghan gave one to a young girl named Mary Riley, who lives in Wellington-street, and each female prisoner was wearing one of the stolen articles when appre- hended by P.C. Holbrook. Mary Ann said a young man she did not know gave her the shawls, and Keenaghan said he found one hidden in some straw behind Mr. Lea's stables. The mother was discharged, and the other prisoners were each sentenced to a months's hard labour.—Mary Jane Doyle, a young woman, was charged with stealing a shawl, value 3s 6d, the property of Thomas Fleming, of 22, Bed- ford-street, and she was sentenced to one month's hard labour. BRUTAL KICKING CASE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, George Hayes, a labourer, about 40 years of age, was charged with maliciously wounding his brother-in-law, William Dem:lett, a wiredrawer' of 22, Tithe- barn-street, Appleton. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, defen- ded. It was alleged that on the afternoon of the 15th March the prisoner went to the door of Dennett's house and made use of foul language towards Mrs. Dennott. Bennett said if the-prisoner used the words again he would make him pay for it. Upon this, the prisoner struck Dennett on the chest, knocking him to the ground. He then kicked him several times on the legs. Upon rising Dennett found he could not use his left leg, and was leaning against the wall, when the prisoner seized him by the scarf, dragged him several yards across the road, threw him to the floor, and again kicked him. Dennett was helped into the house by his wife, and next morning Dr. McCambridge was sent for. The doctor discovered that Dennett was suffering from a fracture of the left leg above the ankle. His leg was also bruised, and so swollen that the splints could not be applied until the following Sunday. He would not be able to use the left leg for another month. The prisoner was appre- hended on the previous day by P.C. Almond, and in answer to the charge said "It was a drunken do."—lu cross-examination by Mr. Knowles the prosecutor said if the prisoner would make him some compensation he should be quite satisfied. He did not want him sent to prison.— Mr. Knowles appealed to the Bench to deal with the case as one of common assault; and besides imposing a small fine, order the prisoner to give some compensation.—The Bench , committed the prisoner to the Quarter Cessions for trial. WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY.—The members of this society gave their last concert of the season in Lacey-street School on Thursday evening. There was only' a moderate attend- ance. The first part of the programme consisted of the following selections from Mendelssehn's "St. Paul ": Chorus, "Lord thou art God"; recit. Miss Sowerbutts, "And many that believed " ; chorus, "Now this man ceaseth not to utter blasphemous words " ; air, Miss Sowerbutts, " Jerusalem that killest " ; recit. Mr. Carey, " And they stoned Him " ; chorale, "To Thee 0 Lord " ; chorus, "Happy and blest " ; recit. Mr. Carey, "And Saul made havoc of the church"; air, Mr. Lea, "Consume them all " ; recit. and air, Miss Johnson, " But the Lord is mindful of His own " ; chorale, "Sleepers wake " ; solo (Mr. Lea) and chorus, "I praise Thee 0 Lord" ; recit, "And Paul came to the congregation"; chorus, "How lovely are the messengers" ; air. Mr. Carey. " Be thou faith- ful unto death " ; chorus, "0 great is the depth." The renderings of the chorus and principals were above the average, and were much enjoyed by those present. Mr. Argent conducted with his usual ability; and the accom- panists were Miss Greenall, of Birkenhead (pianoforte), and Mr. W. A. Watts, M.A. (harmonium.) The second part consisted of miscellaneous items, and opened with the glee "Merry boys away, away" by the choir. An enthusiastic recall rewarded Mr. and Miss Argent for the skilful execu- tion of the duet (piano and violin) "William Tell." A charming interpretation of "Lo hear the gentle lark" by Miss Greenall was encored, and a similar mark of favour was awarded Mr. Morrison for a capital rendering of the ballad "Then you'll remember me." Miss Argent perfor- med a violin solo with much skill. Misses Leatharbarrow and Johnson sang "In the dusk of twilight" with consider- able expression,and were recalled, and Miss Bond was loudly applauded for an effective vocalisation of "Voices of the woods." The glee, "0 by rivers," brought the concert te a elm.

ADDRESSES TO WORKINGMEN AT WIDNES.—The Rev. R. G. Hughes preached the second of a series of addresses to workingmen and their wives in Milton Congregational Chapel on Sunday. The title of the discourse wa2 "The busy little member." RUNCORN STARR BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETIES —ln connection with these societies, two appropriations took place in Bethesda Schoolroom on Tuesday night. The result was that Mr. William Cartwright, of South Bank, re- ceived an allotment of £2OO, and the son of Mr. Williams,- butcher, Ellesmere Port, an allotment of £lOO.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—At this Court on Wednesday, William Barlow, a sailer, and two women, named Mary Jane and Elizabeth Basnett, were charged with stealing 121bs. of pork from the ship Alert, lying at Weston Point. A tine of £1 was imposed upon each. Prisoner Barlow paid, and the women went to gaol for a fortnight. THE RETIREMENT OF MR.' F. SAMONS FROM THE CUS- TOMS.—The Committee of the Royal National Life Boat Institution have, through the Commissioners of her Majesty's Customs, presented Mr. F. Samons, late collector of Customs and hon. secretary to the Lifelaoat Institution, Runcorn, on his retirement from the service, after serving upwards of 40 years, their vote of thanks, recarded on vellum and beautifully framed. FIGHTING FOREIGNERS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Wednesday Joseph 'Jouster' a Pole, who lived in Cromwell-street, was charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm upon another Pole, named Charles Merchant Cavish, who lives in Wellington-street. Inspector Wood said the prosecutor had bad to be conveyed to Virhiston Workhouse Hospital, and he asked that the prisoner should be remanded. The prisoner was remanded for a fortnight. WIDNES NATIONALISTS AND THE HOME hULE SCHEME.— On unday afternoon last, at the meeting of the Widnes Branch of the National League, the following resolution was passed on the motion of Dr. O'KeEfie :—" That we recog- nise in Mr. Gladstone's scheme of Home Rule an honest attempt to deal with this all-important subject, and we be- lieve, with certain amendments, it is capable of satisfying the legitimate aspirations of the Irish people. We tender to the right honourable gentleman cur heartfelt thanks for this, his message of peace, to our distracted country."

SALVATION Aunt MARRIAGE CELEBRATION AT RUN. comq.—There were great rejoicings amongst the members of the Salvation Army at Runcorn, on Tuesday, on the oc- casion of the marritge of "Captain" Moore with " Cap- tain " Fanny Goodwin. Tille marriage as by law established took place at Frodsham in the morning. In the afternoon, at the Forester's Hall, a "Wedding banquet " was partaken of, by a good number, and subsequently an outdoor proces- sion took place. The band of the Widnes and Runcorn corps headed the parade. In the evening the "Salvation wedding " of the happy couple was celebrated, Major Sowerby, of the Liverpool and Cheshire Division, officiat- ing. Addresses were delivered by several captains appro- priate to the occasion, and hymns were also sung. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery on Wednesday, Mr. W. Littler pre- siding. Present—Messrs. Moss, Whittaker, • Rogerson, Coleburn, Imison, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The Secretary reported that during the year ended the 25th March there had been 336 interments, against 381 in the previous year. The fees received showed a reduction of £67 16e 31. Since the cemetery was opened on the Ist March, 1860, there had been 7,116 in,erments, viz :—Dis- senters, 3,663; Church of England, 2.870; Roman Catho- lics, 583. On Thursday evening the annual ratepayers' meeting for the purpose of receiving the accounts of the . Board was held in Bethesda Schoolroom. Mr. W. Sutton presided, and there were only three other persons present. The balance sheet was adopted, and a copy will be found in our advertising columns. t CEYLONESE EXHIBITION AT MANCHESTEB.—TIIIS exhibition, for the accommodation of which very elaborate preparations are being made in the Agil- cultural Hall, Pomona, is announced to open on Wednesday next, the 21st inst, and will remain open for several weeks. We refer the reader to our advertising columns for details. . THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO LIVERPOOL.—The Queen has intimated her intention of prolonging her visit to Liverpool. Her Majesty will arrive on the 11th May, and instead of leavincr, on the following day, as she at first intended, will remain until the 13th. The City Council, en Wednesday, formally sanc- tioned an application from the military authonties for permission to encamp half a battalion of infan- try in Newsham Park. The soldiers will furnish guards and escorts during her Majesty's stay in the city. . OPENING OF AN INDEPENDENT METHODIST -MIS- SION-ROOM.—A mission-room in connection with the Independent Methodists of the Warrington Circuit Was opened at 15, Bridge-street, Earlestown, on Sunday, when in the afternoon and evening services appropriate to the association were con- ducted by _Messrs. Thomas Holbrook and W. llud- son of Warrington. There were encouraging atten- dances, and a cordial ' invitation was extended to all who attended the services, which it was an- nounced would be continued each Sunday afternoon and evening. THE BANKRUPTCY OF A CHEST-1111:g WHEEL- WRIGHT.--At Warrington County Court, on Thurs- day, Edward Pennington, wheelwright, Preston Brock, came before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes on his adjourned examination in • bankruptcy. Mr. Fox, from the office of Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., said that he was instructed by the bankrupt to ask that an answer, given to a question put by the Official Receiver, should be altered. Mr. Fox said that the question referred to an item of ..ClO which was deposited with his firm by the brother of the bankrupt as a guarantee for costs. The bankrupt had nothing to do with it, the money did not pass through his hands, and it was deposited on condi- tion that it was to be returned if not required. He asked that the case should be adjourned to allow of the attendance of the brother to confirm this. Mr. Worsley, deputy official receiver, intimated that he had no questions to ask; and his Honour adjourned the examination until the 6th of May. THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER'S FAREWELL OF AUSTRALIA.—The Adelaide Register has the following telegram from Melbourne, under date 7th March: —" Mrs. Moorhouse, the wife of Bishop Moorhouse, was on Saturday presented with an illuminated ad- dress and a souvenir in the shape of a diamond brooch and pendant, subscribed for by the ladies of ' the diocese. Lady Stowell made the presentation. The Bishop preached his farewell sermon this morn- ing at St. James's Cathedral, which was crowded, hundreds of persons being unable to get admission. Dr. Moorhouse preached a very eloquent sermon from the words, ' And now abideth faith, hope, and charity, these three, but the greatest of these is charity." He asked from his hearers their sympathy in the new work to which he was going, and their prayers that he might be made a more faithful Minister of Jesus Christ. The congregation were visibly affected." Dr. Moorhouse is expected to ar- rive in London on Monday evening or Tuesday morn- ing next.

THE PRESCOT WATCH TRADE.—On Wednesday evening, a meeting of the watchmakers and others interested in the trade was held at the Assembly Rooms, Prescot, "to consider the best means to improve the trade, and •to adopt resolutions there- on." Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., presided, and there was a large attendance.—The Chairman said though he was not in the trade himself, he knew it to be in a very depressed condition. It was not practic- able with the present fiscal arrangements of the country to put any duty upon watches; but they might ask for protection of another kind—protec- tion of their trade against the brand of the foreigner and he was afraid he must say against the malprac- tices of some of their own people. (Applause.)— Mr. T. P. Hewitt proposed "That the deplorable state of the trade at present is largely owing to the practice which has sprung up in recent years of placing foreign movements in English-marked cases, and thus far causing the public to believe that they are purchasing watches of English make; and, inasmuch as the reputation of English makers . thereby . damaged, and the public grossly deceived, it is desirable that a measure should be passed in Parliament making this practice illegal, and im- posing heavy penalties for any infringement of the law." He maintained that they were perfectly justified in asking that nothing but English manu- factured goods should have the Hall mark.—Mr. C. B. Johnson seconded the motion, and said the Goldsmith's Company were willing to assist the English watchmakers in any efforts they might make, and were wishful they would succeed n pre- venting the improper stamping of foreign cases.— i The resolution was carried amid applause.—Mr.. T. S. Preston moved—" That, in the opinion cf this meeting, a serious injury is caused to the English watch trade by English shopkeepers putting their own name to watches of foreign manufacture and selling them as of their own make, thereby leading purchasers to believe that they are buying watches of English make, and that, with the view of pre- venting this fraudulent practice, it is desirable to form a trade association, or committee, to consider what action it may be necessary to take, in the in- terests of the trade, on the Merchandise Marks Bill being submitted to Parliament."—Mr. J. Robinson seconded the resolution, which was carried.—A committee was subsequently formed to carryout the objects of the association, and the proceedings closed with the usual votes of thanks.

WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.—The number of drawings sent from the School of Art. this year to compete for marks, certificates, and prizes reaches a total of 3,450, there being 3,150 art drawings, and 300 science drawings. The number of drawings iient this time last year was 2,988.
