WIDNES MAY DAY PROCESSION ASSOCIATION.— The Secretary of the May Day Procession Association has received the following letter from T. C. Edwards-Moss, Esq., M.P. :—" Sir, I beg to enclose a postal order for £1 as my subscription to your association, which I trust you will accept with my best wishes for the success of their seventh celebration.— I am, yours faithfully, T. C. EDWARDS- MOSS." STARE PLATS AT RUNCORN PIIBLIC HALL.—A special session was held at Runcorn on Monday, the magistrates being Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, Messrs. A. Thomas, C. Reynolds' and F. Rigby, for the purpose of hearing an ap• plication by Mr. A. SallMd for a license to perform stage plays in the Public Hall. The license was granted, and Messrs. W. Whittaker and W. F. Salkeld were sworn as sureties. ELECTION OF RUNCORN GUARDIANS.—The votes in the I contested election for the township of Runcorn were counted at Dutton yesterday week, by Mr. H. Linaker, the return- ing officer' with the following result :—Messrs. William Whittaker 982; Samuel Taylor, 900; Philip Speakman, $55; William Fisher, 843; William Farrell, 723; Robert Shaw, 596. The five first-named gentlemen were certified as duly elected. ROUNDERS.—Sinim's Cross v. St. John's, Liverpool: This match was played on the ground of the latter in Newsham Park, on Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for the visitors by an innings and 12 runs. Score :—Simm's Cross (one innings): W Smart, 0; J Rvlands, 1; J Lomax, 1; W Pearce, 1; W Baggridge, 8; J Real?, 5 ; J Ford, 3; W Lomax, 8; W Lamb, 9; T Harrison, 1; II Rice, 1; extras, 3; total, 41.—St. John's (two innings) : H Warburton, 7; W Bramham, 3; W Burton, 0; W Brumpton' 1; W Brown, 1; G Pendleton, 8; G Pierpoint. 0; Cr Crierie, 0; R Gran, 3; T A Bramham, 1; A C Allsop, 3; extras, 2; total, 29. ACTION AGAINST A WIDNES FRIENDLY SOCIETY.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday George Plumpton, of Crow-wood, summoned the trustees of the Farnworth Friendly Society for £7 for sick pay. Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Heler.s, said he was instructed for the plaintiff, and Mr. &gar, barrister, instructed by Mr. J. W. Knowles, was for the defendant. They had come to terms which were satis- factory to his client, and he thought also to the defendants. The summons would with their worships' permission be , withdrawn. It appeared that in 1869 the society agreed to pay Plumpton' who was then incapacitated.from work, 3s 6d for the rest of his natural life. It was thought at that time that he was permanently disabled, but he had since re- , covered, and the society repudiated the agreement. The settlement affected was to pay the complainant £6 Gs and costs, the agreement to be cancelled and the complainant to take his position in the society as an ordinary .nember. ENGLAND 100 YEARS AGO.—Under this title the Rev. J. Colwell, of Liverpool, on Monday evening lectured to a good congregation,in Victoria-road Chapel, Widnes. Mr. B. ' Brown presided, and expressed his regret that Mr.R. Shaw, of Runcorn, who had been announced to occupy the chair, was unable to attend. Although he was not doing God's work at Widnes, hewas doing God's work at Runcorn. As most of them were aware, the proceeds of that lecture would go towards providing for Lacey-street school a read- room, increasing the number of books in their library, and providing an improved library cupboard :for the custody of the books. The contemplated outlay was about £llO, and they had now got the promise of between £7O and £BO, and the proceeds of that lecture would considerably increase the amount. (Applause.) The Itev. J. Colwell then delivered his lecture in which he dealt with the political, social, and intellectual condition of England 150 years ago in a manner which frequently elicited applause. He described the political corruption which prevailed 150 years ago, the dense ignorance of the masses, the drunkenness of all classes from the peer to the peasant, and the absurdities of the attire of both male and female were touched upon. On the proposition of Mr. Swale, seconded by Mr. T. Sadler, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Colwell. A similar compliment was also paid to the chairman. FOOT RACES AT ST. HELENS.—rOn Saturday afternoon two important maches were decided at the Star Inn Recrea- tion Grounds, St. Helens. The first was between J. E. (alias Choppy ") Warburton and J. Concannon. of Wid- nes, who met to run four miles for £25 aside, " Choppy " conceding his more youthful opponent a start of 50 yards. Both men are well known, and Warburton's performances on the running path extends over a long period. A con- siderable amount of interest was evinced in the match, as there was a capital attendance. Warburton was made ft warm favourite, odds of 6 to 4 being laid on him. An ex- cellent start was effected. but Warburton seemed to gain but little on his opponent until the half distance, when he de- creased the gap considerably. Entering the last mile War- burton was within a few yards of his opponent, but although he drew level with him several times, the veteran was unable to get past. The pair were running side by side, and cries were heard on all sides of "Choppy ' wins," when the latter all at once was seen to fall, and the race was at an end. Before be bad risen Concannon was some 50 yards in front, and, as Warburton then retired, Concannon walked the remaining distance, and was declared the winner. —Afterwards a race, distance 100 yards, for £5O, wee de- cided between Thomas Smith, of Whiston, and George Cook's novice, of Prescot. Smith was trained at his own home, and Cook's novice at the Navigation Inn, St. Helena. Wilkinson got the men away to a beautiful start, and al- though Smith seemed to be winning well after going u eighty yards, he faltered a few yards from the tape, and Cook's novice got p and won a most exciting race by a
foot. CHLOBO-LINSEED COUGH LOZENGES. medicated linseed tract. 64; postage. 24. Kay Bros.. Stockport. and all Chemist.. —Advt.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday at Alforde Chambers. There were present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. J. Houghton, S. S idler, H. Gaskell, jun., J. Taylor, F. Heves, B. Dutton, D. Vright, E. Cirey, 'l'. Hindley, B. Brown, J. I'. Allen (clerk), 1. Girt. (engineer), Higgiuson (surveyor), Dickson (inspector).

div.head: ELECTION.
div.p: THE ELECTION.

The Chairman reported the result of the recent election, and remarked that there were more papers delivered than in 1885, and a very great many less bad ones returned. In 1885 there were 415 papers returned blank, and this year 665-1 considerable increase.—Mr. Gaskell remarked that unpaid canvassers accounted for that.—The Chairman said there were about 200 more papers than in 1885.—Mr. Carey : More 'musts, I suppose.—Mr. Wright: There are more houses tenanted than there were last year.—Mr. Carey: That is very gratifying.—The Chairman went on to say that the expeopps of the contest amounted to £O7 17s 6cl. as against £74 7s 61 last year. (Hear, hear.) He must express his pleasure that the amount was reduced. and ' also the opinion that the cost of these elections should he still further reduced.—Mr. Carey: In what way, Mr. Chair- man ?—The Chairman : I think in regard to refreshwents. —Mr. Carey: Oh.—On the motion of Mr. Handley,seconded by Mr. Wright it was decided that a cheque be drawn for the returning officer's expenses.

div.head: INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.

The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, who formally sanctioned the borrowing of £2,600 for an infectious disea,es hospital, and stated that it would be unnecesary to hold an inquiry when it was decided to spend the further sum of £l4OO in carrying out the coin• plete plans at some future period —Mr. Handley moved, and Dr. O'Keeffe sec nded a resolution that the amount sanctioned be borrowed, and it was carried.

div.head: FREE LIBRIkRY.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRIkRY.

A letter was also read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the borrowing of £7OO for the building of a public library, and it was resolved to borrow that sum, on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Heyes.

div.head: GREAT SAVING OF WATER
div.p: GREAT SAVING OF WATER

IThe minutes of the Gas and Water Committee stated that the mean rainfall for the month had been l•SSO inches, and on the 24th March there was in stock 5,353,433 gallons of water. The illuminating power of the gas during the month I had averaged 17*13 candles.—Mr. Gaskell, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said a Deacon's Waste Water Meter had been fixed at the corner of Ann-street and Lugs- dale-road, and also at West Bank. So far the meters had given extremely satisfactory results. At Sutton's-lane, where they first put one in, one half of the water previously supplied to that district was waste. The waste amounted to 100 gallons per hour; the committee had now succeeded in reducing the waste to 100 gallons per hour, through the use of the meter. At West Bank the waste was about 1.000 gallons per hour, but as the meter had only just been got in working order it was impossible to say what the reduc- tion would be, but the committee hoped to save nearly all the waste water. They expected to save 1,500 gal- lons per hour, which at the cost price of 2d gave a saving of over £lOO per annum. At the selling price of 5d per 1,000 gallons, the saving would be nearly .-C3OO per annum. The cost of the two meters was from £75 to £BO. The meter was the invention of Mr. U. F. Deacon, the water engineer of Liverpool.—Mt. Wright seconded the motion, which was carried. IMPORTANT HIGHWAY MATTERS.. _

The Surveyor reported to the Highway Committee that after the snowstorm of the Ist March 2500 loads of snow were taken off the roads. The Committee recommended that the offer of Mr. R. Bradshaw to sell land required for the widening of Birchfleld-road, about 280 yards at Sc per yard be accepted. Mr. J. Valentine offered to sell about 300 yards of land at 3s 6d per yard for the widening of Albert-road, Halton View. Recommended that the offer be accepted. Mr. G. Tienbath drew attention to the recent deviation in the building line of streets, and it was recom- mended that a petition be sealed and sent to the House of Commons asking that a clause be inserted in the Public Health (Improvement Expenses) Bill now before Parlia- ment, providing for uniformity in the line of buildings. A plan showing approach road to Farnworth Bridge and pro- posed alteration was submitted. The committee recom- mended that the alteration be not made. NT, S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Union, had forwarded a copy of letter from the Local Government Board respecting relief labour. Tbe Clerk was instructed to reply that the Local Board had for several months been doing what the Local Government Board suggested, but were quite w fling to confer with the Guardians on the subject. it was recommended that the salary of Mr. T. Hughes, assistant to the surveyor, be in- creased by 5s per week. It was decided that application be made to borrow a further sum of £1,650 for ten years for private street improvements. The estimate of the commit- tee's expenses for the six months ending 30th September next was approved.—Mr. 'Carey moved the adoption of the minutes, and said the fencing of Lugsdale-road would cost about 2s per yard. He referred to a statement prepared by Mr. Higginson showing the cost of road making in the township. The roads during 1885 had cost £55 per mile to keep in repair. The Board possessed about 30 miles of road.—Mr. Sadler seconded the motion.—Mr. Wright, refer- ring to Farnworth Bridge, said some years ago the railway company promised to carry out that road as nearly level as possible, with a width of 42 feet. It seemed because an ' official of the Board's failed to carry out the instrucions he , received from the the Board, the railway company took ad- vantage of the Board, and were determined net to do the work. Although perhaps not legally bound, the railway I company was morally and honourably bound to construct the road as promised.—Mr. Brown inquired why part of Deacon's road was made and then left ?-3.1r. Carey replied that the Clerk was negotiating with the landowners to obtain the land necessary to finish the road.—The minutes were passed.
THE NIGHTSOIL CONTRACT: IMPORTANT SUGGESTION.

The Health Committee's minutes contained the report of the medical officer, who stated that daring March /here were 107 births and 53 deaths, being at the rate respectively of 46.69 akd 23.12 per 1,000. The deaths occurred amongst children under one year, and 12 between one and five years. There were four inquests. Nightsoil Work: A letter dated 6th April was read from E. Percy referring to recent come plaints of neglect, and anthorising additional penalties in case of future neglect. E. Percy also attended, and stated that the recent snow and frost had delayed him. He was informed that unless arrears of work are cleared up. and current work in a satisfactory state, before the next meet- ing, probably the Board would be advised to take the con- tract out of his hands.—The estimate of the committee for the six months ending 30th September next was £598 163. —Dr. O'Keeffe moved the adoption of the minutes. He re- marked that the committee were still of opinion that it would be advisable to abolish the charge of is per day to patients in the Accident Hospital, but they had determined to leave the question to the new Board. He hoped the nightsoil contractor would ful fit his promise to conduct his contract in a more efficient manner.—Mr. Dutton said the nightsoil question ought to be dealt with in a more drastic manner than had been the custom in the past. Owners of property and tenants were constantly making complaints. Mr. Dutton expressed himself in favour of the nuisance in- spector having entire control of the nightsoil department of the whole district.—Mr. Gaskell drew attention to the filthy condition of the back passages. Frequently the men em- ployed by the Gas and Water Committee had to remove a toot of nightsoil before they could get to a stopcock.—Mr. Brown remarked upon the difficulties the contractor had recently had to encounter. He did not consider it fair to I put the blame of the state of the back passages upoh the contractor. He thought the back passages should be paved, and then they would be kept clean.—Mr. Gaskell said he did not blame the contractor, but the committee who were responsible to the Board.—Mr. Sadler said if Mr. Brown would step 20 yards from his works he would find a back passage 15 inches out of level through the cause mentioned by Mr. Gaskell. He referred to Back Victoria-street. —Dr. O'Keeffe thought the measures a`doptel by the committee would cause the contractor to pay more attention to his work. He was of opinion that if back passages were paved the laying of nightsoil in them would be to a great extent prevented. It was a matter worthy the attention of the Highway Committee, who he considered should see that the back passages of new streets were made.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: FINANCE. On the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Wright, the minutes of the Finance Committee, who recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £3,224 4s Bd, were passed.
div.p: FINANCE. On the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Wright, the minutes of the Finance Committee, who recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £3,224 4s Bd, were passed.
PARLIAMENTARY _PETITIONS.

The General -Purposes Committee ,recommended that a petition be sealed and forwarded to the House of Commons, against the Borough Funds Bill now pending, which pro- poses to do away with the sanction of the ratepayers before the promoting or opposing of bills in Parliament by local authorities ; and that a petition be sealed and forwarded to the House of Commons in favour of the principle of the Waterworks Rating Bill now pending before that House.— Mr. Carey, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said it was the opinion of the committee that the feeling of the Board at the last meeting was that £lOO should not be ex- pended upon purchasing books for the Library at present, and the committee therefore bowed to that :decision, and had not given the matter further consideration.

LIJOSDALE BRIDGE. Mr. Wright drew attention to the fact that the railway company bad lengthened their wall at the Warrington-road side of Lugsdale Bridge, and the approach was made so narrow that it could be conveniently stopped with a gate. Either a dozen yards of the wall would have to be removed or several of the houses on the other side.—Mr. Carey said he was very much obliged to Mr. Wright. The Highway Committee would visit the spot on the earliest opportunity

SINGING THE PRAISES OF WIDNES. Mr. Carey, at the conclusion of the business, proposed a cordial vote of thanks to the Chairman for the way in which he had conducted the business of the Board during the past year, and the way in which be had presided over their deliberations. He had been a member of the Board for a good many years, and he did not remember a single year in which they got through the business in a more satisfactory manner than they had done this year. He thought it was greatly due to Mr. Gossage's unvarying courtesy and kindmss to the members. They had all had their say, and he believed they had all had fair play.—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded the motion with great pleasure. He could only reiterate what had been said by Mr. Carey, that it was owing to his (the chairman's) bonhomie. his tact, and his ability in conducting the affairs of the Board that such a great amount of excellent work bad been done. The Highway Committee, over which Mr. Carey presided as chairman had had the principal portion of the work in their hands, and he knew that a great deal indeed had been done

in that department which was of immense beneßt to the ratepayers There was the very heavy wcik of the sewer to c irry on, and they had had to make roads. In his opinion there were not many roads in the kingdom which were bet- ter than that near by which was cilled after Her most Gracious Majesty. Amongst the new matters was the building of the Public Offices. In speaking of that under- taking, the only regret he had was that the Town Hall was not proceeding part passu with it. He hoped, however, that the erection of the Town Hall was only temporarily deferred, and that it would be built in the immediate future, because he thought nothing would conduce to the moral elevation of the inhabitants of Widnes than to have splendid public buildings where they could meet and consider their own property. He referred to toe excellent work done by the Waterworks and Finance Committees, under the chairmanship of Mr. Gaskell and Mr. Handley respectively, and said when Mr. Gossage had so many good things done under his superintendence the members could only hope that he might be longer amongst them, and that in the future as in the past the members would be able to support him. (Applause.)—The vote was carried by acclamation.—The Chairman, in reply, said had he been a conceited man he should have been completely overcome by the good things said about him, but be did not lay all the flattering unction to his soul that he might do from what had been said. He could not see that his virtues were se great. He had always found such reticence in ob jecting to the ruling of the'chairiean, and such a feeling of good faith amongst all the members that his thanks were due to them for having put up with his shortcomings. There was no doubt that tliere was quite as earnest spirits on Widnes Local Board as there were in any such body in the kingdom, and he thought they could honestly and without conceit point to a great many things in Widnes which were far in advance of towns of its size. He only wished to re- turn to the back passages for a moment. He thought ore ef the greatest benefits ever conferred upon Widnes y when he first came upon the Board. The Board had the good judgnv nt to make all back passages not less than nine feet wide, which gave them not only goon air space behind the houses, the area of yards also being regulated, but also permitted the removal of the nightsoil direct to the cart, in. stead of the abominable system necessary with passages three feet wide, which were frequently to be found in Man- chester, Liverpool, and many otuer places not the size of Widnes. He thatieed tilitim most heartily for all their kind expressions towards him. He hoped to live many yearS amongst them, and as long as he was there his services would be at their disposal. (Hear, bear, and applause.)— The meeting then terminated.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The usual fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held in the Board-room at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. Lieut.-Col. John Ashton occupied the chair, and there were also present the Revs. J. J. Lockwood, ,J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs.. Hadfield, Aaron, Hightield, Wallington, Williamson, Thomas Lewis, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and Dr. J. Adams (medical officer of health.)

• NOTICES OF Nionote.—Mr. Hadfield gave notice that at the next meeting of the Authority he would move the ap- pointment of a Parcchial Committee for Frodsham town- ship, the members to have the same qualifications as Guar- dians, and another member gave similar notice of motion in respect to Frodshani Lordship. NUISANCE AT Vi'esrox.—The Deputy Clerk said that with reference to the nuisance at Weston there was no doubt that the whole of the owners of the land along which the ditch runs were responsible for the condition of it, and were liable to prosecution. The nuisance was caused by sewage matter coming from cottages into the open ditch. It WAS decided to give notice to the owners that proceeding& would be instituted if the nuisance was not abated. 11lescert.exeors.—The Local Government Board wrote sanctioeing the temporary le-appointment of Dr. Adams as medical officer for the Authority, and, further, sanctioning the payment of 55" to the Clerk as remuneration for his services during the past year..—The seal of the Board was attached to the mortgage relating to the Frodsham Lord- ship loan of 166 for -drainage purposes, the mortgage hav- ing been duly perused and proved by the Clerk to the Authoritv.—Mr. Farrington, inspector of nuisances, pre- sented his usual report. _ _
This concluded the business of the meeting, which was :he list one of the Authotity as at present constituted.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The foitnightly meeting of this Board was held on Tutu* day afternoon in the Board Room at Dutton Workhouse. Lieut.-Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also pre- sent Mr. Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Speakman, Handley, Wallington, Hadfield, Lewis, Aaron, Hewitt, Wilkinson, Forster, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). THE ELECTION.—The Clerk handeg in a list of the Guar- dians elected to serve for the coming year. CENSURING AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER.—The Local Gc- 'vernment Board wrote transmitting a copy cf a letter ad- dressed by that Board to Mr. H. Davenport, requiring him to resign the office of assistant overseer for the township of Appleton. The letter was as follows :—"Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to inform you that they have had under consideration the explanatiens contained in your letter of the 2ad ult. relative to the report made by by Mr. Dolby, district auditor, after his audit of the accounts kept by you as assistant overseer of the parish of Appleton in the Runcorn Union for the half-year ended at Michael- mas last. The Board regard your explanation as most un- satisfactory. It appears you have altered the valuation list and ratebook, and, according to your own admission, have signed the name of one, at least, of the overseers without any authority. You also failed to attend the audit at the time fixed, although you admit that you had seen the ad- vertisement as to the time and place of audit, and you neglected to have your accounts made up at the proper time. In other respects, you have disregarded the regula- tions relating to your office, and under these circumstances, and having regard also to the correspondence which has previously ta,ten place with respect to your neglect of duty. the Board do not feel justified in permitting you to hold the office of assistant overseer. They must, therefore, require you at once to place your resignation of the office in the hands of the overseers of the poor of the parish." The letter was signed "C. N. Dalton, assistant sec."—ln reference to this matter, Mr. North wrote from Stockton Heath that he had been appointed by the justices assistant overseer for Stockton Heath ; Mr. North offered securities through the Guarantee Society.—Mr. Handley proposed, and it was seconded and carried, that the security be accepted. THE POLICE RATE.—A circular letter from the county treasurer stated that the local police rate for Runcern was estimated at three-eighths of a penny to produce £322 13s 10d.

FINANCIAL.—The Rev. .1. Lozkwood read a summary of expenditure for the past quarter, the adoption of which he proposed. The summary gave :—lnvoice account, £497; salaries, £298; election, LGO ; registration, vaccination, and extra medical fees, £59; lunatics, £198; coffins for outdoor paupers, £3 19s; and otner sundries, which made up a total amount of £1,152 8s 11d. The return was adopted. COMPLIMENTARY.—Mr. Hadfield proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman and vice-chairman for their services during the past year. He thought that all the members would be agreed that the business of the Board had been conducted in an efficient, courteous, and business-like man- ner. The business of the Board, as also that of the Rural Sanitary Authority, had been got through with despatch and efficiency.— The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously, and a brief reply from the chairman and vice-chairman terminated the public business of the meeting.
STRANGE DEATH OF A CHILD AT WIDNES.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, on Monday afternoon held an inquiry at the Police Station, Widnes, into the cir- cumstances attending the death of Edward Lewis Connor. —Mrs. Connor, wife of Edward Connor, chemical labourer, Lea-street, Widnes, said deceased was her son, and was four years of age last July. In August he complained of the toothache, and appeared unwell. He was poorly for two or three days before she obtained medical assistance, but after- wards Dr. Cooper's attention was called to him. He gave deceased a bottle of medicine, but did not attend the child afterwards. Dr. McLennan did so, however, and lanced his throat. Witness afterwards took the child to Dr. Stewart, of Liverpool, who examined it, and said the child was suffer- ing from blood poisoning through the glands having been cut, and the matter having run into the stomach. Dr. Stewart said the wound should have been poulticed and allowed to get to a head, and it would then have burst itself. She continued to take the child to Dr. Stewart, who told her to apply a poultice twice a week, as that was the only way of curing it, and it would take a long while to do so under those circumstances. She was confined in November, and had to give over taking the deceased to Liverpool, and he was again put under the care of Dr. McLennan. in Feb- ruary she took the child to him, when be said " Well, Mrs. Connor, you are a poor woman, and it is no good bringing your son to me. I can d 9 it no more good, but if it takes a change for the worse let me know immediately." The child did not seem to get worse until last Friday morning, when witness awoke and found it in a fit. She ran out of the house to ask someone to go for a doctor, when a person went for Dr. McLennan, who said he would follow imme- diately. Witness waited until half-past eight, when she sent again. This time the doctor was baying his breakfast, and he said he would come when he had finished it. The child lived until eleven o'clock, when it succumbed, the doctor not haying arrived. In answer to questions, witness said Dr. McLennan was not the parish doctor. She had told him she did not care how much it cost bar so that the child was cured. Witness afterwards stated that when she asked Dr. McLennan how it was he did not come, be said he forgot the name of the street.—Another witness corroborated part of the last witness'e evidence, and a verdict of" Death from natural causes "was returned.

WARRINGTON UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE Com- urrTsn.—The meeting of this committee was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. Derbyshire, the chairman, presiding. The Attend- ance Officers, Messrs. Shearer and fiarnett, reported that there had been a considerable increase in the attendance at school during the past month over the previous month. The annual reports of the offi- cers were also submitted, and showed a slight in- crease upon theprevious year. A vote of thanks was accorded the chairman, on the motion of Mr, Foster, seconded by Mr. Greening..

div.head: POLIC E INT ELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLIC E INT ELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. liorrwor.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies. and Councillor Greening A ROUGH CIISTOMER.—MichaeI Ward was charged with being drunk and disorderly in St. James-street, on Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Fearn and Mr. Edward Johnson. Prisoner was committing a nuisance, and assault- ed Mr. Johnson for remonstrating with him. The police were called, and prisoner assaulted Fearn and conducted himself in a most violent maniter. He was sent to prison for a month. Perron AND Toss.—Charles Pollard was fined 103 and costs for playing at pitch and toss on the previous afternoon. TCESDAY.—Before Councillor C. Broadbent and Mr. E. J. Guest. ABSENTEES.—WiIIiam Bevan, charged with using an absentee from the Warwick Militia, was remanded, as was also Mark O'Brien, charged with being an absentee from the Bury Militia. DRIINIENNESS.—Edward Rowe was fined 53 and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street, on the -previous night. SMASHER."—Patrick Duggan was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street, on the previ- ous evening. There was a further charge against him of breaking a window of the Lower Angel Vaults, and doing damage to the amount of L 2. It was stated that prisoner smashed a vaivable glass panel with his hand, but his de- fence was that be fell against it, and did not break the glass wilfully. The Beach fined him 103, including costs. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Pickmere and Chandley, and Mr. John Fairclough. DESERTION.—Wm. Beavan, charged with deserting from the Warwick Militia, was remanded to Strangeways to await escort.—Mark O'Brien was charged with absenting himself from the 3rd Battalion Lancashire Fusiliers, during 1885, at Bury. It was stated that he had once before deser- ted, and been sentenced to imprisonment by a military court.—He was fined 40s and costs, or one month's hard labour. STEALING SITIRTS.—John White, who stated that he was a labourer and came from Cardiff, was charged with steal- ing two men's shirts, value ss, from the draper's shop of Sarah Fell, 15, Mersey-street, the same morning. When apprehended, a abort time after the theft, prisoner was wearing the two shirts to avoid detection.—He pleaded guilty, and was sent to prison for a month. -41'stratmes.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster Darentatexass.— Bodelia Knockton and Bridget Mc- Donowgh were charged wtth being drank and disorderly in Scotland-road on the previous night. They received bad characters and were each sent to prison for a month. SLEEPING OCT.—Three boys named Quinn, Whittaker, and Fairhurst were charged with being on the premises of the Bank-street School with intent to commit a fei.onv ore be previous night. The constable who arrested them, P.C. Hennessey, said that it was a regular custom of the boys to sleep out at nights. The Chief Constable said that on the previous eight Trinity eb.ools were broken into and some money stolen; the robbery had evidently been done by boys. Quinn and Whittaker were each gent to prison for a month, and Fairhurst was ordered to receive twelve -strokes with the birch rod, and to be kept in custody uutii six o'clock in the evening. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Dr. Gornall. DESERTION.—Joseph Mellor was charged with having, on or about August last, deserted from the South Stafford- shire Regiment, stationed at Manchester. He was remanded to Strangeways to await eacort. STEALING CoAL—Patrick Yates, an elderly man, was charged with stealing a quantity of coal, value 4d, from Arprey, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. Prisoner had a pocket extending all round his coat, into which he had put the coal. He said that he had not stolen it, but had picked it up on the rail- Way line. He was sent to prison for a month. NEGLECT OF FAXILY.—Peter Lee pleaded guilty to leav- ing his wife and two children, aged three and one years, chargable to the funds of the Warrington lanien. Mr. Shearer (relieving officer) said that prisoner's wife and family were aamitted on the 2nd of March. A warrant was taken oat for the apprehension of prisoner, who was a labourer, and who had run away and enlisted, leaving his family totally unprovided for. P.C. Monaghan apprehen- ded prisoner at Dublin on Thursiay. The magistrates passed sentence of a month's imprisonment.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FEUDAL—Before Messrs. H. Stanton, W. Long, and C. Lister. DoG Casxs.—William Dale, farmer, Massey Brook, was -charged with being the owner of two dogs which were al- lowed to be at large on the 21st March, and also with un- lawfully keeping a dor without having an excise license on the 22nd March. Both the charges for allowing dogs to be at large were dismissed, and a fine of is and costs, Sa 6d, was imposed in regard to the charge of being without a license.—Matthew D. Woodhead, Lymm, was charged with allowing a dog to be at large, and was fined 2s 61, in- cluding costs.—Arthur G. Banning, for a similar offence at Lymm, on the 26th February, was fined is and costs, 95 63. ASSAULT.—John Eccleston was charged with having, on the 13th March, unlawfully assaulted John Murphy, a la- bourer. P.C. Dutton said that on the night of the 13th March he saw the defendant push Murphy to the ground just outside the Spread Eagle Hotel, Lymm, and kick him in the side. Murphy was drunk but Eccleston was not, and he got two men to take the former home. It was stated by Sergeant Harrington that the two men did not take Murphy all the way, and he had been severely assaulted and lay out in the snow the same night. The next morning he had to be taken to the Infirmary at Warrington, in which he re- mained about a fortnight. The landlord gave evidence to 'the effect that Eccleston had assisted him to put Murphy out of his house because of his being drunk. A fine of is and costa, 12s 6d, was imposed. DRUNKENNESS —Ralph Jackson, a young man, was fined ss, including costs, for having been drunk and disorderly at Lymm on the 19th December.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell, junr. DIIIINICEN/cass. John Walsh, Thomas Moran, James Rawlinson, Michael Gormley, and John Brennan were each fined for this offence. James Malone for fighting in Marsh-street, on Saturday night, was bound over to keep the peace. NHOLECT OF FAMlLY.—Richard Jones, chemical labourer at Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Co.'s, and formerly living in Church-street. was charged with nehlecting his wife and lamily.—Mr. Scannell, relieving officer, said the defendant's family became chargeable to the union funds on the 25th February, and remained so for about three weeks. Defend- ant now owed £2 lie 6d including costs, but had only £.2 I.os 6d, which Mr. Scannell agreed to accept.—Mr. Gasket' said he would set the prisoner at liberty, as he did not wish him to lose his work, but he must be careful to con- duct himself better in future, or he would be committed to prison.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY. Before Messrs. George Pilkington and J. C. Gamble. MISCRLLA.NIIOI7B.—Mary M cCafferty, Catherine Matthews (37th appearance), Catherine Lancaster, and Catherine Owens. were each fined for drunkenness.—Ellen Roberts and and Thomas Butler were each bound over to keep the peace on charges of creating disturbances.—Thomas Carr, John Lyons, and William Ellis Grayson, young men, were each fined 2s ad and costs for having, on Sunday, the 4th April, obstructed the footpath in Farrant•strest, Widnes.—Mary Sullivan summoned Mary McNulty for using defamatory language, and the defendant was bound over to be of good behaviour.

MONDAY.—Before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst• and Mr. F.

Rigby. ALLEGIED Funious DRIVING. - Edwin Finch, a young man, was charged with furiously driving a horse on the 3rd April, in Lord-street. P.C. Millington deposed that the de- fendant galloped a horse in a trap along Lord-street at a furious rate. The constable shouted to him to stop, but instead of drawing up he commenced to beat the animal. He, however, drew up at the bridge, where there were 200 or 300 people assembled; and it was a wonder no one was run over.—By defendant : The horse was going at 16 or 17 miles an hour. The horse stopped within two hundred yards.—Mr. Rigby said it was quite clear that if the de- fendant had been going at the rate stated be would have gone at least two miles.—The Bench dismissed the case. DRITIcKENNEss.—David Jones, Bernard Kay and Thomas Murpby were each fined for drunkenness.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The final meeting of the "old "Board of Guardians for the Prescot Union was held at the Workhouse Whiston, on Thursday, when there were present Mr. J. Workhouse, (in the chair), the Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. Jackson, W. Newsome. W. Birchall, J. Matthews, J. Lowe. J. Fisher, E. Svder, W. Gerrard, R. Leigh, R. Tnson, T. F. Hill, 3. Kenwright, J. Griffiths. %V. Swift, J. Ellison, P. Longton, T. Heald, W. B. Longton, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). STATISTICS.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 482 inmates of the workhouse this week, 498 last week, and 442 in the corresponding week last year. There were 51 vagrants relieved against 37 in the corresponding week last year. THE ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR WOOLTON.—The Clerk read a copy of his reply to the communication from the Local Government Board, enclosing copy of a memorial from several Guardians, asking for a new election in regard to the assistant overseership of Woolton. In his reply the Clerk stated that he was placed in an unenviable position, and he disclaimed any desire to espouse the cause of either Baxter or the unsuccessful candidate, Spencer. He stated the steps taken by the Guardians to till the vacancy, and he believed the election had properly taken place, and that the votes were properly recorded. He had not yet received any reply from the Local Government Board. At a later period of the meeting the Clerk read the following report from the Government Auditor : "Waterloo, Liverpool, 10th April, 1886.—For the informa- tion of the Guardians of the Prescot Union. I have to regret that at my audit of the accounts of Mr. J. R. Wood, late assistant overseer for the Woolton district for the half-year 'lending at Lady Day last, I certify the following sums to be due from him :—Hale £8 is 2d, Halewood £l3 5s Bd, Speke £l2 9s 7d, Tarbock £47 14s 6d, Little Woolton £627 les 2d, Much Woolton £699 163 sd, Halewood (special expenses !sanitary rate) £79 3e 3d, total £1,488 Go 9d.—Yours, G. Hezmiußsr."—The Clerk observed that towards the deficiency they would receive £1,900 from the Guarantee Society, and he suggested that anount should be divided pro rata among the townships in WIWI the defalcations oc- curred.—On the motion of Mr. Newsome, seconded by Mr. Griffiths, a motion to that effect was passed. THE RAINFORD MEDICAL OFFICER.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board sanctioning the appointment of Dr. Murdoch as medical officer for the township of Rainfordi at silary of £25 per annum, for the ensuing twelve months. PA?itNi 10 tin CLEIIK.—The Board awarded the sum of £2O to the clerk for his services in conducting the recent election of Guardians, and on the recommendation of the Finance Committee a cheque for £lOO was ordered to be made in his favour as clerk to that Authority. DESERTED FAMILIES.—Mr. Newsome drew the attention of the guardians to the deserted families in the Union dur- ing the past three years. He found that they bad expended £1,632 is id up,n deserted wives and 251 children, and at the present time they had 141 deserted persons in the Workhouse who were being maintained at a cost of £35 per week. He thought that state of things deserved the con- sideration of the Guardians. ECCLESTON ELECTION.—Mr. Tyrer said there had been many complaints in the township of Eecleston that rate- payers had not been able to vote on account of not having paid their rates. They stated most distinctly that they had never received demand notes, nor had the assistant overseer called upon them for the amounts said to be due. As a matter of fact, out of £1.900 which ought to have been col- lected, £1,500 was still outstanding. He moved that the matter be referred to the Finance Committee of the new board to thoroughly investigate the circumstances.- Mr. Newsome, who was defeated in Eecleston township, sec- onded. He said the mysterious surroundings ef the non- collection of these rates led him to think there was some- thing very nasty underneath. Among 7,000 voters only 1,000 papers had been delivered.—The Clerk said he could only issue papers to those who had paid their rates. The district auditor had spoken strongly on the subject of the rates not being collected, and threatened to surcharge the overseers with the amounts not collected.—The motion was carried.
THANKS.—Tbe thanks of the Board were tendered to the chairman (Mr. Leatberbarrow), vice chairman (Mr. Lowe), and deputy vice-chairman (Mr. Fisher) for their services daring the past year.

The Conservatives of the Central Division of Bradford have adopted Mr. Brodie Hoare, of Tunbridge Wells, as their candidate. EXTRAORDINARY MURDER.—At Manchester, on Monday, John Holland was remanded on a charge of murdering his child. Prisoner had lived apart from his wife, but on Satur- day he met her and asked her to return to him. She refused, and he snatched the child from her and threw it over the bridge, and it fell on the road twenty-six feet below, and was killed immediately. The wife's screams attracted the police, and the prisoner was arrested. The child was four- teen months' old. FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. FORSTER.—rhe remains of Mr. W. E. Forster were interred on Saturday at Little Wharfedale, Burley, Yorkshire. Special trains were run from Bradford and intermediate stations to Burley, and by these large numbers of persons travelled to take part in the ceremony. The procession was about one mile in length. Mr. John Bright had intended to be present, but was pre- vented at the last moment. The funeral was conducted strictly according to Quaker tenets. COAGULINE.—Cement for Broken Articles. 6d. is, 2s: postage 2nd. Bold everywhere. Kay, Bros., filtockport.—Acirt.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 17. 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 17. 1886.

by his brilliant play afterwards. All the backs on the part I of Aspull played well, Roberts being the pick, his kicks be- ' lag of great advantage. Teams :—Warrington: Buxton, Boardman, Barnes, Jolley, Speakman' Gilbert, Fair. Turner, Ashton (captain), Povey, W. Dillon, Haves, Rigby, E. Dil- lon, Davies, and F. Turner. Colour, white. Aspull : Daw- ber, Roberts (captain), Seddon, Samuels, Halms, Cartwright, Hampson, Hesketb, Lindsay, Lawson, Haydock, Brooks, Bramwell, Monks, and Pilkington. Colour, blue. At the finish of the game a rush was made to the grand stand, where the challenge cup was to be presented to the Warrington team. The players were received with enthusi- astic cheering. Barnes was carried shoulder high to the place of honour, while Fair. Turner and Ashton were re- ceived with loud shouts of welcome. When the cheers had died away, and silence had been restored, Mr. C. A. Cron- shaw, of Wigan, said it had been intended that the Mayor of Liverpool should have been there to have presented the cup to the winners, but unfortunately he could not be present, and he as one ^f the Vice-presidents of the Union, had at the last moment been requested to present the cup to the win- ning team. (Loud cheers.) He need nbt:dilate upon the advantages of football to such an ebthusiastic assembly as that, but he would say that, as one if the promoters of the Union, he felt exceedingly proud that they could number among their ardent supporters such a nu.nber of gendemen as they saw there that day. (Cheers.) Warrington were the first winners of the West Lancashire Cup—(cheers)— and as one of the Vice-presidents he congratulated them most heartily, and he honed they had set the stone rolling which would prove them to be one of the best clubs they had in the county. (Cheers.) In the name of the commit- tee of the West Lancashire and Border Towns Rugby Union be begged to presect to Mr. Francomb, President of the Warrington Football Club, the challenge cup. (Loud cheers.)—Mr. Francomb was greeted with loud cheers, and _ . . _

said that on behalf of the -Warrington Football Club he begged to return hearty thanks. Ele was sure everybody from Warrington was delighted with. the bravery and the determination with which the cup had been won. (Cheers.) The Warrington team bad fought many wonderful battles, but he thought they had not once been doubted in their honour and their fairness to their opponents. (Hear. *tar.) He believed that football was a thing that would encourage men to be brave in whatever position of life they were placed, and the game ought to be played fairly, and let the victors gain fairly. He believed that the Aspull men had played thoroughly well—(loud cheers)—and they should only be too delighted if on some future occasion they bad the honour of carrying the cup to Aspull. (Cheers.)—Mr. Parry, hon. sec. of the -Union, announced that the gold medals for the Warrington team would be presented in a few days at a grand dinner. Silver medals will also be awarded to the Aspull team. The crowd then dispersed.

RUGBY RULES. FINAL TIE FOR THE WES C LANCASHIRE AND BORDER TOWN'S UNION CUP. GREA.T VICTORY FOR WARRINGTON. 'through innumerable difficulties the Warrington team on Saturday last found themselves in the final for the above

- - - cup, their opponents being the sturdy collier lads from As- pull. "Warren's lads" have not succeeded without a hard and tough struggle, meetieg in the first place Lymm and Oughtrington, then Widnes, St. Helens, Runcorn (twice), and lastly Aspull ; scoring in all 175 points to 14, which re- flects great credit on them. It will be seen from the above that they have had to encounter some of the best clubs in the Union. From the commencement, the home players have been pretty confident that they would win; and their supporters equally so, it being a common remark during the past few weeks to ask what they would win by. During the past week the town has been in a state of excitement. On Wednesday week when the team went to Southport hun- dreds assembled to wish them success, but this was further beaten when the team arrived at the station to be in time for the 1-55 to take them to Fairfield. Fully 2000 spectators accompanied the team. Others availed themselves of the route by the L. fic. N -W., whilst a few went on "shanks' pony." One of the committee men met a crowd of young- sters from Warrington who were singing witti great gusto, and astonishing the natives with the following lines Our cup's come home to-day. Our cup's come home to-day; For Tommy Barnes has dropped a goal. And brought it home to-day.

Of course this was after the match when on their way home' the team arrived at the Central Station. Liverpool, at 2-30, the secretary, Mr. J. R. Calvert, having arranged for a 'bus to meet them there and to drive them to their destina- tion, where they arrived about 3-0. The Union Committee had made ample arrangements as regards dressing, /sc. After all preparations for the struggle had been gone through, Ashton led the boys in white to the ground, their appear- ance being greeted with a good deal of cheering, which was renewed when Johnny Roberts and his party put in their appearance. On looking round it was seen that all round the ropes were packed with an excited throng of people, whilst crowds were on the grand stand, where the cup was placed in the middle; fully 6000 being present. The weather was beautiful for play—scarcely a breath of wind in the air—but the ground was soft owing to sleet and rain falling in the morning. On spinning the coin in the air, the choice of goals to defend fell to the Aspull captain, who elected to play with the slight hill in his faveur.
Aspnll won the toss, Frank Turker kicking off, with the sun in the eyes of the Warricgton team. The Warrington forwards, in the first place, rushed the ball into the Aspull

quarters, but their forwards soon returned it into the War- rington ground. From a line out Fair. Turner got hold and made a dashing run, a scrimmage taking place. Several exciting scrimmages then took place, both teams being pretty equally matched. Gil eert now showed up with a nice dribble, but was stopped by Seddon before looking dangerous. Good scrimmages again took place, Aspull hiving a slight advantage. Gilbert now got hold and punted to Roberts, who made a pretty return, the ball rolling into touch about half way. Barnes relieved by a short run, Jolley seconding his efforts by a further run, and Gilbert and Barnes took play to the Aspull 25. The Aspull forwards, however, gallantly defended, and soon took play back to the centre. Barnes obtaining possession got in a nice run and kick to the Aspull 2,5, play being for some time confined to the neighbourhood of the goal line; but the Aspull forwards seemed determined to prevent the War- ringtonians from scoring, for by a determined rush they toot the ball to their opponents' 25. For off-side tacking Buxton claimed a free kick, from which not much was gained, the same player stopping a determined rush. Gil- bert next showed up with a good punt, which caused play to be confined to centre. The Aspull contingent slightly gained ground in the packed scrimmages, Roberts further aiding their efforts by a good kick to the Warrington 25. The Warrington forwards, with Ashton, Frank Turner, and Rigby at their head, next put the Aspull backs on the de- fensive, until Roberts relieved by a good kick, and following well up looked dangerous, eut Barnes tackled him in the Warrington 25. Gilbert obtained a free kick, the ball fall- ing into the hands of Seddon, who transferred to amuels, who was brought down by Gilbert. Fair. Turner, Povey, Ashton, and Davies now came through, and with a combined dribble they took play to the Aspull quarters. Cartwright now put in is pate to Samuels, who made some headway Until brought to grief by Rigby. Speakman next tried a bit of his stratagem play, but was held, and the Aspull for- wards improved matters for their side by taking the oval with a rush to the Warrington 25, Buxton foiling their attempt to score. Fair. Turner and Ashton by a strong rash however relieved, but Roberts, with his sure kicking, again confined play to the Warrington quarters. Povey, Davies, and Frank Turner relieved the pressure, Barnes seconding their efforts by obtaining a free kick. The return kick was charged flown by Ned Dillon, who galloped to centre line. Aspull, by loose play, again took the ball to the Warrington stronghold, bet Davies, Heyet' and Rigby promptly retaliated. By the good play of Cartwright, Samuels, and Seddon, the oval was taken back, Buxton kicking to Roberts, who replied with a long punt towards I the Warrington citadels. Good scrimmaging now took I place, until J. Barnes got in a long kick, when play raged furiously on the line. The collier lads, however, thought they would not yet let the Warringtonians score, for by combined dribbling they took the ball to the centre flag. Rigby, Povey, Ashton, and Davie, however, were not to be denied, and shortly afterwards a minor resulted on behalf of Warrington, • Roberts being compelled to touchdown, Jolley having a free kick, but Fair. Turner failed to convert it into a major point. Shortly afterwards half time was called with the ball in the centre of the field. It was a great surprise to many of the Warrington supporters that Aspull had done so well in the first half, for with the exception of the minor scored against them, their form was quite as brilliant as that of the Warringtonians. The ques- tion now was, would they be able to hold out, for the War- rington team are noted for their grand staying powers, and if the collier lads could not in the end keep pace with them, their efforts in the first half were of no avail. After both teams had been looked after they got ready for the resumption of play. From the kick out nothing much came, scrimmages taking place in the centre. Aspull slightly gaining ground, good kicks were exchanged between Barnes and Roberts, a free kick being conceded to Aspull. Frank Turner was now I seen in a bit of his best form—it never having been known before that he could run,—for by a smart rush he took the ball to the Aspull 25, and all but scored. Good combined forward play on the part of Aspull, bcwever, took the leather to centre. where H. Boardman got in one of the nicest rani of the day, close to the Aspull goal-line being the Scene of action, the Aspull lot in the end Wag compelled to touch down. From the kick out Fairfield Turner obtained hold, and by one of his litti.e rushes again took play to the Aspull quarters. Some good passing by Gilbert and Jolley im- proved Matters, but the Aspull forwards by determined play relieved the pressure. Roberts now saved a rush by the Warrington forward, but another free kick was allowed Warrington for the off-side collaring of the Aspull team, Samuels returning and Gilbert retaliating with interest. Speakman put in a nice little screw kick, after which the Aspull lot tried hard to get away, but it was of no avail, their efforts being frustrated by the grand tackling of Gil- bert. Speakman, and Rigby. Speakmaa now passed to Barnes, but he was tackled by Seddon before he could get in a fair kick, Roberta returning with a long punt to the War- rington territory. Buxton, however, being on the alert, Promptly propelled the leather back again. By a low pass by Speakman toßarnes a lot of ground was gained, Gilbert taking the ball to touch. From the line out the ball ex- changed bands in quick succession, until it came to Barnes, who nicely dropped it over the crossbar, although surrounded by his opponents. The cheering for some time was terrific. The kick off was well followed up by the Aspull forwards. Buxton misjudging the distance, let them in, and shortly afterwards they scored a minor. This little mistake on his part he shortly afterwards rectified by a good kick and ran to Aspull quarters; the Aspull forwards tried hard to equalise matters and removed play to the opposite side of the centre flag; Povey, Davies, Ashton, and Rigby replied by a good strong rush, and Barnes gained ground from a pass by Gil- bert Some tight scrimmages were next witnessed, and on the ball becoming loose Jolley got hold and made a dashing run, being brought to grief by Samuels. The Aspull forwards now pulled themselves together for a final effort, and suc- ceeded in getting past Buxton, who kicked in touch. The Warrington forwards, however, relieved the pressure, and play took place about half-way. Speakman now stopped a rush and put in a dodgy run. Roberts' sure kicking told for his side. until H. Boardraan got in a good run and kick. The Aspull men now showed signs of weakness, but they sturdily resisted all attempts to get over their lines, the war raging for some time just outside the Avail 25. Gilbert put in a punt. but Roberts again relieved by a good kick. The collier lads followed up, but conld never again get past half-way. H. Boardman again showed up with a nice run, and Fairfield Turner gained a lot of ground by a determined rush, but was brought down by Cartwright before he could score. Good play on the part of H. Boardman and E. Dillon brought about time, and thus came to an end one of the best and closest contests fought in the cup competition. The Aspull men played up with indomitable courage until the last second. The game strictly sneaking was a forward one. In the first half both teams were pretty evenly matched, Aspull having perhaps a slight advantage, and in this portion of the game it seemed as though the Warringtonians were rather too confident. In the second half, however, they un- mistakeably showed their superior staying powers, no doubt owing to the excellent preparation they have received at the hands of their trainers, Messre. Smith, Jones, and Foster. H. Ashton, the captain, displayed wonderful form. Fair. Turner played well, but not so effective as at Widnes, being unwell. Rigby deserves an especial word of praise, his play this week being marvellous, and more so when it was known that he was playing with an injured leg. Of the forwards it may fairly be said that their play can scarcely he praised too much. With regard to the Aspull forwards Lindsay and Lawson several times showed that they were men worth their place in their team, whilst Hampson and Brooks manifested good form. As far as the backs are con- cerned they all played a good game, but Barnes must be singled out as the hero of the day. Jolley played a good game, but must improve in his picking up, his tackling be- ing a sight to witness. H. Boardman quite justified his selection; Gilbert and Speakman also being in first rate form. Buxton made one mistake, but quite made up for it

div.head: E CUP.
div.p: E CUP.

We give an accurate representation of the cup :—The trophy (says the "Athletic News ") for the purposes of the annual competition of the West Lancashire and Border Towns' Union, which is the production of the emin- ent firm of Messrs. Ylkington and Cs., of Church-street, Liverpool, is in many respects a remarkable work of its kind, and altogether a unique example of the silversmiths' craft. The cap is fashioned in solid silver, standing, with the pedestal, close upon thirty inches high, and takes the form of an antique classid vase in the Grecian style of art. The surface is elaborately and richly chased in repousse work, representing the national emblems of the rose, shamrock, and thistle, prominence of course being given to the Lanca- shire rose, which is conventionally treated. Entwined round the central shields are the national products—wheat. barley, and the hop plant—artistically arranged, whilst a bordering of rich ornamentation of like character introduces a series of Norman shields, on which it is proposed from time to time to record the winning clubs. The side handles are of a richly-chased foliated character, being in strict harmony with the design of the vase, the cover of which is surmounted by an exquisitely modelled figure of a football player in correct Rugby style. The two principal shields present admirably conceived and skilfully executed "kick off" and 'first scrimmage" scenes; while the ebony pedestal is mounted with a silver shield, which com- pletes the design of this beautiful and model challenge cup. We may add that the value of the cup is sixty guineas.

RECEPrION OF TRH VICTORIOUS TEAM. The reception which was given to the victorious team on their return home with the coveted troy was, to say the least, remarkable for its spontaneity and enthusiasm. Not- withstanding that a very large number of the most ardent patrons of football bad accompanied the players to Fairfield, it was manifest throughout the day that a general interest prevailed amongst the people of the town as to the result of the match, and in the latter part of the afternoon large throngs gathered in various parts of the principal streets, and anxiously waited for the latest news. The opinion was pretty confidently held that Warrington would become the abiding place of the cup for the next twelve months, but at the same time it was admitted that a team with the hand- some record of that of Aspull was not to be despised, so that there was just enough uncertainty about the issue to work up the excitement. When, therefore' telegrams giving the final result were posted up in several places of business in the town the enthusiasm was very great, and mutual con- gratulations w ere freely indulged in. It was known that the victorious team would return to the Central Station towards eight o'clock, and, as there seemed to be a general desire to give them a suitable reception, towards that hour an immense crowd gathered in Horsemarket-street and Winwick-street. From the further side of the railway bridge to Market-gate the street seemed to be literally packed with human beings. For the time being all vehicu- lar traffic was stopped, and even for pedestrians it was no easy matter to edge their way through the crowd. The train containing the footballers arrived at the Central Station aeon after eight o'clock, and as the winners of the cup descended to the street they were greeted with vehe- ment cheering. They, accompanied by Councillor Fran- comb, the president of the club, were accommodated on a wagonette drawn by four horses, which was in waiting, and, as they proceeded towards Market-gate, preceded by St. Paul's and Mr. Fletcher's Brass Bands, they were loudly cheered along tho whole route. From one of the upper stories of Mr. P. Caldwell's business premises there was an illumination of coloured light, which lit up the street in a most 'striking manner. Tbo procession was continued, amid frequent outbursts of cheering, from Market-gate by way of Sankey-street, Parker-street, Bridge-street, Butter- market-street, and Scotland-road to the Griffin Hotel, the head-quarters of the club. Here Councillor Francomb from 'one of the windows briefly addressed the large crowd which had gathered in front of the hotel. He said that a splendid victory had been won, and he thanked the people for having given such a magnificent reception to the victorious team. Several short complimentary speeches were also made by other gentlemen. and the remainder of the evening was spent in a festive manner, music and singing enlivening the proceed- ings. At a late hour the cup was taken by the winning team to the house of Mr. Francomb, where it was de- posited.

div.head: MEETING AT THE GRIFFIN HOTEL.
div.p: MEETING AT THE GRIFFIN HOTEL.

_ On Tuesday evening last the Griffin was all alive, the team and friends being invited by the host and hostess (Mr. and Mrs. Pritchard) to assemble and drink to the future success of the Warrington Football Club out of the cup. A goodly number of members had assembled, a few influen- tial gentlemen of the town also being present. For a short , time Mr. A. Pennington was kept on the move in attending Ito their wants, and all being supplied from the flowing bowl. The Captain (Mr. E. Warren) then proposed the health of the host and hostess, which was drunk with the usual musical honours.—Mr. W. Dillon next enlivened the company with a song, rendered in his best style.—Mr. Prit- chard, in responding, to the toast, said that it gave him great pleasure in seeing so many present, and they might rest assured that he would always do his utmost to attend to their wants. He was very proud of their victory, and said that it was one of the happiest moments of his life when he saw the cup triumphantly brought into the. Griffin on Saturday last.—The Hostess also thanked the team in a very appropriate speech for their patronage, and also Mr. Warren for his kind wishes.—An amusing incident next oc- curred, Mr. Calvert saying that he had that day received a

note from a person signing himself "A Tradesman." which was to the effect that he had enclosed in a box 20 "silver medals," to be given to tbe team, secretary, treasurer, cap- tain, umpire, eirc., and hewed that they would wear them on their manly chests. The medals were then presented amidst roars of laughter.—Mr. Peacock next added to the harmony of the evening by singing a song entitled " Pictures on the wall." after which the healths of the ladies who serve at the Griffin was proposed and received with entbus;asm.— Mr. A. Pennington next congratulated the team in a few well-chosen words, after which Mr. Warren rose and said that it gave him great pleasure in welcoming one of the old players amongst them, and asked them to drink to the health of their esteemed and worthy friend, Mr. S. Sutton, who had come amongst them that evening to congratulate them upon their success, and at the same time to christen the cup.—After this aas done, Mr. Sutton ably replied, express- ing his pleasure to be amongst them. He also gave an ac- count of Rugby football in Warrington in its infancy, but his chief aim was in congratulating Mr. Warren on the successes which the Warrington Club had obtained during the present season. He also mentioned the fine play shown by Tommy Barnes, and said he had seen many good men on the field, but none better than the little goal-kicker. He concluded by wishing the Warrington Football Club every success in the future.—Several other speeches were given during the evening, and the shout which went up for the healths of the secretary and treasurer was deafening. The following gentlemen also enlivened the proceedings by singing some capital songs, viz.: Messrs. Jones, Whittle, Crosby, and Reddish, Mr. F. Booth, Mr. Lee, Mr. J. Hampson, Mr. Pennington. The party broke nip at a quarter to eleven after spending an enjoyable evening. RUNCORN AND THEIR DEFEAT BY WARRINGTON. BY A RUNCORN MAN. Enthusiasts of football in Runcorn are much depressed at the defeat of the local club by Warrington on Wednesday at Southport. Until the very last they had confidence that Runcorn would just manage to beat their sturdy opponents, and large numbers do not accept the wrecking of their hopes with a good grace. When the result of the match became known in the town shortly after seven o'clock on Wednesday evening the crowds that had assembled dispersed in different ways with slow stride's and glum looking faces, and set about finding excuses for Warrington's victory. A most surprising rumour was set afoot. It was to the effect that Harry Speakman, the clever three-quarter back, had sold the game through some influence exerted upon him in War- rington on Saturday, and it was strange to find that the statement gained credence in many quarters. Lunt did not play with his accustomed skill and dash at Southport, and when he arrived at Runcorn station at half-past ten he was met by an excited crowd, who hooted him and cried "Sold the game for SIO." Lunt, we believe, vows he will not play with the team again, but he will doubtless alter his decision on cool reflection, and take no notice of the rash and totally uncalled for display of feeling on the part of a disappointed crowd. The allegation against Speakman is generally voteel as childish, and when it is remembered that Runcorn is his native town, and that he is idolized as a footballer by thousands, no one with a grain of common sense will accept as truth the charge made against his char- acter. Now that the somewhat bitter struggle for the cup is decided, it is hoped that good feeling will again reign between the rival teams, and Warrington's visit to Runcorn in a fortnight to play the return fixture is looked forward to in anticipation of a reversal of the last decision, should the weather be calm and favour an open and passing game. The stormy weather, it may be mentioned, is considered to have done much to spoil Runcorn's chance.

ASSOCIATION RULES. GOLBORNE MUFFERS "v. " DUFFERS."—The most mink-provoking match ever witnessed at Golborne came off on the Recreation Ground on Saturday afternoon, before a large crowd of spectators, the competitors being the " bluffers " and " Duffers "of the district—all noviccs at the game. The two teams—wearing tall hats and dressed in knee-breeches and highly-coloured jackets—were led on to the field by the Golborne Brass Band. From first to last the spectators were kept in a continual roar of laughter, frequently heightened by the fall of the " tall "hats, which were unceremoniously kicked abeut the field. After an exciting game, the result was declared a draw—three goals each.

NEW SPRINGS V. EARLESTOWN (" A" THem).—This re- turn match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the New Springs Club. The Springs captain lost the toss, and Taylor started the ball with the wind in his face. The Earlestown forwards soon came down on the Springs goal but the ball was returned, and play raged in neutral terri- tory for some little time, until the visitors' forwards made another onslaught on the Springs goal, and. the ball was shot between the home uprights, the visitors thus drawing first blood. Taylor kicked off, and in a very short time the visitors had registered a second goal. At half time the score stood 4tol in favour of the visitors. The teams changed ends and the Springs forwards added three goals in a remarkably short time, and the visitors managed to put the leather past the Springs custodian twice in the second half, the game ultimately ending in a victory for Earles- town by 6 goals to 4. WELLINGTON CUP. . . _

Saturday was the day for the -completion of the first j round of the competition for the Wellington Challenge Cup, open to clubs within a radius of seven miles of Earlestown, and several ties excited considerable interest. Reports of the games are appended : Sr. HELENS ASSOCIATION V. EARLESTOWN VIADUCT STARS.—These teams met on the ground of the latter, when the visitors won by six goals to one. HAYDOCIC ST. JAMES'S V. CHERRY-TRIM ROYAL (PARR).— The game was of a very one-sided character, the St. James's winning by ten goals to none. MILLFIELD ROVERS V. MOSS ROSE ROVERS.—This match resulted in the defeat of the latter by five goals to none. Sr. HELENS Sr. MARES V. HAYDOCK WANDERERS.—These teams met on the ground of the latter, on Saturday week, when the home team, after an exciting game scored four goals to three. One of the Haydock points was disputed, however, and the committee decided that the tie should be re-played. The teams met at Haydock last Saturday when the former verdict was reversed, the St. Helens team winning by four goals to two. The losers protested against two of the goals awarded to St. Helens, and the protest was heard at a meeting of the committee on Monday evening at Earlestown, when the tie was awarded to St. Helens.

STURSHAW CROSS WANDERERS V. ASHTON RECREATION (IST).—The Stubshaw Cross team, on Saturday week, beat Ashton by four goals to one, but the tie was ordered to be re-played owing to the ineligibility of one of the players for Stubshaw Cross. The teams accordingly met at Ashton on Friday night, when after an exciting match Stubshaw Cross won by two goals to one. ASHTON RECREATION (2ND) V. EARLESTOWN ROVRES.— These teams met at Ashton, the play was of an exciting character, and Ashton scored four goals to three by the Earlestown Rovers.—The latter protested against the tie being awarded to Ashton owing to the spectators crowding In the field and interfering with the players, and at a meet- ing on Monday night the committee directed the tie to be re-played on the ground of the St. James's club at llaydock some night during the present week. EARLESTOWN IST V. EARLESTOWN OLYMPIC.—This match , was played on the ground of the first-named, the MesneE., on Saturday afternoon, when a fair number of spectators were present. The home team had much the best of the ' game, and scored four goals in the first half. In the second half they added three more, while their opponents failed to ' , notch a single point. The Earlestown first thus won by seven goals to none. The winners were represented by Appleton, goal; R Green and J Green, backs; Whalley, Bowker, and Duxbury, half backs; Rich and Caldwell, right wing ; Dagnall, centre ; Sims and Siddeley left wine. DRAW FOR SECOND ROIIND.—A meeting of club represen- tatives to make the draw in the second round of the compe- tition for the Wellington Cup was held at the Wellington Inn, Earle-street, Earlestown, on Monday evening, when there was a very large attendance. Several protests were considered by the committee as stated in preceding para- graphs. The draw for the second round was as follows : Earlestown 2nd v. Haydock C.B. and F.O. Bt. Hel.ns Association v. Stubshaw Cross Wanderers. Haydock St. James's v. St. Helens St Mark's. flaydock Ramblers v. gartestown Ist. Millfield Rovers v. Ashton Recreation 2nd or Earlestown Rovers. The first-named club in each fie has the choice of ground. and all ties have to be played off on or before to-day (Satur- day.

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

THE MISSION AT VlThosst.—The special mission a the Vulcan—in the schoolroom—under the Manchester City Mission, has been continued each evening during the present week. As last week, the services have been con- ducted by Mr. W. H. Pritchett, assisted by Mr. Dring, the Earlestown town missionary. GOOD TEXPLARY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day evening, under the presidency of Bro. George E. War- burton, W.C.T. After the transaction of formal business, suggestions in regard to the election of lodge deputy mid electoral superintendent were considered. DRINK Ai:max.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Patrick Heavey , of Earlestown, was brought up in custody, having failed to answer a summons, for being drunk and disorderly at Ear- lestown on the 3rd inst. He was fined 20s and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment in default of payment. FOOTBALL: EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. EARLESTOWN ROYERS.—These teams met on the ground of the first named at Newton Common on Tuesday evening, when the Wan- derers won by three goals to one. A second match between the two teams took place on the same ground on Wednes- day evening. The game came to an abrupt termination by Ike bursting of the ball after 20 minutes' play. No goal had been scored by either side during that period. TRH Bows FIDE TRAVELLER QuEsnorr.—At the New- ton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Michael Holleran was summoned for being found on licensed premises during pro- hibited hours, and further with falsely representing himself to be a traveller. The defendant did not appear. and P.S. Commina stated that on the previous night, a little before 10 o'clock, one of the constables met him with another man at Wargrave. The defendant was then drunk, and he said he was going away and did not intend to appear in answer to the summons. A warrant was issued for the defendant's apprehension.. TEMPERANCE MEETING.—On Saturday night a pub- lic meeting and entertainment were held in the Good Tem- plars' Lodge Room, Bridge-street. The •chair was occupied by Brother George Clarke, District Coun., who gave an appropriate address. The programme included songs by Brother J. McDonald, Brother John Taylor, Brother George Clarke (chairman), Sister E. Clarke; recitations by Mr. Barlow (Wigan), Brother J. Waddington, Sister Morris (Ashton), A. White, Brother John Warburton- readings by Brother E. Newman, Brother J. Barnard, Brother E. C. Matthews; and a duet by Sisters E. and J. Clarke. A cordial vote of thanks to the entertainers closed the pro- ceedings. NEWTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION: LETTER FROM Mn. GLADSTONE.—A fortnight ago, at the finish of the business of the annual meeting of the Liberals of Newton Division of South-West Lancashire, a vote of confidence in Mr. Gladstone and the Government was unanimously passed, and the chairman (Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P.) was directed to forward a copy of the resolution to the Premier. On Friday last the following acknowledgment was received :—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, April 8, 1886. Sir,—l am directed, by Mr. Gladstone to inform you that he has received the communication which you have done him the honour to send him, and to convey to you his thanks for the expression of approval and confidence in Her Majesty's Government which it contains.-1 am sir, your obedient servant, G W. SPENCER LVTTLETON. C. Pilkington, Esq." SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO Mn. SAMUEL HRWITT.—On Saturday afternoon the well known and highly respected veterinary surgeon, residing in Park-road, Newton, met with a serious accident. About half-past one o'clock Mr. Hewitt and his ND, Mr. Samuel John Hewitt, were driving in their gig along Mill-lane, and just as they got beneath tbe railway arch at Newton Bridge station an express train passed overhead and momen- tarily startled the horse. The animal fell, and as both shafts smashed, the occupants of the vehicle were thrown out. The son fortunately alighted on his feet, and escaped unhurt; but Mr. Hewitt, Ben., fell heavily upon his left side, and it was immediately discovered he had sustained serious injury. In addition to the violent shock, his left shoulder had been dislocated. Mr. Hewitt was conveyed home in one of his cabs (called from the stand at the elation), and was subsequently attended by Dr. Hannah, of Ashton, and with the help of Dr. Watkins, of Newton, the limb was set. Since the accident Mr. Hewitt has made pro- gress towards recovery. CHILDREN'S CONCERT.—The annual concert by the members of Mr. H. J. Darman's Juvenile Singing Class was held in the Co-operative Hall. Earle-street, on Wednes- day evening. The gatherhus was in every respect a most gratifying success, and the densely-crowded hall testified to Mr. Darman's continued popularity. The juvenile vocalists looked exceedingly pretty, and the splendid style in which the various . selections were rendered evidenced careful training. Mr. Durman accompanied his pupils on the piano. 'forte. The vocalists were Misses Maggie Conway, Betsy Smith, Polly Jonas, Ruth Urin, Polly Owen, Susannah Warburton, Eliza Lord, Agnes Gosling, Jessie Limond, Hettv Hill, Maggie Edwardson, Lizzie and Lucy Winetan- ley, Bertha Jackson, Becca Jones, Nellie Lawrence, and Masters Willie Owen and William Robert Sutton. Warm applause followed each piece, and the enthusiasm of the audience was maintained to the end. Before the last piece was sung Mr. Durman, who was heartily applauded, stepped forward and thanked those present for their kindness in attending that gathering, and thereby encouraging the young children in their efforts.
