div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

_ What animal always plays a leading part in life ?—A blind man's dog. A bar in the river and a bar on shore have the same name, because water is scarce in both places. "Do make yourselves at home, ladies," said a lady to her visitors the other day; "I am at home myself, and I wish you all were. Old age is the night of life, as night is the old age of the day. Still night is full of magnificence, and for many it is more brilliant than day. It is said of a popular lecturer that on announcing to his wife, who had her own opinion about his talents, that he was going to lecture at Sheffield, the lady replied, "At Sheffield! I'm so glad; I always hated those Sheffield people." Mrs. Partington Bays the only way' to prevent steamboat 'explosions is to make engineers boil the water on shore. In her opinion all the bustin is done by the. very careless prac- tice of cooking the steam on board the ship. •Sterne, who used his wife very ill, once said to Garrick, The hasband who behaves unkindly to his wife deserves to have his house burned over his head." "If you think so," :said Garrick, "I hope your house is insured." "Curr-Citler."—" The name Eve," says Baxtorf, in his Hebrew Lexicon, "is derived from a root signifying talk." It was perhaps from this that the Rabbins derived their 'tradition that twelve baskets of "chit.chat " were rained down into Paradise for Adam and Eve to amuse themselves with, of which twelve Adam picked up three, and Eve the 'other nine. "What is Smith doing now ?" "He is travelling with a -circus." "Pretty hard work, isn't it ?" "No; he has .nothing to do except to stick his head in the big lion's .mouth twice a day." Cause AND EFFECT.—A. lady in a fashionable London -aquare has a cat which in the course of last year broke fifty .plates, six cream jugs, two brass candlesticks, three soup -tureens, fifteen teacups, and one poker, and has eaten no leas than thirty chickens, two sweetbreads, seven turkeys, three legs of lamb, ten gooseberry pies, and three pots of ,Dreserved apricots. Nevertheless, this cat is the greatest favourite with the cook and all the servants. Rtarroinc.—The clergyman who thus described an every- 'day horse transaction was on his high horse of rhetorical sublimity "You may kindly guide the prancing steed to : the crystal brook which babbles down the hillside in the summer sun, but you cannot coerce him to stoop and slake his thirst in the silvery stream if he be not willing to accept your proffered kindness." A Spanish miser fell into a river. A peasant, seeing that the current would carry him away, held out his hand, cry- ing, "Give me your hand!" Give! He had never done such a thing in his life, and would sooner die than begin! Luckily for him, the stream carried him close to a fisher- man, who said, "My man, take my hand!" As soon as it was a question of taking, it was all right; and he was

saved. Anotrr THE EMILY WOH3f.—A father had been lecturing his young hopeful upon the evils of staying out late at night and getting up late in the morning. "You will never be good for anything," he continued, "unless you turn over a new leaf. Remember that the early bird catches the worm." "How about the worm, father ? " inquired the young man. " Wasn't he rather foolish to get up so early?" "My Km," replied the old man solemnly. " that worm hadn't been to bed at all ; he was on his way home." When Mr. W. S. Gilbert was in America two or three years ago, a Mrs. Malaprop who met him, and probably mistook him for the musical partner of the firm of Gilbert and Sullivan, asked him a number of questions that re- -Tealed a plentiful lack of information on the subject of contemporary music. winding up with a query as to whether "Batch" (Bach) was composing anything just now. "No, madam," Mr. Gilbert replied, with perfect imperturbabiliM " Batch ' hasn't composed anything for years. Ele's de- coppoeing just now." Fon HOLDERS OF THE GHLVITATION THEORY RH- smarm° GLAClERS.—Professor Geikie, with some geological friends, once paid a visit to Kingston in East Lothian, and was examining some rocks there which slope down to the public road, when a ploughman passed. Therustic overheard .the professor's remarks about the striking indication thee.
GENERAL NEWS.

The Corporation of Dewsbury has resolved to erect a ne town hall at a cost, including land, of about £38,000. There appears to be little room to doubt that the price of wheat has now reached a point so low as to discourage its cultivation in the United States. Mr. Joseph Cowen, M.P., writing to a correspondent at Newcastle-on-Tyne, says :—" The present Parliament will soon be finished, and with it my parliamentary duties will terminate." LINSEED LOZENGES, solidified linseed tea, laxative and de- mulcent, lid; postage 2d. Kay, Brothers, Stockport, and all Cbemists.—Advt. The possibility of an increased duty being placed on French wines is causing great activity amongst the wine growers; 8000 cases of champagne were landed at Dover on Monday, and there are 20,000 more at Calais waiting ship- ment. THE VACANCY AT BRADFORD.—At the meeting of the I Executive of the Bradford Liberal Association, on Monday evening, it was unanimously resolved to invite Mr. Shaw- Lefevre to become the candidate for the Central division of the Borough. THE STEPNEY ELECTION PETITION. Judgment Was given in the Stepney election case on! Monday. Of the Hanoverian voters who had been struck off the poll, 16 had voted for the petitioner, Mr. Isaacson, the Conservative, and seven for Mr. Durant, Liberal, who, therefore, retains his seat. DESPERATE STRUGGLE WITH A BURGLAR.—TWO Police- men at Sheffield, named Crawford and Moore, on Saturday evening succeeded, after a desperate struggle, in capturing two thieves who bad broken into the ivory warehouse of Mr. J. A. Horton, in that town. Crawford was considerably in- jured in the struggle. A VICTIM To GAMBLING.—At Manchester Police Court, on Monday, a traveller named Dunkerley, in the service of a firm of wholesale provision merchants, was charged with embezzling nearly £lOOO from his employers. Prisoner ad- mitted his guilt, and said he had lost all the money in betting on horses. Commencing with small bets he had grown reckless, and betted £lO. £2O. or £lOO at once. He , was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment. Condy's Fluid is not poisonous, and has no smell. The Tones says : Condy's Fluid is the best purifier and disinfectant known to science. Caution—To prevent imposition, ask for CONDY'S I FLUID, and see that you get it—Advt. GERMAN ENTERPRISE IN THE TEXTILE INDUSTRY.—The German textile industry is engaged in a great undertaking by which it is hoped to extend the fame of German manu- facturers in various parts of the world. The idea is to equip two new vessels to serve as floating exhibitions of the products of the German textile mdustry. The exhibi- tion is to be thoroughly representative, and it is especially intended to visit the new colonies for the purpose of in- troducing the manufactures there, but all the chief seaport markets of the world will also be visited. Some of the large textile manufacturers are at the bottom of the project. PASSENGER STEAMERS WRECKED.—SERIOn Loss OF LIFE.—The steamer Taiaroa' belonging to the Union Steam- ship Company, New Zealand, and coasting between Welling- ton and Christchurch, has been wrecked near Kaikoura. The vessel struck during a violent gale. Three boats which were lowered capsized. one of them containing 29 persons, of whom only three -escaped. The total loss of life is un- known. The Italian steamer Oxford struck on a rock off Panta Campanella on Monday, and has become a total wreck. A large number of persons were drowned. The captain, horrified at the loss of his vessel and passengers, shot himself. TEN SHOP Harms REGULATION BILL.—On Monday morn- ing the secretary of the Pawnbrokers and Traders' Associa- tion of London was called before Sir John Lubbocles Select Committee to give evidence in opposition to the Shop Hours Regulation Bill. The entire trade, he said, bad come to the conclusion that the bill was dangerous, and they could not see where it would end. The hours which young people worked were not excessive, and he bad never known a case of ill-health arising from overwork. He was of opinion that it was a mistake to limit the hours of employment. as by so doing it was detrimental to the people. The longer the hours of labour the better the condition of the people. Saturday half holidays led to much mischief and extravagance. (Laughter.) A MERCHANT SENT TO PENAL SERVITUDE.—Robert S. Bourne, 41, a colonial merchant, was indicted at the Cen- tral Criminal Court, London, on Saturday, for having in his custody, without lawful excuse, a certain stone upon which a certain part of a bank note ofillte Colonial Bank was en- graved and made. The prisoner is a colonial merchant of considerble standing in Barbadoes, and Game to London for the purpose of making his annual purchases for his stores. The explanation offered by the prisoner in defence was that he was a large advertiser, and intended to fill up the spaces with advertisements connected with his business. It was mentioned, as showing the prisoner's eccentricity in the matter of advertisements, that be had in Barbadoes started bicycles, which he had painted red, placing upon them olack men painted white.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced by the recorder to five years' penal servitude. THE SOCIALISTS' TRIAL.—Tbe trial of the London Socialists, Messrs. Hyndman, Burns, Champion, and Wil- liams, was resumed at the Old Bailey on Saturday. Hynd- man addressed the court in defence. Be took the fullest responsibility for his actions, but contended that be had not I used any language which would be calculated to excite to riot. He had spent a large fortune in the cause of Socialism, which he believed had already borne fruit. He maintained that England was the most Socialistic country in the world. and in support of his case quoted from the writings of Adam Smith.—The Attorney-General, replying on the whole case, said the speech for the defence had no relevance to the question at issue, which involved no question of the right of speech. If the defendants used language contrary to law' motive could be no excuse. He denied that the defen- dants had the right to claim that they were the only cham- pions of the poor. He proceeded to urge that the methods adopted by the defendants were not constitutional.and law- ful, and that there had been no real attempt made to deny that defendants bad made use of violent and inflammatory language to forward what they called the social revolution. —The jury returned a verdict of "Not Guilty," but ex- pressed the opinion that the language of Messrs. Burns and Hynnman was highly inflammatory, and greatly to be condemned, although they acquitted them of seditious in- tent. Tho foreman added that, considering the circum- stances of the public excitement at the moment, and after the reports in the press of the speeches delivered, the jury were of opinion that the prosecution was rightly in- otituted. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY. The new members enjoy the advantage and privi-

lege of seeing the House- of Commons at its very best. Through four successive sittings the debate on the introduction of the Home Rule Bill has been maintained at high pressure, and when the House of Commons works at high pressure it is without a rival. The distinction of creating the necessity for chairs to be placed on the floor of the House remains reserved to Mr. Gladstone; but on other occasions the Chamber has been densely crowded, and all the principal speakers of the House save one have joined in debate. The one is Mr. Bright, who has sat at- tentive night after.night, but has shown no indication of desire to speak. During Mr. Gladstone's speech on Thursday, he occupied the corner seat below the gangway, from which in times past he delivered all his memorable speeches. On that occasion Mr. Chamberlain had in the rush been landed above the gangway. • But on Friday night, when his turn came to speak, he induced Mr. Bright to lend him the corner seat, and he has since retained it, Mr. Bright sitting just below him. There were, of course, rumours that Mr. Bright intended to speak. Possibly he will before the second reading is agreed to. But on a first reading there was no call for him or any one else except ex-Ministers charged with the delivery of personal explanations. The motion for leave to introduce a bill is usually regarded as a . formality, meaning little more than obtaining per- mission to get the bill printed. We have had the Home Rule Bill debated for four nights, and joy in this formal success is tempered by the knowledge that on the second reading we shall have from the same orators speeches very much to the same effect. The first reading was agreed to without a divi- sion, a conclusion which has greatly distressed the advisers of the Conservatives in the London press. The Times, which has become almost maudlin in its opposition, shrieked aloud that every stage of the bill must be divided upon. But the Conservatives .re.membered how a month or two back they were advised upon the same authority to contest- every seat vacated by the nomination of a Minister in Mr. Gladstone's Government, a scheme which, as far as it was carried out, did.not greatly benefit them. Wiser counsels prevailed, and at an early hour of yesterday morning, in a crowded House amid loud cheering, the bill was read a first time. Mr. Glad- stone, who seems to get younger and stronger, amidst the difficulties of the situation spoke again. At ordinary times he strictly observes the injunc- tions of the doctor, and abstains from late atten- dance at the House. On Tuesday night he sat it out, winding up the debate with a speech of great vivacity and power. Amid the gloomy prognostica- tions of the day he alone stands hopeful—even certain. "My plan," he said, "holds the field. It has many enemies. It has not a single rival." The political situation stands in a very curious and complicated state, but I fancy on the whole it is tending in a direction favourable to Mr. Glad- stone. His strong point is touched upon in the de- claration quoted above. He has a plan and no one has an alternative. He is also ready, as indicated in the speech of Tuesday night, to accept any modi- fications that may recommend themselves to the majority of the House, and may promise improve- ment on the original scheme. The opposition of Lord Hartington, Mr. Chamberlain' Mr. Trevelyan, and Mr. Goschen is in no degree modified. But they do not make adequate impression upon the mind of the average member, who has been waiting for months to make up his mind, form a definite opin- ion, and take an absolute side. He is now moving towards Mr. Gladstone, and will doubtless end by espousing his cause. Various estimates of the result of the division on the second readisig are current, most of them giving a majority larger or smaller for the bill. Twenty- five is a figure which meets with general favour. That is, however, not sufficient to carry such a bill through the remaining stages, much less to induce the House of Lords to alter their pre-determination to throw it out. A nominal majority of 25 would actually, setting aside the Irish vote, be a minority of GO. /With command of the solid vote of 85' which the Irish members seem inclined to secure him, it will bp difficult to defeat Mr. Gladstone at any stage of the measure. But the Lords will make short work of it, and then the country will be asked to say what it thinks of the definite measure. The suicide of Lord Shaftesbury has created a painful sensation which is, perhaps, more connec- ted with the familiar title than with its latest bearer. To the English people there has been for the last half century only one Lord Shaftesbury—the tall, grave-faced gentleman who devoted his whole life and resources to the benefit of his fellow men. • The unfortunate man who has just died by his own hand was a stranger to the public. So little was he known that when Lord Shaftesbury died many people looked upon his second son, Evelyn, as his successor to the title, unaware even of the existence of the elder brother. Lord Ashley, as he was till but the other day called, was a plain man of unambi- tious turn of fnind. Thirty years ago he was in the navy, and to the last affected something of the sea- man in his dress. He was the last man that might have been suspected of the intention to commit suicide; and yet he hit upon quite a new thing in the art. Suicides have many eccentric ways of ac- complishing a purpose which is usually suggested by madness. But never before did one hire a four- -wheeled cab in the centre thoroughfare of a great town and there kill himself. It is curious that Lord Shaftesbury, having entered the cab with deliberate suicidal intent, carefully bargained with the man for the amount of his fare. Cabby was to drive up and down, from the bottom to the top of Regent- street. "What will be the fare," said Lord Shaftes- bury. "I don't know, sir," said the wary cabman. "Then say a shilling a turn." "Very well," said the reasonably pleased cabby, and before three shillings was earned he had a corpse for his fare. The craze of table turning has absolutely gone out of fashion, and it is quite a long time since we heard of our old friend Planchette. I hear of a new thing, much more wonderful than Planchette, that is now coming into vogue. It consists of a rect- angular board two feet long by eighteen inches wide, on which are placed all the letters of the alphabet. A miniature three-legged table on small rollers is placed on the top of the board. Two per- sons sit down with their finger tips on the table in the old fashion suitable for table turning. A.ques- tion is asked and the table forthwith moves about and with its legs pointing to successive letters of the alphabet spells out the answer. There is some- thing novel about this, though it is not likely to succeed in reviving the excitement which once gathered about moving tables and revolving hats. Just now London, as far as it is turning its atten- tion to matters of this kind is concerning itself with mesmerism. But, on the whole, this falls a little fiat. The excitement of events at Westminster has brought down the Prince of Wales with great fre- quency. He was there last Thursday when Mr. Gladstone delivered his great speech, and has once or twice since been seen in the gallery. It is noticed, as an odd circumstance, that he avoids the seat over the clock which he has been accustomed to take ever since his first appearance in the Peers' Gallery. On Thursday, this favoured place was left for Prince Christian, the Prince of Wales sitting next-but-one below the Duke of Cambridge. On Friday night His Royal Highness again selected another seat. It is said that he was annoyed at a picture in "Punch " which, illustrating the familiar newspaper report "The Prince of Wales occupied his usual seat over the clock," drew him seated in alternative positions, one in a chair set on the top of the clock, the other cross- legged over the barrel of the clock. That, however, seems a too absurd sensitiveness not like the Prince of Wales. I never saw him looking so well as he does just now. Early in the year he suffered a good deal from dyspepsia, and has lately submitted to dieting himself. Lean mutton and stale bread form the principal items in his daily food. They seem to agree with him very well. There is talk in high, life of a divorce case which will put in the shade the Crawford v. Dilke scandal. All the persons concerned belong to the highest rank. The respondent, though not what is , known as a professional beauty, is very handsome. There are no less than four co-respondents, one of them holding high office, and all bearing familiar and distinguished names. To the petitioner, the respondent, and one of the co-respondents a visit to the divorce court will be no new thing. They have figured in earlier cases. To the other three co-res- pondents the experience will be novel. Efforts are being made to keep the case out of court, but it is believed they ipust of necessity fail. The dis- closures that wAI be made are calculated to shake our comfortable faith in the purity of the Victorian court as compared with the Georges for example. The fact seems to be that whilst at the present day greater effort is made to hide guilt, society is really no better than it was when George the 111. was Xing.

Sir,--One of your readers reminded me the other day of my promise to give another three-course vegetarian dinner recipe, through the medium of your valuable journal. I therefore hasten to filial my promise.

NO. 2 DINNER FOR SIX PERSONS. LENTIL Sou.—One lb. lentils, 2d ; one or two onions, and pepper and salt to taste, Id ; cost, 2id. Directiogs Wash the lentils, put them with the onions (sliced) into tive pints of boiling water, and boil fast for one hour, adding the seasoning a few minutes before serving Whole lentils make the best soup. Let them boil rapidly without stop- ping for twO to three hours. More onions or other veget- ables and a little oil or butter may be added. ' MACARONI CHEESE.—HaIf lb. macaroni, 2,id ; 4oz. cheese., 2d ; I-pint milk, id; I egg, id ; a few breadcrumbs, a little butter, mustard, allspice, pepper and salt. id ; cost. 74d. Direct;ons ; Drop the macaroni into boiling water, slightly salted, keep at boiling heat until tender, put half into a dish, sprinkle on it half the cheese (grated or chopped fine), then use the rest of the macaroni and cheese in the same way, beat up the egg, add to it the milk, with a little mos- tard, salt, pepper, and ground allspice, pour this mixture on the cheese, sprinkle a few breadcrumbs on the top, adding two or three small pieces of butter, and bake 20 minutes. Four lbs. of potatoes, cost, 2d. Two los, of carrots, boiled, cost id. DATE Pununto.--Three-quarters lb. maize meal, td ; IMb. dates, 3l; 6oz. sugar' id; cost, 413. Boil the meal as a porridge for 20 minutes, carefully pick over the dates, and stir them with the sugar into the sauce- pan, turn into a disb, and bake one hour. Total cost is 6d. As my attention has been drawn to my first letter on this subject by other individuals, I will with your permission continue to give other sample dinners from time to time ; -since it is gratifying to know that the question of diet is receiving attention from all classes of society. Warrington, April sth, 1886. W. H. CHAPMAN.

div.head: TEMPERANCE REFORM.
div.p: TEMPERANCE REFORM.

Sir,—Scveraf-letie; have appeared in your columns of late respecting the great drink question, but none of them, so far as I have observed, approach the question from a free trade point of view. I humbly opine that it would be in- finitely better, instead of passing repressive measures for the regulation, and indeed discouragement, of the traffic, to treat the sellers of drink in the same way as the sellers of any other article of legitimate commerce—that, is giving to any man absolute liberty to open a public-house or club, and sell drink without licence and without restraint,except in the way of insisting upon the drink being consumed off the premises. It might be advisablr, perhaps, to insist that no loitering shall be allowed in any place in which drink is procurable, and this might be effected without the rights of the citizen being tampered with in a greater degree than at present—such, for instance, as the loitering in streets and public places of individuals whose freedom is restricted for the good of the State and the safety and welfare of all good citizens. I imagine that thousands of men and worcen would never have become drunkards but for the inducements held out to them by the bar, taproom, or snuggery in public- house or club. There they come in contact with their friends; and for the good of the house, and in order that their friends may not consider them stingy, they must needs " stand treat," regardless of the fact that they may already have had quite as much as is good for them. Were drink sold over the counter only, as I advocate should be done, no roan would take more than he wanted for his or his friends' consumption in his own house; and as a necessary re- sult of the abolition of drinking saloons, clubs on temper- ance principles would spring up which would provide for that social rntercourse which, I take it, is the chief attrac- tion that at present draws so many of our countrymen and ' countrywomen to the dramshop ; and not the drink, which I believe to be Quite a secondary consideration, if indeed it be a consideration at all to anyone, but to the miserable wretch in whom the fierce appetite has been created, and who so swiftly pursues the steep and dangerous course which leads to Avernus,—Yours, &c.,
COBDENITE.
TOXTETH AID SOCIETY AND THE UNEMPLOYED AND DESTITUTE CHILDREN.

Sir,—A number of our kind friends and donors having I expressed a wish to have a full account of our work in aid- ing the poor unemployed men and families, we trust you will permit us, through your valuable paper, to do so. Since we commenced two months ago we have aided 10,000 per- sons, men, women, and children; 4000 large loaves and 3500 packages of tea and sugar, 300 bags oatmeal, 200 bags rice, a large quantity of sago and barley, meat and potatoes; 121 r tons of coal have been sent to 250 families, giving them lcivt. each; 1500 families have had a good supply of rice milk, broth, and soup; 100 sick persons have had meat and bar:ey sent to them to make beef tea; 200 persons have had warm garments put on their naked bodies; 100 poor poor destitute children have had warm stockings and shoes and other clothes put on their poor starving bodies. Be- sides all this, our society have given 300 aged poor a boun- tiful te.. and also 1000 destitute children. We have ex- pended in this good work over one hundred pounds. The soup and milk is sent every week by two kind ladies, and all the clothes have been sent by a number of others. Every week through tbe kindness of a young gentleman (Master Tony) a large number of destitute children are provided with a bountiful dinner. We are at present issuing 600 tickets for bread and groceries, and 200 for milk and soup every week. This is the work the society has performed since it commenced, and, therefore, we feel justified in say- ing it is the greatest work of any society in Liverpool. There is no paid official—all are doing the work without fee or reward. We have a noble band of visitors. They go into the lowest courts and hovels and visit these poor men, women, and children, and, with words of comfort and also the aid in their hands, do all they can to cheer them in this their time of misery and sorrow. Many a P;.:A. Led has been comforted by the good Lee; tea sent to them, and many a dying. ,eased by the thoughtful kindness of our visitors. Our committee-rooms in Mann-street are a sight to be recnentzred on Monday and Wednesday even- ings. The hall is filled to overflowing at six o'clock, al- though the committee do not sit until 7 p.m. From six to seven a beautiful service of prayer and praise is held, and to see the way these poor men and women join in it would do any person's heart good. Last week from two to three hun- dred tried to get in, although the hall was full, and two policemen had to keep back this large crowd of unemployed men until those inside were relieved. It is the same every week, and since we have had from lack of funds to refuse 200 families, the eight has been sad and pitiful enough to melt the hardest heart.
We ask all to read our appeal on your front page, and to send us help at once. Help us to feed these poor hungry men, women, and children.— We are, sir, your obedient terYants,

W. L. SEWELL, Chairman. T. SHAW, Mr. FLETCHER, Mr. W. CHRISTIAN, Visiting Mr. JONES, Committee Mr. KAY. Mr. ASHBROOKE, I'. E. HALL, Treas., 259, Grafton-street. D. WILLIAMS, Hon. Sec., 98, Isaac-street. Committee-rooms, Wesleyan Mission-hall, Mann-street.

have to report that the Ladies' Sewing Class has continued to meet every day this week at the Town Hall, where they have nobly and generously employed themselves in making clothes mainly for the poor children, all of whom were in a wretched and deplorable condition of semi- nakedness. To see the poor little waifs after their "re- habilitation" in clean warm clothing was a sight to be remembered, and to.make glad the hearts of the contribu- tors. If it is a luxury to do rood, the working ladies at the Town Hall must be enjoying an Elysium, for, irres- pective of religious or social conditions, they have, and are, zealously working together for one common purpose, establishing among themselves, for the time at least, a bond of union by which they hope to ameliorate the condition of those less favourably placed than themselves.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 17. 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 17. 1886.

It will probably be remembered that on the 30th ult. a I public meeting was held at the Town Hall, to consider the propriety of establishing in Warrington a p-rmanent " Re- lief Society," and after some discussion it was adjourned to that day three weeks, in other words to Tuesday next, the 20th met, at 3-30 p.m., when, in addition to the resumption of that question, the Sub-Relief Committee will be glad to have the opinion of the General Committee and contributors as to the desirability of discontinuing, or otherwise, the re- I lief, inasmuch as there are conflicting opinions on that point, as well as on the mode of distribution, on which the Sub-Committee will be glad to receive instructions. The system at present adopted does not seem to give unqualified satisfaction, and it must be confessed that dry bread is rather cold cheer, and we are told that' Mara cannot live by bread alone." It is a question whether it would be better to do as they have been doing at Manchester, distribut- ing tickets to the unemployed, through the instrumentality of ladies, clergymen and Nonconformist ministers, medi- cal men, and others, and so enable them to get what they want at the shops, while avoiding the expense and repulsive machinery of red tape and the inquisitorial officialism of an organised "Relief Society." Decent but distressed working people must not be treated like the chronic pro- fessional pauper class. They must be treated with some consideration, and not to be made to feel too keenly their humiliating dependence. Want of tact in the administra- tion of eleemosinary aid to such recipients not only detracts from the gratification the service of the gift might other- wise impart, but may also have the effect of lessening in- stead of promoting a genuine feeling of gratitude. To give I gracefully, without jarring on the feelings of the recipients, requires a charity that is many-sided in thought as well as In deed; hence the necessity for entrusting such duties to persons of large sympathies, yet not lacking firmness and discrimination, and in these respects women are certainly not inferior to men. On the contrary, their quicker power of perception enables them almost intuitively to appreciate nice distinctions and shades of character, which are not so readily distinguishable to male eyes. Therefore, whatever is resolved upon on Tuesday next, it is to be hioped the lady element will be well represented.—l am. sir, your obedient servant. J. HARRISON, Treasurer. Town Hall, 16th April, 11186.

the church had been bard at work, meeting together once a week to produce the beautiful articles they saw for sale arouqd them. The object of the bazaar hardly required any words from him.to recommend it. They would agree with him that there were few things more important for us as a cation, and as individuals, than the proper education of the children of this country. (Hear, bear.) He had always held that no education was worth hav- ing unless it Was accorapanied with rel,gions teaching, and be rejoiced that he was able to take part in the proceedings that day, the object of which Was to promote the religions teaching of the people of Widnes.' (Hear, hear.) ThJugh he himself belonged to the Church of England. yet the members of that church recognised in all other Christian communities valuable allies against the Increasing power of atheism and infidelity. For his own part be should always be glad to help those Christian com- munities in every possible way be could. (Applause). He concluded by wishing the promoters of that effort every success, and declared the bazaar Open. The Rev. J. W. Chisholm, of leiyerpool, proposed, and Mr. Whitehead seconded, a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Edwards-Moss.

The motion was carried by load acclamation, and Mr. Edwards-Moss briefly replied. The "fair traders," to quote a phrase of the hon. members then commenced the sale of their wares. The btalls had been arranged round the building, and were flied with a `large assortment of goods, chiefly the result of the skilful use of the needle, and thimble by the ladies of the congre- gation. Valuable contributions had, however, been made by many friends and well-wishers, and the display was one which was a credit to all concerned. The room bad been adorned with flags and bannerettes, and appropriate mottoes, I and with the parti-coleured articles offered for 'sale presen- ted a bright appearance. The goods stalls, four in number, were superintended v Mrs Vause, Mrs Savage, Miss Hough- ton, Miss Betney, Mesdames Birkenhead, F. Atherton, Rush- ton, Boyle, Burgess, J. Betney, Wilson, Wright, and Greg. The Sunday school stalls were in charge of Misses Harri- son, A. and E. Betney, Robinson, Rimmer, and Mrs. Loch, and the refreshments were distributed by Mesdames White- head, Scrivens, Perrin, Wilcock, John Betney, Ogden, and Blundelfield. For the amusement of visitors an gallery had been arranged by Mr. John Betney, junr., and Mr. Greig, and a museum of curiosities was under the con- trol of Mr. James Waters and Mr. W. Savage. A working model of a steam engine was exhibited by Mr. T. Gibson. Mr. J. H. Hargreaves produced in the presence of the au- dience beautiful lines of harmony by a swinging pendulum termed the " harmeniagrapb." The role of an " amateur photographer " was taken by Mr. J. Ireland, and a galvanic battery, the cause of much amusement, was manipulated by Mr. Lloyd. During the evening Mr. John Betney, the musical conductor of the church, arranged and conducted a concert in which the choir rendered glees and Miss A. Bet- ney and Mr. Price contributed songs. Mr. A. Ogden. the accompanist, performed a solo on the piano. The takings on Wednesday amounted to about £5O. The sale was continued on Thursday, when the sales amounted to £3O. As there was still a large number of articles unsold, the bazaar was also open last evening, when the sum of £l7 was realised. The total amount of the fund for the erection of the school is now £145.
LATEST NE WS.
Tne Rutland Liberal Association have unanimously re: solved to invite Mr. Jesse Collings to contest the county at next election.

KILLED ON ins WEDDING DAY.—On Thursday evening just before six o'clock, Martin Perritt, a Welshman em- ployed at the Preston Dock Work?, was instantly killed, being crushed between to waggons. He was twenty years old, and married on Thursday afternoon. THE PREMIER AND THE EASTER HOTADAYS.—A Chester correspondent states that Mr. and Mrs Gladstone will spend the Easter recess at Hawarden. The right hon. gentleman is expected to arrive there on Tuesday evening next. The Rev. Harry and Mrs. Drew have been occupying the castle since their return from the honeymoon, and the Premier will consequently reside with his son, the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, at Hlwarden Rectory. THE PIMLICO CASE.—Yesterday, Mr. E. Clarke, Q.C., addressed the jury for the defence. He contended that the deceased, having given his wife to Dyson, and suffering from great pain, knowing his wife had possessed herself of chloroform to subdue his passion?, rose in the night and took the fatal draught. He appealed to the jury that the medical testimony was utterly opposed to the theory that Mrs. Bartlett could have administered it.—The case was adjlurned.

THE CYCLONES IN MINNESOTA. NEW YORK, FRIDAY.—Later details respecting the cyclones in Minnesota show the number of fatalities to be much greater than at first reported. THE CHOLERA OUTBREAK AT BRINDISI.

ALEXANDRIA, FRIDAY.—Owing to the sudden outbreak of cholera at Brindisi, the Sanitary Council have imposed seven days' quarantine upon all ves:els coming from Venice, Ancona, and Brindisi. THE CROWN PRINCE OF PRUSSIA'S ILLNESS.

BERLIN FRIDAY.—The Crown Prince, who is suffering from measles, passed a very good night owing to the com- plete development of the eruption, which tas alrea'dy begun to subside. The fever has completely disappeared, and the catarrh nearly so.

The House met at four o'clock.

The Lord Chancellor, Lord Sudeley, and Lord Collonson were the Royal Commis • sioners. QUESTIONS.—There was a full attendance of members for some time previous to prayers, but the excitement fell far short of that of last Thursday. At prayers every seat in the House had been taken, and after that the Peers' Speakers' and Strangers' Galleries were opened, and in a few minutes every seat therein was occupied.—Mr. GLAD. STONE, replying to Sir M. Beach, said he did not think it would be in his power to give any information in relation to Turkey and Greece and the Powers before Easter. The Crofters' Bill would lee proceeded with next Monday. THE RESIGNATION OF THE CLERK OF THE HOUSE.— Mr. GLAUSTONE, in feeling terms, moved a vote of thanks to Sir Erskine May on his retirement from the office of Clerk of the House..—Sir M. BEACH seconded the motion, and expressed deep regret at the right hon. gentleman's re- titement.—Mt. C. RAISES and Mr. PARNELL added their regrets to those which had been expressed.—The motion was Carried item con.
THE IRISEI LAND BILL. MR. GLADS fONE'S SPEECH.

Mr. GLADSTONE, amid cheering, then rose io ask leave to introduce a Bill to amend the provision for the sale and ply-chase of land in Ireland. He commenced by observing the difficulty of the subject and the diversity of opinion that existed. The Government in their. Irish legislation asked the House not merely to make arrangements for the good of Ireland and Irish matters by Irish laws, but also to make a serious endeavour to settle the land question.iThe first question he proposed to ask was--Is it necessary to deal with the subject at all? In pursuance of this necessity, he quoted extracts from Froude's English in Inland as to the origin of agrarian crime, which was continued throughout the past century with at times a terrible facility to expand to alarming dimensions. There was one union, be said, that never failed of terrible issue. When oppression was married to misery the issue was a fatal and hideods progeny of crime. Continuing the second question, he asked, Why should Great Britain be encumbered with an endeavour to settle this difficulty? He urged that Great Britain could not escape responsibility in respect of the matter, for the deeds of the Irish landlords were our own deeds. In proof of this responsibility he reviewed the legislation of the century on behalf of both the landlord and the tenant. Coming to the provisions of the measure, he stated that it was to take effect on the same day as the Irish Government Act. Purchases were to be made in a Three per Cent Stock, to be. issued to the amount of £180,000,000, under regula- tions made by the Treasury, the object of the bill being to give to all landlords the option of being bought out. As re- garded agricultural land, a State authority, appointed by the Legislature in Dublin, would act as the middle term be- tween buyer and seller. As a rule, but with one or two ex- ceptions, applications must be for the whole of a tenanted estate. They must be registered, and would rank according to priority. Power would be given to the Land Commis- sion to refuse applications in exceptional cases. The pur- chase price is to be based upon the net rental for the year ending last November, and the net rental to be ascertained by deducting the rates and outgoing of such as had charges and management expenses. The basis of the calculation was to be that where the laud was in good condition the landlord was to have twenty years' purchase. As to the financial aspects of the scheme, it was proposed that in respect to notices issued during the financial years 1887, 1888. they should issue £10,000,000. In each of the two succeeding year, they would authorise the issue of £20,000,000, making £50,000,000 which would be the sum authorised to be spent by the Act, the £180,000,000 being the total stock created. He argued tkat a landlord, with a gross rental of £1,200 and a net rental of £960, at the nominal rate of compensation, at 20 years' purchase, would receive £19,400. It was proposed to appoint a receiver general for Ireland, through whose hands all Irish revenues should pass, and by whom not one shilling would be allowed to be apnropriated to Irish purposes until the interest on the new stock was met. He then examined in detail the position of the landlord, and tenant, and state authority in giving effect to the Act. After pointing out that the British taxpayer would incur no serious risk in consequence of the operations of the Act, he concluded by urging the measure on the House as a necessary complement of the Irish Government Bill. (Cheers.) Mr. CHAMBERLAIN made a further explanation, as to his reasons for leaving the Government, and adversely criti- cised the new measure. The debate was continued by Mr. W. H. Smith, Mr. Forwood, and other members.

div.head: WIDNES UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH.
div.p: WIDNES UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH.

A numerous company assembled in the Unitel Methodist Free Church, Zion Chapel. Oakland-street, Widnes, on the occasion of the opening of a two days' bazaar, having for its object, the augmenting of a fund which has been started for the purpose of erecting a new Sunday school. At pre- sent the children are taught in the chapel, under inconve- nient and uncomfortable conditions, awl unburdened by any debt the cemmittee have come to the wise decision to build a Sunday school on laud already in the possession of the trustees of the church. Amongst those present at the opening ceremony were—Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. for Widnes Division, the Revs. W. Vanse, J. W. Chisholm, George Bond, M.A. (vicar of Farnworth), Major Cross, Messrs. J. H. Hargreaves, G. Pride. J. Matthews, W. Treacv, , D. Wright, John Betney, T. S. Swale, W. A. Savage, A. ' Houghton, E. Gandy, J. W. Hargreaves, J:c. After devo- tional exercises, The Rev. W. Yause called upon Mr. Moss to open the baler. He mentioned that Mrs. Paynton. who would have been very glad to be present, bad been very ill for a long period, but she had kindly sent £5 towards their funds. (Ap- plause.) Other small sums had been received, so that they started that bazaar with about £lO in hand towards the amount they hoped to realise. (Applause.) Mr. Moss, who bad a very cordial reception, said that a few days agn it was very doubtful whether he should be able to visit Widnes, because the tremendous crisis which existed in Parliament might entail his presence in the House of Commons that day. But he could assure them that it was with very great pleasure that he found he could get away at a late heur last night and fulfil his promise to be present with' them. (Applause.) He considered it a great honour to be asked by a body of men amongst whom he was sure there were many political opponents of his. He could only assure them that it would be his endeavour and his pleasure always to do all he could for the interests of his constituents, of whatever class, political party, and religious denomination they might belong. (Applause.) He believed that members of this church were as a rule Liberals—(laughter and applause)— and he had no doubt that the teachers in the school which was about to be built wouid probably be Liberals also. (Laughter.) That reminded him that en one occasion the late Lord Cairns, a great and good man, who did much to- wards education, was told by a friend that the Conservative outlook was dark, because most of the schoolmasters of the country were Liberals. "On the contrary," said Lord Cairns, with a smile of quiet humour, "I see in this the great hope of our nation, for the boys are certain to be Con- servatives." (Applause.) He sincerely hoped that that would be the case in that school. (Laughter and applause.) The little band which founded the church met some 13 years ago for the first time, and within 12 months of that meeting the foundation stone of that building was laid; and 'in the process of time this building was completed. •The cost was about £5OO. It spoke very well for the energy and enthusiasm of that small band when he told them that within two years that sum was entirely paid off. (Hear, hear.) Then there were only the bare white walls of the building and a few forms, and in a short time it was found that certain improvements were required. These improve meets were carriedout_at a further cost of £2OO, which sum was entirely paid olf two years ago, so that this church is entirely free from debt. (Applause.) He only wished that some other churches:with which he was still more closely cennected were in the same condition (Hear, hear.) Tbere were now 300 scholars attending school, and a staff of 40 teachers. The consequence was that it was absolutely necessary that there should be better accommodation. It was proposed to build a new Sunday school on land adjoining that building. The school would be 58 feet by' 30 feet. with two vestries, and the cost was estimated at £4OO. The land was already in possession of the committee. The amount of money subscribed to the school fund was now about £5O. A harveet festival last September produced £23, an entertainment realised £5, a tea meeting brought in £l5, and other small sums had been received. They hoped by that bazaar to raise £2O0— (hear, hear)—and he was perfectly certain that they would agree with him that they had every chance of doing so. The members of the church had not been idle; and the ladies of

div.head: _ IRIS H QUESTION,
div.p: THE _ IRIS H QUESTION,

Sir.—" The hour has come; the fateful hour for which two nations wait." Hitherto we hive been used to look upon England, Ir.land, Scotland. and Wales as forming parts of one kingdom, and for at least eighty years some attempt has bean made to govern the people, with the ultimate view of self-government. From the quotation given above, the "Barrel Organ" of Truth would lead us to infer that not one nation, but "two nations," have been waiting "to cut one Parliament in two to make two nations one." English- men are now brought to face one of the most important problems this country has prodeced, and the question—bow shall we solve it ?—is of a most perplexing character. That the time has arrived when Nome Rule of some kind must be accorded to the Irish, as a right, none can deny; or that what we want is Home Rule of a kind that will foster the principle of federation, and not of a kind that will tend to- wards driving nations further apart. In the "Freeman" of March 27th, the Irish are represented as asking for "the greatest amount of self-government compatible with the unity of the empire." This must be the accepted principle upon which we hope to see our statesmen work. Mr. Gladstone has now brought the people of Great Britain to the point, and their answer will very soon have to determine the question. Are we to have the scenes of the past ten years re-enacted ? Is Ireland to be again given over to the tender mercies of the " village tyrant " ? Are we again to see Engl and and her noble buildings at the mercy of bands of dynamiters? It would be interesting to see the sum total spent on Ire- land duriog the past eighty years in trying to preserve peace. I can fancy the amount paid in providing soldiers and police, to keep her Majesty's loving Irish subjects in order, would be an eye opener to many an Englishman. Yet we have Mr. Gladstone's word for it, that the coercion of the past has been but "fencing and skirmishing." If resorted to in the future, it must "be adequate to the attainment of Its end," and not "a spurious and ineffectual coercion." Sir, I feel these are words that may well m'ake us pause and con- eider what we are about. The ties of party will, I have no doubt, be strong with us all, but will it be unfair to ask those wbo oppose the Government proposition what is 1-their alternative. Being, as we are, "between the devil and the deep sea," how are we to get out of the difficulty? I must at once say that with the Government proposi- tion, as a principle, lam in sympathy. Give the bill the benefit of amendments worked out on the lines of Mr. Cbam- berlain's critical speech, and Ireland would receive Home ' Rule of a kind Mr. Isaac Butt never dreamt of. 1 The position of our Tory friends during the present crisis is something ludicrous. The only policy they seem to have lis one made up of the imploring cry, "come over and help us." Even that arch-anarchist, Mr. Chamberlain, would be welcomed into their ranks now, if only he would help the Ulster Tories to line the hedges and ditches of Ireland with swords and bayonets to keep off those terrible Lend Leaguers. The next thing I expect to hear is Lord Randolph pleading with Mr. Bradlaugh to help to preserve ; our glorious constitution. Stranger things than this have happened, during the past two years, in the Tory camp. One cannot eaaily forget what happened in Warrington ' last November. The advent of Mr. Biggar and Mr. T. P. 1, O'Connor upon us poor Warringtonlans was something that causedthe Greenallites to shake with laughter and delight. The fervid oratory of Mr. Loughlin, given forth in the deep and solemn tones he knows so well how to assume, is still ringing in my ears. I wonder if he is prepared to take the chair now, after reading his co-patriots' speeches in the House of Commons, in a demonstration against the "Ci.O.M.?" I guess not. Yet there N one thing he might do ; taxation should go hand in hand with representation, and his duty should just now be to make Irishmen in War- rington see this.

With such knowledge RS is at present to be obtained re- specting the Irish Land Bill, I must acknowledge to feeling a decided opposition to the land purchase portion et the scheme. What in the name of goodness are we to pay £120,000,000 to a lot of land grabbers fer ? I see it stated now that £60,000,000 is the sum likely to be fixed by Government. I should like to know on what basis this or any other sum is fixed. To me the position seems clear enough. Grant the Irish a parliament of their own and let the landlords deal with the Irish as a nation. Why should our National Debt be further saddled with each enormous sums?

The " Freeman " says :—" Irish landlords have better pe ior fair Consideration at the needs of their own fellow countrymen than at the hands of Englishmen." Sir hmes Caird says:—"! should fear that from the land any econo- mical rent has for the present disappeared." The "Times" says that there are 538,000 holdings averaging £6 each, now subject to a rent of £3,572,000; and it goes on to declare that "it is not too much to say that the rental of the 538,000 holdings is practically irrecoverable by anybody, whether landlord, English Government, or Irish Govern- ment." After this statement I ask how can any one have the conscience to ask Englishmen to pay into the pockets of the landlords anything like the sums mentioned? or any sums other than the precise value of the land? The Irish land question has an interest in it of far mere Importance to English workmen than they seem to be aware of. It is an established fact that the population of Ireland is yearly growing less. Why Is this? It is not that their fecundity has become abnormal. Nature and the religious training of the Irish prohibit this. The answer is, that the Irish are driven out of Ireland into our English towns by the inhuman land laws that at present exist. The English peasant and the Irish peasant are I driven off the land and forced into competition with the urban population, thereby increasing local rates and reduc- ing landlord's expenses. 621,000 people have, within the 'past 20 years, beer: forced into the towns in consequence of a determination to find what Mr. Disraeli called the three Iprofits, vii, the landlord's, the farmer's, and the labourer's. There is but one profit to be had from the land, and it be- longs to him who tills the ground. It is clear from this that the Radical Programme is fast becoming an accom- plished fact ; the lend must belong to the people And not to individuals; the profits of labour must belong to the worker, and not to the investor, using the word worker is its best sense.—Yours, kc., 'CLIFFORD DIX. April 12th, 1886.

SHOCKING DEATH OF AN OFFICER.—Lient. Evans, of the Chatham Division of Marines, was found with his throat cut in his quarters at the Marine Barracks, Chatham, on Tuesday morning. Deceased had been cohabiting with a woman named 'Vaughan, and after the discovery of his death she was found in the quarters of another officer. An inquest was held on Tuesday evening. Bessie Vaughan, who was found in the room at the time of the tragedy, de- posed that she visited the deceased at his quarters shortly after midnight. He complained of her being late. They had a quarrel, in the course of which Lieut. Evans took a revolver from a table, placed it to his head and fired. He fell to the Moor, and she ran and obtained the assistance of two offiurs. She saw the letter produced lying on the table. The letter was read, and was as follows :—‘• I have killed myself solely because Hettie Vaughan, the only girl I ever loved, has been untrue to me. Anything of mine she may wish to have please give it to her in memory of a man who she only appreciated a short time.—EDGAR EVANS." The inquiry was adjourned until Thursday next. On Thursday the jury returned a verdict of suicide during temporary insanity. THE NEW QUEENS'S CHAPLAIN.—The Ven. Arch- deacon Blakeney, D.D.' Vicar of Sheffield, has been graciously appointed by the Queen to be one of Her Majesty's Chaplain's in Ordinary. This distinction is well merited. The new Queen's Chaplain was formerly curate to his brother, the late Canon Blakeney, Vicar of Christ Church, Birkenhead. From ,1 there he was appointed to the important living of S. Paul's, Sheffield, where he did much good among the working classes. He was next selected to be Vicar of Sheffield, a position of great responsibility in which he has made himself most popular and earned good repute. He subsequently became Archdeacon of Sheffield, to the satisfaction of the clergy generally. He is likewise a Canon of York. He is an able organizer and administrator; and a sound preacher and a learned divine. Archdeacon Blakeney married the eldest daughter of the late , Mr. B. Darbyshire, J.P., of Birkenhead, a lady emi- nent for her Christian usefulness and efficient zeal among the poor of Sheffield, and who is greatly be- loved by all classes. div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
THE POLLING DISTRICTS.

On Thursday evening a special meeting of the Warring- tion Town Council was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, to receive the report of a committee appoin- ted to consider the present arrangement of the polling dis- tricts of the borough. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also present Alderman Burgess, Councillors Broadbent, Hutchinson, Roberts, Jolley, W. Pierpoint, J. Pierpoint, Fleming, Sutton, Greening, Mackie, Brown, Francomb, Taylor, Dixon, Belton, and Whittle; Mr. Longdin (borough surveyor). Mr. Chorley (borough treasurer), and Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk.) The committee, which was composed of Alderman Bur- gess, and Councillors Roberts, Sutton, Greening. Francomb, Wright, Jolley, and Wm. Pierpoint, met on the 9th inst., and, having appointed Alderman Burgess chairman, passed a resolutioh that it was desirable and necessary that addi- tional polling districts should be provided. The committee further resolved that it was desirable that the North-west Ward be divided into five, the North-east Ward into four, the South-east Ward into two, the Seuth-west Ward into two, and Latchford Ward into two, polling districts. At a second meeting, held on the 12th inst., it was resolved to submit a report to the. Council of the arrangement of the different polling stations, with a recommendation that it be approved, the resolution to take effect as regards municipil elections on Nov. Ist, 1886, and as regards Parliamentary elections on January Ist, 1887. Alderman Btu:toms, in moving the adoption of the report placed before the •Council the reasons that actuated the committee in recommending it. They had previously, he believed, had five polling stations. In view of the fact that the Corrupt Pri.ctices Act imposed upon almost every elector the necessity of walking to the polling booth they considered it desirable in the first place—and that was the first and greatest reason—to have the polling stations as near the houses of the voters as could convenienieutly be done. (Hear, hear.) A second reason was that it would prevent overcrowding in the streets in which booths were situate, and a third was that it would prevent confusion, tumalt, and perhaps riot, that might ensue as a consequence of such overcrowding. Under the Corrupt Practices Act, many had now to walk long distances, which, to the infirm, the aged, and the sick, was possibly in some instances an insuperable barrier. The overcrowding that took place in a street like John-street, where 2,500 voters had to poll, was not at all desirable, and the probability was that, if the excitement grew, as was the case sometimes at elections, turmoil and even a riot might follow. If there was any increase at all in the cost it would be an infinitesimal one.

Councillor FRANCOMB seconded the proposition. There had, he said, been only one desire on the part of the com- mittee' and that had been to keep free of putting any addi- tional burden on the rates and to give the voters as much convenience as possible. He believed that every member of the committee was perfectly convinced that the rates would not be increased in any way. Personally he had tried to vet information en the subject, and felt convinced that no more expense would be added to the rates. Tha convenience to voters would be very great. Last year he took a prominent part in tke election and was stationed in John-street, where, at times, they were literally packed, and it was impcssible for people not engaged in voting to pass through the street. To bring so many people together in a narrow thoroughfare must certainly be a great inconve- nience to business people. Many men had to get from work for the purpose of voting, and if the polling booth was not far away the masters did not object, as it did not Interfere with the progress of business, but if men had to go from one end of Warrington to the other it often happened that they did not get back to work again that day, and inconvenience and loss of money resulted.

Councillor 111AcKtz asked if the possible extra expendi- ture referred entirely to the rates? Alderman Burgess did no qualify it in that way, but Councillor Francomb had done so. He should also like to know whether the proposal af- fected Parliamentary as well as municipal elections. They must take into account the fact that at a Parliamentary election at any rate, it was a matter of serious importance to the candidates, possible and probable, that there should be no items ended to the already heavy expenses connected sith an election, in regard to which the sum to Le expended was tied down to a rigidly small sum for certain duties. Three times the number of polling booths would mean three times the number of clerks—(Voices : "No.")—and it would require a responsible head man at each booth. He had no wish to oppose the scheme, but desired to put it out of the power of any respectable working-man—such as there were many of in Warrington—being compelled to say that it was utterly impossible for him to stand. He had strong opin- ions on the working-man candidate question, and felt that every pound added to the expenses of a candidate was another nail in the coffin of any man of that class standing as a candidate.

Alderman BURGESS then rose to speak. Councillor BOLTON : I rose last time to a a point and I was not allowed to weak. " Alderman BURGESS: But you aro not an alderman. (Laughter.) aldCeormunacni.llorlfßyooLuwaLwßounte ylouhasvheoutldhealslaomwearniochtesr.as an Alderman BURGESS said that they did not go to London for guidance in this matter—nor to Montrose, nor to Perth, or to anywhere else—but they had taken for their guidance the experience of the Town Clerk and the gentlemen in his office. The information they there received was that the only charge to the rate in Parliamentary elections was for police, which might be about £2O to £25. At municipal elections presiding officers and poll clerks were required, but no additional expense would be incurred. Councillor JMIN PIERPOINT said that Dr. Mackie feared that if there were 15 instead of five or six stations it would take a larger number of hands to work them. He reminded Dr. Mackie that at polling stations there were a certain number of compartments according to the number of voters. Under the proposed alteration they would be distributed in various parts of the town, but he took it that a similar number of compartments would be fixed, and the same number of officers required. (Hear, hear.) He did not see where there would be any increased cost. Councillor Borirox said Dr. Mackie wanted to know if a candidate's expanses would be increased. As far as his knowledge went, the expenses of a candidate was fixed by Act of Parliament, according to the number of voters. if there was a multiple of committee rooms there would be a multiple of expense. That did not add anything to the total cost, but simply took expense from something else. There would he so much less for the lawyers and printers. (Laughter.) Councillor JOLLEY said that the question had been care- fully considered by the committee, and all had agreed that it was the best scheme that could be produced. Mr. Roberts, the representative of the Liberals, and Mr. liampson, the representative of the Conservatives had made suggestions which had brought the thing out so well. There was really no point that could be raised against it. They need only look at the names of the committee to be satisfied of that. (Laughter.)
--Councillor SUTTON said that nearly all the officials at an election had to be volunteers and, therefore, it could not make much difference to the expense of a candidate or any- one else.

- Councillor BROADBENT thought it had been clearly shown that the scheme would convenience voters both at Parliamentary and Municipal elections. Dr. Mackie, not having been on that wonderful, clever committee Mr. Jolley had alluded to, had brought forward the point of view of

'The l‘lnvou expressed his confidence in the committee; he believed it was rear immaculate as possible. (Laughter.) The way in which they had solved the problem redounded to their credit.

Councillor BROADBENT proposed a vote of thanks to the committee for the manner in which they had carried out their duties, especially mentioning Councillor William Pier. point as haying been the first to move in the matter. The MAYOR, in seconding the proposition, said it was very gratifying to see a young member of the Council take up a matter like that, and bring it to so successful a teimi- nation.

Councillor BOLTON said that Mr. Broadbent and a few others originated the scheme. The MAYOR said he was not in the secret of tbat. Mr. Pierpoint was the first be heard speak of it, and, whether he originated it or not, he hid taken a warm interest in it, and had greatly facilitated the committee in arriving at their conclusions. (Hear, hear.) The proposition having been carried, Councillor W. PIER- POINT, in reply, said the scheme, though new to Warring- ton, was old to many of the surrounding towns. He did not want to take all the credit on himself, and must say he had had to consult the borough surveyor very often with reference to the divisions, and at his (the surveyor's) sug- gestion, and with his help, they made, he thought, a very fair division of the wards and polling districts. There- fore he thought more credit was due to Mr. Longdin than himself. The meeting then terminated. _

THE UNE -tj-RGE.NE---APPEAL FOR-AID FUR W: PLoYED ARTiZARB AND DESTITUTE CHILDREN OF TOXTETH PARE. The Toxteth Aid Society wish to make a Special and Urgent Appeal through your valuable papers on behalf of the hundreds of poor deserving men who from no fault of their own are now In great and terrible need. God alone knows what they suffer. Borne have had no work for months. They have sold all they possessed to tuy food for to keep their poor wife and little ehildrep from starvation. Once they had happy times; now all is changed. Tne poor man goes out in the morning and eturne in the evening with the same sad and heartrbroken cry, "God help you, my dear wife and children; I have got no work yet." The poor children have hardly a rag to cover them, and many a day they have to go to school without any food. Some families have not had any food for two days. This is the sad condition of hundreds of poor men, women, and children in Taxteth Park to-day. We ask all your kind readers to read our letter in your paper. and they will see the noble work we have performed in helping these poor fellow crea- tures. We appeal for help at once to go on. We are greatly in need of help. All our funds are nearly eslitusted. We appeal to all to feed the hungry atAl clothe the naked. May God dis- pose all hearts to do se Donations of clothes. will be gratefully received and acknowledged by T. R. HAM Ron. Tress., 259, Grafton-street ; or by D. WILLIAMS, Ron. The doctor, in going his rounds, came to his bedside and asked, "Well, my man, how do you feel this morning ?" Pat: "Party well, cur." Doctor : "That's right. I hope you get every attention from the attendants?" Pat: "That I do, surr. Share, yer honour, thir's only wan thing wrong in this establishment." Doctor : "And what may that bee Pat "Share, sur, I only git as much mate as wad fade a !sparrow, stir." Doctor: "Oh, you're getting your appetite, are you?' SOLVING A DIFFICEILTY.—When Mr. Howard Paul was performing in one of the small towns in the West of Ire- land, the hall in which the entertainment was given was approached through a large gate, which, by accident or mishap, had fallen to the ground. Mr. Paul, on making the discovery, instructed the hall-keeper—a wild-looking, thick-headed Paddy—" to hang the gate immediately." The fellow trudged away as if to execute the order, and, after some time had elapsed, returned to Mr. Paul, who asked him if he had done the job. " Och, yer honour," said Pat, "I tried a long while to hang the gate; but faith, sir, he wouldn't hang !" "Where have you put it, then ?" "I have settled him, yer honour." "Why, what have you done with it ?" "Shure, master, I tuk hould of him and threw him into the pond and dhrowned him lu "Are the contractor and the inspector always happy in their relationship--always mutually trustworthy ?" asks a writer in a trade contemporary. "Not always, as was in- stanced to me," he goes on to relate, "a little while ago in going over some works with a friend, a contractor's engi- neer. He was using large quantities of cement, and the name on the bags attracted my attention. 'You are using A.'s cement?' I remarked. 'Well, no,' he replied, with a twinkle of the eye ; we are using his bags, but it's B's cement.' 'How is that?' Oh, a trick of the trade! When we began work here A. and B. both supplied us with 1 cement. They were equally good; but A. was five per cent. dearer, so I ordered from B. The inspector, who I have reason to suppose was getting the five-per-cent. commission on A.'s accounts, objected; so I just got my cement from B. all the same, but I put it in A.'s bags. The inspector is satisfied, so am I.' 'Was this your own idea?' No ;it is as old as Punch and Judy. There is no possible dodge, I think, which contractors have not already dis- covered:"
